title: Reform's plan to turn council workers into 'Trump-style deportation… - TBIJ
description:
Andrea Egan, Unison general secretary, said: “The idea of conscripting council workers to a Trump-style deportation police force is absurd and sinister in equal measure.
Food inspectors, fire safety officers and their colleagues work every day to protect us all from harm and are already seriously overstretched.
“Reform’s back-of-a-fag-packet proposals would risk public safety.
Council teams including trading standards and licensing officials occasionally take part in joint immigration operations led by the Home Office.
This is obviously going to hit migrant businesses the hardest.” Shrivastava said the council would resist any attempt to impose such a policy in Lewisham.
text:
A visit from a food hygiene inspector can make or break a business. A rating of five reassures customers that standards are very good. On the other hand, would you risk eating at a cafe or restaurant that’s rated a one or zero?

Inspections, as a result, are a stressful experience for business owners and their staff. Imagine, then, how much more fraught the process would be if, once they’d finished checking fridges and worktops, inspectors declared: “Right, let’s check your immigration status.”

That scenario is on the cards should Reform win power in Westminster.

As part of its plan to focus “every organ of the British state” on hunting down, detaining and deporting “illegal” migrants, a Reform government led by Nigel Farage would require food hygiene, fire safety, trading standards and many other inspectors to do immigration checks on top of their other duties.

The proposal, announced last week, has been described as “absurd and sinister” by the union Unison and an “intensification of the hostile environment” by the mayor of a London council which, earlier this year, became the first local authority in the UK to refuse to help the Home Office undertake immigration raids.

Reform claims that immigration checks could be “easily” incorporated into inspections undertaken by staff at local authorities and other public bodies, such as the Health and Safety Executive, because they “do not require highly technical qualifications”. Doing so, it estimates, would increase the immigration enforcement capacity by up to 40 times.

PCS, a union that represents UK government workers, told us immigration officers perform a “highly specialised” role that requires “extensive training, detailed knowledge of complex immigration legislation, as well as intel and the ability to make decisions with serious legal and human consequences”.

A spokesperson added: “Reform's suggestion that immigration checks do not require technical expertise and can simply be added to the responsibilities of any public sector inspector fundamentally misunderstands the nature of the work our members perform.

“It also demonstrates a clear disregard for the need for humane, lawful and properly-trained approaches to immigration enforcement.”

Councils would be encouraged to cooperate by receiving a share of fines handed out to those who employ illegal workers. That money would also pay for the recruitment of more inspectors.

Andrea Egan, Unison general secretary, said: “The idea of conscripting council workers to a Trump-style deportation police force is absurd and sinister in equal measure. Food inspectors, fire safety officers and their colleagues work every day to protect us all from harm and are already seriously overstretched.

“Reform’s back-of-a-fag-packet proposals would risk public safety. They’re part of a nasty campaign targeting our migrant friends, neighbours and colleagues. The very people who do so much to keep our public services, and our whole country, running.

“This racist agenda is completely contrary to the values of public service workers, and Unison will continue to oppose it every step of the way.”

Reform says these immigration inspectors would be expected to relay information to a new “Deportation Command” and the “Migrant Identification Centre”.

Council teams including trading standards and licensing officials occasionally take part in joint immigration operations led by the Home Office. Local authorities also share data with the government relating to a person’s right to work (when someone applies for housing or social care support, for example).

However, a growing number of councils, including seven in London, are refusing to cooperate with immigration raids where they legally can. Lewisham was the first to do so, passing a motion to that effect in July.

Mayor of Lewisham Liam Shrivastava said of Reform’s plan: “It is, in many respects, a continuation but intensification of the hostile environment [the name given to policies, aimed at undocumented migrants, introduced by then home secretary Theresa May in 2012] where ordinary workers, whether they’re council officers or teachers, are being made to behave like border guards.

“This sort of enforcement regime creates a climate of fear. Many workers and businesses are going to be terrified. This is obviously going to hit migrant businesses the hardest.”

Shrivastava said the council would resist any attempt to impose such a policy in Lewisham.

“There would be huge legal and practical questions around how you can compel officers to do that – I think we would be very against it,” he added.

Reform’s policy announcement also included plans to effectively end the asylum system for up to five years, and deport thousands of asylum seekers before their appeals to remain in the UK are heard.

We previously wrote about the public inquiries into the proposed expansion of Campsfield and Haslar Immigration Removal Centres.
To recap: the Home Office plans to create around 1,000 additional detention spaces, expanding the UK’s detention estate by approximately 40%.
We must stand together to stop this expansion plan, as we work towards abolishing detention altogether.
We are therefore absolutely delighted that JCWI (the Joint Council of Welfare for Immigrants) and Asylum Matters agreed to be the lead endorsers of Right to Remain submission.
Expanding immigration detention harms all of us: so we all need to come together to prevent it.
text:
We previously wrote about the public inquiries into the proposed expansion of Campsfield and Haslar Immigration Removal Centres. To recap: the Home Office plans to create around 1,000 additional detention spaces, expanding the UK’s detention estate by approximately 40%.

We cannot let this happen, and Right to Remain is challenging this, with all of you.

Thanks to a large number of people who wrote to oppose the Campsfield planning application, there is now an public inquiry into this matter, and we will be formally giving evidence as an interested party. Our submission is based on the evidence provided by many of you in our community, especially by people who have first-hand experience of detention – thank you.

We must stand together to stop this expansion plan, as we work towards abolishing detention altogether. We are therefore absolutely delighted that JCWI (the Joint Council of Welfare for Immigrants) and Asylum Matters agreed to be the lead endorsers of Right to Remain submission.

Lavanya Pallapi, Chief Executive of the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants said:

“We unequivocally support Right to Remain’s submission to the inquiry, and oppose the expansion of Campsfield.

Immigration detention is a cruel and inhumane punishment that this and successive governments have used against migrants and people seeking asylum, many of whom have faced horrific and traumatic journeys to seek safety in this country. This expansion is a costly, punitive and unnecessary solution to the government’s aggressive increase in forced removals.

People caged in these detention centres are not able to access the necessary trauma-informed healthcare that they need, leaving them with significantly worse physical and mental health if or when they are able to get out, as well as ruptures to their relationships, housing, education and employment. People detained are often also prevented or restricted from accessing proper legal advice, to which they are legally entitled. Despite this, most people detained are still ultimately released.

People have repeatedly been subject to violence and trauma in these dark prison-like institutions, where they can be held indefinitely, and which have repeatedly been found to systematically violate people’s human rights.

We must seek to invest in and build communities, not cages.”

Lou Calvey, Executive Director of Asylum Matters said:

“1,000 more beds at Haslar and Campsfield means thousands more people suffering completely unnecessarily. It means thousands more people trapped in fear and uncertainty; thousands more families, neighbourhoods and communities torn apart; thousands more people left trying to recover from the trauma of detention.

And, at a time when racist, anti-migrant sentiment is being spread aggressively in the UK, continuing to push for this expansion means our Government giving in to those who want to divide our communities. Expanding immigration detention harms all of us: so we all need to come together to prevent it.

We stand with everyone who has been directly harmed by immigration detention, and we support Right To Remain and all those intervening in the public inquiry against this plan – it’s vital that we all unite against this cruel expansion.”

If your group also would like to endorse our submission, alongside JCWI and Asylum Matters, please contact Ally(at)righttoremain.org.uk. You can find out more information about it here.

title: Video of ICE agents detaining man in Long Beach draws criticism from local leaders
description:
Video showing a man being detained by ICE agents in Long Beach is drawing criticism from state and local leaders.

"They tased him, and it was just horrible," said Patty Villarrel, who lives in Long Beach.

“ICE agents brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and U.S. citizen," Garcia said in an X post.
text:
Video showing a man being detained by ICE agents in Long Beach is drawing criticism from state and local leaders.

Neighbors say they rushed outside when they heard the commotion, and that's when they saw the man on the ground being held down by agents.

Cellphone video shows a man being detained on the ground by what appears to be ICE agents in North Long Beach Saturday afternoon. However, the video does not show what happened leading up to that moment.

Many neighbors say it was disturbing to watch and allege that the encounter was violent.

"They tased him, and it was just horrible," said Patty Villarrel, who lives in Long Beach.

"They were even kicking him when he was handcuffed on the ground," neighbor Ashley Brust said. "That was kind of crazy. That was kind of traumatic."

The encounter happened near the intersection of Locust Avenue and Ellis Street.

In the video, you can hear the man screaming that his arm is broken and asking for help. Neighbors are also seen in the street demanding federal agents leave the man alone.

The family confirmed to NBC Los Angeles on Sunday that the man is a U.S. citizen.

"I love it, and that’s why we have a community that gets together, and I am very grateful we have a community in North Long Beach," Villarrel said.

Long Beach police say they were requested by the Department of Homeland Security and ICE for assistance due to a vehicle vandalism and a person needing medical aid. When officers arrived, they found the handcuffed man detained by ICE bleeding.

Police say they took the man to a nearby fire station, where they removed the handcuffs, and Long Beach Fire personnel took him to a hospital for treatment.

Long Beach police say they were not involved in any immigration enforcement and did not make any arrests.

Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson posted his reaction to the incident on social media.

“Our residents shouldn’t be put in these situations," Richardson said. "Families shouldn’t have to live in fear in their own neighborhoods. I’ve asked our city team to verify exactly what happened and to document everything."

Congressman Robert Garcia, who represents Long Beach, also condemned the encounter.

“ICE agents brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and U.S. citizen," Garcia said in an X post. :The videos are horrific and should concern not just our community but the country. I’m proud of the neighbors who documented and stood up for the family being terrorized by ICE. Donald Trump and his inhumane and illegal deportation machine must be stopped. Long Beach stands with our community and our immigrant families. ICE is not welcome in Long Beach. Abolish ICE.”

U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli responded to Garcia’s message with the following:

“You’re a sitting member of Congress and you’re encouraging people to obstruct immigration agents enforcing laws enacted by Congress? Shame on you. These incidents would be less common if the targets complied with lawful commands. You’re intentionally fanning the flames and increasing danger for the community and officers. I’m proud of the men and women of law enforcement who risk their lives every day to keep us safe. We will not hesitate to arrest and prosecute anyone who assaults them.”

NBCLA reached out to ICE, DHS and CBP regarding the incident but has not received a response.

title: US citizen injured during California ICE incident, officials say - CNN
authors: Julianna Bragg, Celina  Tebor, Sarah Dewberry
description:
A resident of Long Beach, California, was injured during an incident involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Saturday, according to federal and local officials.
Ricardo Gonzalez, a former Long Beach city employee, was reportedly found by Long Beach police after he and other community members called 911 after becoming concerned about unmarked vehicles, Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson told CNN on Sunday.
ICE personnel had requested emergency assistance from the Long Beach Police Department in response to vehicle vandalism and a person in need of medical aid, Long Beach police said in a statement Saturday.
CNN has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security, the city of Long Beach and Long Beach police for more information.
Long Beach police officers took Gonzalez to a nearby fire station, where his handcuffs were removed, police said in the statement.
text:
A resident of Long Beach, California, was injured during an incident involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Saturday, according to federal and local officials.

Ricardo Gonzalez, a former Long Beach city employee, was reportedly found by Long Beach police after he and other community members called 911 after becoming concerned about unmarked vehicles, Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson told CNN on Sunday.

ICE personnel had requested emergency assistance from the Long Beach Police Department in response to vehicle vandalism and a person in need of medical aid, Long Beach police said in a statement Saturday.

When local officers arrived, they found a man handcuffed and bleeding while being detained by ICE, police said, adding a “large group disturbance” involving the agents was taking place.

“(Gonzalez) called 911 when he saw a circumstance escalating, and so he called and asked for assistance,” Richardson said. “When the police arrived, we know that he was detained. He was on a curb. He was injured.”

It’s not yet known what led up to the circumstances or what occurred before Gonzalez was detained.

A GoFundMe created by Gonzalez’s daughter, Leslie Gonzalez, said he was struck by an unmarked vehicle believed to be driven by federal agents while riding an e-bike.

CNN has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security, the city of Long Beach and Long Beach police for more information.

Videos shared by a witness showed Gonzalez handcuffed and lying on the ground while being held down by an agent wearing a “Police ICE” vest. In one video, the man can be heard yelling repeatedly, “Help me, my arm is broken” and “call a paramedic.”

Richardson, who said he was “outraged” over the incident, spoke with Gonzalez, who told him he is a US citizen, and his family following the incident. CNN is working to verify Gonzalez’s citizenship status.

US citizens have been caught up in the Trump administration’s sweeping immigration crackdown, which has featured highly visible enforcement operations and aggressive tactics that have prompted nationwide protests, legal battles and political backlash.

Long Beach police officers took Gonzalez to a nearby fire station, where his handcuffs were removed, police said in the statement. Fire department personnel then transported him to a hospital for medical attention. Richardson declined to comment on Gonzalez’s current condition, citing his privacy.

Meanwhile, officers remained at the scene in an attempt to de-escalate the situation, the police statement said. When Long Beach police left the scene, some ICE agents followed officers to the station’s parking lot, where the federal agents were asked to leave and told they could contact the department to file a vandalism report.

US Rep. Robert Garcia, a Democrat from California, said in a post on X: “ICE agents brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and U.S. citizen,” calling the videos “horrific.”

The GoFundMe was created to pay his medical bills, the website said. Leslie Gonzalez said her father is currently receiving treatment for his injuries.

“My Dad is one of the hardest working men out there,” she wrote on the GoFundMe. “Because of him I have a roof over my head and I have all the opportunities around me. Our family is everything because of him.”

Richardson said he attempted to contact ICE through its complaint hotline, but has yet to speak with someone at the agency.

What would have been a safe weekend in North Long Beach “turned into a violent incident with no transparency or accountability, and a lot more questions than answers,” Richardson told CNN.

text:
LONG BEACH, Calif. (KABC) -- Dramatic new video circulating online shows U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arresting a man in Long Beach.

The group StopICE.net shared video of the incident, which happened on Saturday morning near 56th Street and Elm Avenue.

The group says in the moments before the video was recorded, ICE agents used a vehicle to run the man down and tackle him to the ground.

Advocates say the man seen being detained is a U.S. citizen from Long Beach.

You can hear his cries for help in the video as he's being held down and restrained by masked agents.

SEE ALSO: UCLA study shows 15,000 people have been deported in SoCal during Trump's 2nd term

"Help me! Help me! My arm is f------ broken," the man is heard yelling.

Witnesses say he was also tased.

The man was eventually taken to a hospital to be treated after Long Beach police arrived.

"He was just riding his bike down a residential street, in his own neighborhood, and here comes ICE, speeding down the streets, going 50 mph in a residential area, kids playing, where there's families, on a Saturday," said Sherman Austin with StopICE.net.

Former Long Beach mayor and current Congressman Robert Garcia responded to the video, saying, in part, "ICE agents brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and U.S. citizen. The videos are horrific and should concern not just our community but the country."

Eyewitness News reached out to the Department of Homeland Security about the arrest but has not yet heard back.

Congressman Garcia's statement prompted a response from First Asst. U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli, who wrote on X, "These incidents would be less common if the targets complied with lawful commands. You’re intentionally fanning the flames and increasing danger for the community and officers."

title: Blunder in, abandon allies and court a dictator: it's the Trump doctrine, now playing out in Myanmar
description:
This sparked a civil war that has now turned into a brutal series of overlapping conflicts between the military, resistance forces and a medley of ethnic militias.
This month the Trump administration decided to upend nearly a decade of united western policy and open direct talks with the Myanmar regime.
The purpose of the talks was not to persuade the military regime to reintroduce democracy or stop its brutal war.
Since the 2021 coup, rare-earth shipments from Myanmar to China have totalled $3.6bn, making up the majority of China’s rare-earth imports.
Many Myanmar resistance figures, including Aung San Suu Kyi, have placed their hope in US help.
text:
Marco Rubio was once adamant that the US had to do everything in its power to end what he described as the “ethnic cleansing” of the Rohingya in Myanmar. In a 2017 letter he signed along with 20 other US senators, Rubio called for “strong multilateral sanctions against specific senior Burmese military officials associated with the gross human rights abuses”. Those responsible for the atrocities should be prosecuted, he argued.

In the years since, the Myanmar military’s crimes have only increased. What was then deemed ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya is now widely viewed, including by the US, as genocide. What little democracy existed in Myanmar was eradicated in 2021 when Aung San Suu Kyi was arrested and imprisoned and her party’s election victory overturned, and the military took full control.

This sparked a civil war that has now turned into a brutal series of overlapping conflicts between the military, resistance forces and a medley of ethnic militias. Around 100,000 people have been killed in the conflict, which has forced 5 million people to flee their homes. The UN estimates that 16 million are now in need of urgent assistance. It is one of the world’s biggest humanitarian disasters – and entirely human-made.

Earlier this year, Myanmar held sham elections, and Min Aung Hlaing – the general most responsible for Myanmar’s genocide and one of the targets of Rubio’s letter – became president.

But Rubio, now the US secretary of state, no longer believes that Min Aung Hlaing should be prosecuted. Instead he’d rather like him to become an ally. This month the Trump administration decided to upend nearly a decade of united western policy and open direct talks with the Myanmar regime. The possibility of lifting sanctions is now being discussed. The move has shocked other western nations – none of which, it appears, was warned.

Inevitably, a Maga figure lingers in the background. This time it’s Roger Stone, the Donald Trump ally who was found guilty in 2019 of lying to Congress, witness tampering and obstructing the investigation into whether the Trump campaign conspired with Russia in the 2016 presidential election.

Stone, who was spared jail after Trump commuted his sentence, recently started working as a lobbyist for the Myanmar regime, helping to “rebuild relations between the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and the United States”.

It seems to be working. Earlier this month Michael Vance, the assistant secretary of ​state for intelligence and research, travelled to Myanmar’s capital Naypyidaw. The trip was supposedly to secure the release of a US citizen, but Vance also held talks with the generals. The purpose of the talks was not to persuade the military regime to reintroduce democracy or stop its brutal war. Instead it appeared to be about securing American access to Myanmar’s rare earth minerals.

In recent years, the race to control a steady supply of rare-earth minerals – elements used in a host of military technology and hi-tech manufacturing applications – has become increasingly fraught. China controls most of the world’s rare-earth mines and almost all of the processing capacity. The Trump administration’s desire to turn the tables has led it to strike one-sided deals with Ukraine and the Democratic Republic of Congo that have placed US business interests over practically everything else.

There are more than 600 rare earth mines in Myanmar, most of which currently supply China. Since the 2021 coup, rare-earth shipments from Myanmar to China have totalled $3.6bn, making up the majority of China’s rare-earth imports. This is the prize the US appears to have its eyes on.

Vance’s trip has handed Myanmar’s generals a propaganda victory at a moment when they are doing everything they can to legitimise the regime. The US, unfortunately, is not the only country welcoming Myanmar’s generals back into the fold. Min Aung Hlaing this month flew to Malaysia, once a strong opponent of the junta, where the prime minister Anwar Imbrahim floated the idea of Myanmar being welcomed back into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean). Trips to Indonesia and Brunei are also on the cards, while the Philippines has indicated that it too would like to see relations normalised.

The junta’s diplomatic victories follow growing military success. Over the last two and a half years, with the help of more sophisticated drones supplied by Russia and China, and the conscription of another 100,000 young men, the junta has regained control over several towns and pushed the resistance back into the countryside.

For Myanmar’s civilians, the long nightmare continues. Last month more than 50 people were killed when the military bombed a busy market in a rebel-held area. Every week brings fresh atrocities, while the hope of a peaceful, democratic Myanmar slips further into the distance.

The one silver lining that those fighting for Myanmar’s freedom can cling to is that the rest of the west hasn’t given up on it yet. British diplomats are adamant that there will be no change in the UK’s position, while Canada, Australia and the EU are all likely to hold the line too. But even here there are concerns.

Campaigners point to the UK’s recent reduction in aid to Myanmar from £66m a year to £55m. Just half of the $889.6m the UN has requested for Myanmar this year has been provided by international donors. They would also like to see Britain and others engage more directly with Myanmar’s pro-democracy camp, including the resistance.

Trump is not the first president to prioritise resources over democracy, as a cursory glance at US relations with Saudi Arabia since it discovered oil in 1938 shows. But Trump’s rapacious attitude to oil and minerals, his willingness to enrich his friends and family, and his brazen support for dictators makes this a very different America. Myanmar is simply another example of the corrosive nature that Trump’s foreign policy is having in every corner of the globe.

The question is whether Trump will get what he wants. US policy on Myanmar has been driven by Congress, and there remains bipartisan support for keeping it in place. The House of Representatives recently passed a bill that would extend the sanctions regime for another six years. Particularly at a time when his support is waning, Trump is unlikely to have much joy in persuading senators and members of Congress who have long supported Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement to turn a blind eye to genocide and war crimes.

Even if he did, the bigger question is whether Myanmar’s generals can give Trump what he wants. The vast majority of Myanmar’s rare earth mines are near the border with China and many are controlled by militia groups, not the junta. “There is no way China is going to let the US get anywhere near the rare earths,” Joshua Kurlantzick at the Council on Foreign Relations told me.

And yet even if none of this leads to any real change, the Trump administration’s decision to open talks with a genocidal regime responsible for one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises is a disaster for those in Myanmar fighting for their freedom. Many Myanmar resistance figures, including Aung San Suu Kyi, have placed their hope in US help. Like other democrats fighting demagogues, such as Volodymyr Zelenskyy, they have been deserted.

Here is yet another example of the Trump administration blundering into a part of the world where it knows little, offering a prize to an authoritarian and leaving with not much to show for it.

In the letter from ICE, director David Venturella focused on how the facility will abide by building standards which will “safely, securely, and humanely house detainees.” In Jones’ counter-response, Jones continued to express concern for the ICE facility.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security was sued by San Antonio to block the opening of the East Side Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center. Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones released a statement that calls attention to the facility that is set to open in January 2027.

“For months, my office and City staff have requested basic information that the people of San Antonio are owed, to include: How do you intend to comply with the NEPA review, how do you intend to use the City’s permitting processes, and how do you intend to consider in good faith the people’s feedback?,” Jones wrote in the statement. The request she referred to was made in July 2026.

Jones is suing on the grounds of the National Environmental Policy Act. Jones alleges that ICE has not shown proof that they have assessed the potential environmental risks of establishing their facility. NEPA requires that all agencies — including the Department of Homeland Security — to also determine societal and economic effects of large scale projects such as the creation of a massive detainment facility.

City Attorney Andy Segovia reviewed how the DHS violated NEPA in a press conference held on Oct. 13. “NEPA requires all federal agencies, including DHS, to conduct an environmental review before undertaking a project of this size and scope.” Segovia stated. “The city is requesting that the federal court vacate the purchase of the facility and to stop anything that is going on until DHS and ICE have fully complied with the requirements of NEPA.”

Concerns about the ICE facility began to grow in February of this year. After Jones requested that lawmakers vote against the funding of a new ICE facility, she wrote a joint letter with other federal and local officials in opposition to the facility’s opening. Jones’ letters received a response on June 22. In the letter from ICE, director David Venturella focused on how the facility will abide by building standards which will “safely, securely, and humanely house detainees.” In Jones’ counter-response, Jones continued to express concern for the ICE facility. ICE did not respond to Jones’ last letter.

Segovia filed legal action on behalf of San Antonio on Oct. 13. This filing attempts to keep the ICE facility from moving forward with operation on the East Side.

During the announcement of the legal action being taken, Segovia stated, “With a facility of this size and scope, within the urban core of San Antonio, these sorts of [environmental] reviews are even more critical. It’s very clear to see that there will be impacts, and the law is there to make sure that those impacts are mitigated.”

In opposition to Jones and Segovia, District 10 councilman Marc Whyte and District 9 councilwoman Misty Spears do not favor the lawsuit filed by the city. Spears claims that the lawsuit reinforces a double standard while Whyte argues that filing the lawsuit is “the wrong fight.”

ICE said in a statement that Araujo "weaponized his vehicle" and tried to run over an officer during the stop, prompting the officer to fire their weapon "in self-defense."

"The driver was struck, and emergency services were immediately contacted. The driver was transported to the hospital, where he passed away from his injuries," ICE said.

Tirado Pantoja has been in the country since 1996 and has a son and stepdaughter who are both U.S. citizens. He does not have a criminal record, according to his habeas petition.

Judge Ellison ordered the government to release Rojas Pliego from custody within 48 hours.

text:
Neighbors in North Long Beach rushed out of their homes yesterday and blocked federal immigration agents from detaining a man they had just violently knocked to the ground, according to first-hand accounts from four residents who spoke to the Long Beach Post.

The man is a U.S. citizen named Ricardo Gonzalez who lives near where he was detained, according to neighbors and an online fundraiser started by his family. He was riding an e-bike near Elm Avenue and 56th Street on Saturday afternoon when an agent jumped out of an unmarked car and tackled him, according to a neighbor who asked to be identified only by his first name, Joe. (Other accounts online said agents rammed Gonzalez with their car. The Post could not locate any video of this or anyone who said they witnessed it first-hand.)

The agent then accused Gonzalez of throwing something at their car, Joe said.

Agents tased Gonzalez twice while he was on the ground, and one agent knelt on his back while Gonzalez yelled in pain and said his arm was broken, according to two neighbors who asked not to be named for fear of reprisal.

As residents came outside to see what was going on, they started yelling and honking, alerting more neighbors.

The area was already on edge, Joe said, because eight or so unmarked law enforcement vehicles had been parked in the neighborhood since early that morning. He said his wife at one point had even called 911 to report the vehicles and ask if they could move because they were blocking multiple one-way streets.

Volunteers with anti-ICE rapid response groups had also brought loudspeakers to warn about the vehicles and urge everyone to stay inside. Instead, when neighbors heard the growing confrontation with agents, many intervened.

“If they try to take one of us, they’re going to have to take all of Long Beach,” said Patricia Velazquez, who has lived in the area for more than three decades.

Cellphone video shows roughly 50 people yelling expletives at masked agents who were carrying handguns and wearing vests that said “ICE.” Neighbors demanded to see a warrant, dragged trash cans behind the agents’ vehicles or stood in front of them, blocking them from driving off.

One agent made racist comments to the mostly Latino crowd, saying they didn’t “look legal,” according to Joe. They also used pepper spray on the crowd, neighbors said.

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to questions about the confrontation.

At one point during the roughly hour-long standoff, agents grabbed two women — both U.S. citizens — and put them in the backs of different vehicles, according to two neighbors. They were soon freed, according to Joe. He described the crowd distracting agents while people sneaked behind their vehicles to open their doors.

Long Beach police soon showed up. In a statement, they said federal agents had called for help providing medical aid to someone and dealing with a crowd that had vandalized vehicles.

One officer attempted to step in immediately but was held back by his partner, one neighbor said. Video shows federal agents then allowed Gonzalez to leave with the Long Beach officers after agents searched his wallet and looked at his identification.

An LBPD officer uncuffed Gonzalez and took him to a nearby fire station. Paramedics then took him to a hospital.

Gonzalez is a Long Beach resident who, until recently, worked for the city, Long Beach City Councilmember Tunua Thrash-Ntuk said in a statement. He was riding through his own neighborhood, she said, “when he was racially profiled and violently assaulted by ICE agents—leaving him with broken bones and crushing medical bills.”

In their online fundraiser, Gonzalez’s family says he is a hardworking man who supports his family. He is still recovering, they said, and asked for help spreading the word about what agents did to him.

Long Beach Congressman Robert Garcia said he was “proud of the neighbors who documented and stood up for the family being terrorized by ICE.”

“ICE agents brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and U.S. citizen,” he said in a statement. “The videos are horrific and should concern not just our community but the country.”

Mayor Rex Richardson said he is outraged by agents’ actions and is demanding answers from the Department of Homeland Security.

text:
The National Human Rights Commission of Korea determined that officials violated foreigners' right to informational self-determination by failing to properly follow consent procedures when accessing their mobile phones during airport immigration inspections.

On October 19, the Commission recommended that the head of the Incheon International Airport Immigration Office improve procedures for accessing and collecting foreigners' personal information from their mobile phones. It also called for the deletion of photos taken without consent.

In October 2025, two Mongolian nationals, one Turkish national, and one German national filed complaints with the Commission, alleging that their rights had been violated when officials accessed personal information on their mobile phones during immigration inspections. Immigration authorities said they had accessed the phones with the foreigners' consent to verify the purpose of their visits and had taken some photos to secure evidence needed for the inspections.

However, the Commission pointed out that the written consent forms did not specify the purposes for collecting and using personal information, the categories of information to be collected, or the retention period. It also determined that it was difficult to verify whether consent had been explicitly given when it was obtained verbally. In particular, the Commission found that consent to accessing a mobile phone could not be interpreted as consent to separately photographing and retaining photos from it.

Immigration authorities revised their mobile phone access consent form during the Commission's investigation. However, the Commission determined that it still lacked sufficient detail, as it described the information to be collected as "all information stored on the mobile phone" and the retention period as "until the purpose has been achieved."

A Commission official said, "Mobile phones contain a wide range of information related to an individual's private life," adding, "Access to personal information during immigration inspections must be carried out in a way that fully safeguards the data subject's right to informational self-determination."

text:
MINNEAPOLIS -- The acting head of Immigration and Customs Enforcement says that two of its officers appear to have made "untruthful statements" about shooting a migrant in Minnesota and may face federal charges for their actions.

"Today, a joint review by ICE and the Department of Justice (DOJ) of video evidence has revealed that sworn testimony provided by two separate officers appears to have made untruthful statements," Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons said in a statement.

"Both officers have been immediately placed on administrative leave pending the completion of a thorough internal investigation. Lying under oath is a serious federal offense. The U.S. Attorney's Office is actively investigating these false statements," the statement said.

"The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct. Violations of this sacred sworn oath will not be tolerated. ICE remains fully committed to transparency, accountability, and the fair enforcement of our nation's immigration laws," Lyons added.

The statement from Lyons comes a day after the top federal prosecutor in Minnesota asked a judge to dismiss charges against two men, including one who was shot in the leg by an immigration agent, citing "newly discovered evidence" in what was initially framed as a "violent" attack on law enforcement during an enforcement operation.

"Newly discovered evidence in this matter is materially inconsistent with the allegations in the complaint affidavit. ... as well as the preliminary-hearing testimony," U.S. Attorney for the District of Minnesota Daniel Rosen wrote in the filing Wednesday evening. It remains unclear what specific new evidence Rosen was referencing.

Rosen has asked the court to dismiss the case with prejudice, meaning the charges cannot be refiled.

"Accordingly, dismissal with prejudice will serve the interests of justice," Rosen wrote.

In the wake of the shooting on Jan. 14 -- a week after an ICE agent fatally shot Renee Good in Minneapolis -- the Trump administration said the man who was shot, Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, attacked a federal law enforcement officer with a "shovel or a broom stick" and that the incident was part of "an attempt to evade arrest and obstruct law enforcement."

Lawyers for another man charged in the incident, Alfredo Aljorna, said surveillance videos did not corroborate the FBI's claims that an agent was assaulted and said Sosa-Celis was shot while standing at his doorway some distance away from the officer.

Earlier this month attorneys for Aljorna also urged a judge to prohibit the government from deporting key witnesses who they said cast doubt that an agent was repeatedly struck with a broom or a snow shovel, Judge Paul Magnuson granted the request.

The reversal on the assault charges for Sosa-Celis and Aljorna comes after several discrepancies emerged between statements from Department of Homeland Security officials and details outlined in court records regarding their arrests.

DHS initially said in statements to media that officers were conducting a "targeted traffic stop" for Sosa-Celis when he fled in his vehicle, crashed into another car and attempted to evade arrest. The agency alleged that Sosa-Celis "violently" assaulted an officer and that two other individuals exited a nearby apartment and joined the attack "with a snow shovel and broom handle."

According to DHS, Sosa-Celis struck the officer with "a shovel or broom stick," prompting the officer to fire what the agency described as a defensive shot "to defend his life," striking Sosa-Celis in the leg.

However, an affidavit from FBI Special Agent Timothy Schanz, who investigated the shooting, stated that ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations agents were attempting to stop a different man identified as Joffre Stalin Paucar Barrera -- not Sosa-Celis -- whom they believed was in the country illegally. According to Schanz, agents later identified the driver DHS agents stopped as a different man, Aljorna.

Schanz wrote that Aljorna struck a light pole and fled on foot toward his apartment building.

Sosa-Celis was allegedly standing on the porch and yelling at Aljorna to run faster, the affidavit says. Aljorna slipped and allegedly "began tussling" with the agent before Sosa-Celis grabbed a broom and began striking the agent, according to the affidavit.

The agent "then saw who he believed was a third Hispanic male approach with a snow shovel, and this male also began striking" him, Schanz said in the affidavit. The third man was identified as Gabriel Alejandro Hernandez-Ledezma by DHS, who accused him of also assaulting the officer.

Sosa-Celis was shot in the leg as he attempted to go inside the apartment, the affidavit says.

Video reviewed by ABC News' Visual Verification team includes a 911 call from individuals identified as relatives of Sosa-Celis, who said agents fired as he was attempting to close the door.

text:
President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he is ready to deploy Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to U.S. airports starting Monday if Democrats don't agree to a funding package to end the Department of Homeland Security shutdown.

"I look forward to moving ICE in on Monday, and have already told them to, 'GET READY.' NO MORE WAITING, NO MORE GAMES!" the president wrote in a post to his social media platform.

In an earlier social media post on Saturday, Trump wrote that unless Democrats "immediately sign an agreement," he will move to deploy ICE agents into American airports and conduct security enforcement "like no one has ever seen before."

Trump said that operations would include immigration enforcement. It's currently unclear which security roles, exactly, ICE agents will take on at airports.

The White House referred ABC News back to the president's post when asked what capacity Americans can expect to see ICE operating in at airports.

Trump's statements come after Democrats on Friday blocked legislation to reopen DHS for the fifth time since the partial shutdown began in mid-February.

Democrats have demanded changes to policy surrounding ICE and Customs and Border Protection in exchange for votes to fund all of the department. Republicans, meanwhile, have rejected Democratic efforts to fund other agencies in DHS like the Coast Guard, Transportation Security Administration (TSA) and Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA).

Thousands of TSA employees have now missed their first full paychecks, and travelers are facing long lines at airports around the country.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, during an appearance on Fox News earlier Saturday, called on Democrats to negotiate with Republicans.

"I just wish they would stop using the American people as leverage. Make them go through pain so Democrats can get what they want legislatively," Duffy said.

On Capitol Hill, in a rare Saturday morning press conference, Senate Majority Leader John Thune also urged Democrats to agree to a funding deal.

"At some point, the Democrats are going to have to take yes for an answer. I know they think this is politically good for them. It is not," Thune, R-S.D., said.

A bipartisan group of lawmakers met behind closed doors with White House border czar Tom Homan throughout the week. The latest meeting concluded late Friday night.

"We need to get the government open, and we'll keep talking until it has," Homan told ABC News after the meeting.

Thune said he believed that meeting was "productive" and confirmed that the Trump administration added to its offer on DHS funding and submitted legislative text, though lawmakers have not publicly discussed what the new offer from the White House entails.

Thune said he hopes additional meetings take place over the weekend.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, in a speech on the Senate floor on Saturday, urged Republicans to support a Democratic effort to fund TSA while other negotiations continue.

"It is unacceptable for workers and travelers and entire airports to get taken hostage in political games, but that's what the Republicans are doing," Schumer, D-N.Y., said.

"It is unacceptable to say we will only pay TSA workers if it is attached to a bill that funds ICE with no reforms, but that's what the Republicans have been doing. Democrats want to pay TSA workers ASAP, with no strings attached," Schumer added.

Schumer said Democrats are "having productive conversations on reforming ICE and CBP," but that the process is "ongoing."

"But we must fund TSA now. Let us keep negotiating the outstanding issues with ICE, but let us start sending paychecks to TSA workers now. Let us end the long lines at the airport now," Schumer said.

ABC News' Lalee Ibssa contributed to this report.

title: Peru Moves to Expel Undocumented Venezuelans — But Due Process Questions Remain ...
description:
Peru and Venezuela are moving to coordinate the removal of undocumented Venezuelans from Peruvian territory, while Lima simultaneously pledges support for Caracas's Plan Vuelta a la Patria — a state repatriation program.
What Peru Has Already Done — and the 2020 Precedent The October 15 announcement did not arrive in a policy vacuum.
Between January and mid-September 2026, Peru's migration authority conducted 5,461 document-check operations, reviewing the status of 83,422 foreign nationals and removing more than 2,800 irregular migrants.
There is also a notable precedent from earlier in Peru's response to Venezuelan migration.
Peru unquestionably has the legal authority to expel undocumented migrants.
text:
Peru and Venezuela are moving to coordinate the removal of undocumented Venezuelans from Peruvian territory, while Lima simultaneously pledges support for Caracas's Plan Vuelta a la Patria — a state repatriation program. The arrangement puts two legally distinct procedures under the same political umbrella, with critical procedural guarantees still unresolved.

The move marks the deepest bilateral cooperation on migration between the two nations in years, arriving less than three months after both foreign ministries announced a gradual resumption of diplomatic relations — and it puts more than 1.6 million Venezuelan nationals residing in Peru directly in the policy crosshairs.

Two Governments, Two Very Different Messages

On Thursday, Fujimori posted on social media that she had spoken with Rodríguez "to address cooperation between our countries, initiate support for her Plan Vuelta a la Patria, as well as coordinate the processes of expulsion from Peru of undocumented Venezuelan citizens." She added that the removals would be carried out "by air, in an orderly and secure manner," with both foreign ministries drafting the protocols.

Rodríguez framed the same call in distinctly softer terms. The acting president said she had reaffirmed her commitment to "strengthen the mechanisms that allow the safe return of our compatriots" through Plan Vuelta a la Patria — language that centers voluntary repatriation rather than forced removal.

The contrast is not merely rhetorical. Voluntary returns allow migrants to self-select, apply through consular channels, and depart without a formal immigration record. Administrative expulsions are state-initiated removals that carry official documentation and can affect future visa eligibility for years. The public announcements from both sides did not clarify how flights designated for voluntary return would be separated from those tied to expulsion orders — or whether they would be the same flights at all.

Who Is Delcy Rodríguez, and Why Is She Running Venezuela?

Readers unfamiliar with Venezuela's current political situation may be asking why Rodríguez — previously Nicolás Maduro's vice president — is now described as the country's acting leader. On January 3–4, 2026, U.S. Special Operations forces detained Maduro, and Venezuela's Supreme Court ordered Rodríguez to assume all presidential powers "to guarantee administrative continuity." She has remained in the role since, even after exceeding the initial 90-day mandate set by the high court.

What Peru Has Already Done — and the 2020 Precedent

The October 15 announcement did not arrive in a policy vacuum. Between January and mid-September 2026, Peru's migration authority conducted 5,461 document-check operations, reviewing the status of 83,422 foreign nationals and removing more than 2,800 irregular migrants. Peru's interior minister, César Astudillo, signaled in September that the pace of expulsions would increase significantly.

There is also a notable precedent from earlier in Peru's response to Venezuelan migration. In January 2020, authorities deported 131 Venezuelans with criminal records following a raid on a coastal hostel south of Lima where weapons and drugs were seized — at the time, one of the largest single expulsion operations Peru had conducted. That operation prompted the Interior Ministry to form a dedicated police unit to investigate crimes involving foreign nationals.

The Diplomatic Reset That Made This Possible

The October 15 call did not occur in isolation. On July 24, 2026 — days before Fujimori was inaugurated — Lima and Caracas issued a joint statement announcing "a gradual process for the full resumption of bilateral relations," ending a rupture that had severed ties in mid-2024. That freeze came after Peru recognized Venezuelan opposition candidate Edmundo González as president-elect following disputed elections, prompting Caracas to expel Peruvian diplomats and cite the "reckless statements" of then-Peruvian foreign minister Javier González-Olaechea as grounds for the break.

By August, the two foreign ministers were already in contact: Peru's Carlos Espa held a call with Venezuela's Félix Plasencia to advance the first stage of normalization — the reopening of consular missions. That thaw directly enabled Thursday's migration coordination conversation.

Amnesty International Has Already Raised the Red Flag

The procedural gap at the center of Thursday's announcement is not a hypothetical risk. In November 2023, Amnesty International warned that Peru's expedited 24-hour expulsion process — introduced under Legislative Decree 1582 — was "incompatible with due process guarantees" and the international prohibition on returning people to countries where they face serious harm. The organization specifically cited Venezuelan refugees — people who fled documented mass human rights violations under Maduro — as the population most at risk of removal without adequate review.

Plan Vuelta a la Patria has operated flights from Lima before: by mid-2021, more than 6,500 Venezuelans had returned to Venezuela from Peru through the program, with Venezuelan state airline Conviasa funding and operating the flights at no reported cost to Peru. That financial model may well carry over to this new phase — but neither government confirmed it on October 15.

What Still Has Not Been Answered

The announcement leaves several material questions unanswered: how many individuals will be included, when the first flights will depart, how the process will distinguish between voluntary returns and forced expulsions, and — most critically — whether individuals with pending asylum or refugee claims will receive adequate legal review before boarding a plane.

Peru unquestionably has the legal authority to expel undocumented migrants. The open question is whether the diplomatic framework agreed on October 15 will produce operational protocols capable of separating the two categories of departure — voluntary and coerced — and whether those with legitimate claims to international protection will have a meaningful opportunity to assert them. Until those protocols are public, Thursday's announcement functions more as a political signal with two different audiences — one in Lima, one in Caracas — than as an enforceable migration agreement.

text:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Vice President JD Vance faced tough questions from voters about the Trump administration’s policies on data centers, high costs, immigration and his own rhetoric in a town hall on CBS News that aired Saturday night.

The string of sharp queries, some from voters who said they had supported him and President Donald Trump, previewed the rocky path he may face trying to answer for the administration’s record if he runs for president himself in 2028.

Join our WhatsApp group

Subscribe to our Daily Roundup Email

Vance, who said during the town hall there’s “of course” a chance he doesn’t run for president, faced an especially pointed question about “a failure of leadership” posted by the widow of one of six U.S. soldiers killed by an Iranian drone strike in Kuwait, which occurred the day after Trump started the war with Iran.

“This literally is the first time I’ve heard of this,” Vance said in response.

As he went on, he said, “This job is an amazing honor, but you live in a bit of a bubble and sometimes information doesn’t filter up.”

Questions about Iran war strategy and costs

After telling the vice president about his late wife, Master Sgt. Nicole Amor, who was killed on March 1, Joey Amor asked about mistakes and fundamental failures that led up to the deaths of those soldiers and how leaders would be held accountable.

Vance seemed taken aback by Amor’s questions, saying, “This literally is the first time I’ve heard of this,” and said he wanted to talk with Amor to learn more after.

But as Vance went on, he acknowledged mistakes were made and said, “there were issues with where troops were located that we realized was a huge mistake that we could do better on, and we have changed that.”

A Michigan man who said he voted for Trump and Vance in 2024 but now plans to vote for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed pressed Vance about the high gasoline prices resulting from the war. In response, Vance said he recognized that gas prices were too high, and said, “I think it’s important to be honest about why they’re so elevated.”

He said it was because of “what’s happening in the Middle East” and said the administration was taking steps to try to lower prices.

“We’ve never had a situation like this where you have effectively, the largest state sponsor of terrorism that’s trying to choke off world energy supply,” Vance said, without acknowledging that situation occurred because of the war Trump launched.

He also blamed former President Joe Biden, saying that during his tenure, America’s refining capacity was diminished.

But when Vance was pressed on the Trump administration owning the current situation, the vice president suggested that looking backward for blame was not the way.

“Fundamentally, we are where we are, and you have to, in my view, I’d like to know what is Abdul El-Sayed’s solution for the problem that we have right now,” Vance said. “It’s easy to criticize something that happened seven months ago.”

Immigration enforcement tactics and the rhetoric around immigrants

A nun who spoke to Vance about their shared Catholic faith questioned the administration’s hardline immigration enforcement tactics, including children who are separated from their parents when the adults are swept up in sweeps, and how that squared with their values.

“We’re trying to strike the right balance,” Vance said. When moderator Tony Dokoupil asked Vance if the administration is not striking that balance, Vance replied, “I think that is constantly a work in progress.”

He admitted that, “Sometimes you have some people who made mistakes. Sometimes you have some people who really screw up.”

When Dokoupil asked for specific examples, Vance said there are a number of cases the administration has investigated that resulted in further training or discipline for immigration enforcement officers, but said they don’t advertise it publicly in order to let investigations play out.

Another voter, who said she became an immigrant five years ago and voted for Vance after becoming a U.S. citizen, asked him pointedly about his recent remarks referring to H1-B visa holders as, “foreign indentured servants,” and accused him of “scapegoating immigrants for the issues you’re supposed to be solving.”

“To the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that’s on me,” Vance said, before explaining that he was trying to criticize the companies that bring in the workers, not the immigrant workers themselves.

Selling access to the White House is ‘disgusting and despicable’

Dokoupil pressed Vance on whether Trump and others in his administration were profiting off the presidency, including the nearly $1.2 billion the president took in from his crypto businesses last year, according to a federal filing. When asked if he’d seen anything in the White House that made him squeamish, Vance said, “I’ve never seen anything like that from the president.”

He said, though, that there is evidence of corruption in Washington, but he doesn’t see evidence of it from the president or the administration.

Vance said he’s read articles about allegations, but said he goes to investigate claims himself and finds that they are not true.

Dokoupil asked Vance about the president’s crypto profits, along with the recent resignation of his ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, over allegations she denies that she was leveraging her position for benefits.

“If somebody’s selling access to the White House, that’s disgusting and despicable and they should suffer consequences,” Vance said.

text:
Purple Sanctuary, a student group organizing against Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Northwestern’s campus, called on the University to take action against ICE at a Thursday event.

The talk was a component of Disorientation Week, a student-led programming series related to campus activism. During the event, Weinberg senior Asha Mehta discussed what she described as the “minimal” policies at NU that protect students from immigration enforcement activity compared to its peer institutions like DePaul University and Harvard University.

Purple Sanctuary also shared its active petition to the University, which lists a series of immigration-related policies that it believes NU should adopt, including transparency from the NU Police Department, free Know Your Rights trainings and clear delineation of public and private spaces on campus. At the time of publication, the petition has more than 100 signatures.

Mehta, a Purple Sanctuary member, said she is disappointed by the University’s limited response to ICE activity around campus.

“This is not the way it has to be,” she said. “It could be better and student pressure really does work.”

NU released an official statement addressing federal immigration enforcement activity on April 1, 2025.

The letter instructed students to call NUPD if they were approached by federal officers on or off campus, urged international students to exercise caution when traveling abroad and provided several “wellness resources,” including NUhelp and NUGuardian.

Mehta, who worked with other Purple Sanctuary members on an analysis of the ICE-related policies at the top 100 universities in the U.S., said the University’s acknowledgment of immigration enforcement activity has been minimal compared to similar schools.

She said nearby colleges like the University of Illinois Chicago and DePaul University maintain immigration-related resource directories and provide specific instructions for how students can report ICE activity on campus. Harvard University requires ICE agents to request permission from the campus police department before entering campus, she added.

The University of Southern California, Mehta said, offers free legal support to immigrant and international students through its law school.

Eighth-year doctoral candidate in physics and astronomy Jorin Graham, another Purple Sanctuary member, said the “ambiguity” of NU’s communication regarding ICE has led to anxiety among students on campus.

“It’s really important that people know their rights,” Graham said. “And as Northwestern is not providing that information, I think it’s really important that we as members of the community step up to do that.”

Leif Thesen, a senior at Bates College who attended the presentation, said she was struck by how differently the University responded to ICE activity compared to her school.

Bates, a small liberal arts college located in Lewiston, Maine, reacted promptly when ICE activity began increasing in the surrounding community, Thesen said.

“(NU has) so many more students,” Thesen said. “There are so many more people at risk.”

She added that Bates President Garry Jenkins sent out an email on Jan. 16 with resources regarding immigration enforcement. The school then restricted buildings that had previously been open to the public to student access only.

Thursday’s event outlined the progression of ICE activity over the past year, including deportations of international students and individuals in the Chicago area.

While Mehta noted public awareness has died down following the influx of federal immigration activity last fall due to Operation Midway Blitz, she emphasized that ICE remains active in the area.

“Even if it’s not in the news, ICE is still definitely a threat to our Chicago community,” Mehta said.

title: Common Cause is Suing to Protect Constitutional Observers
description:
Across the country, constitutional observers have been watching, photographing and recording federal immigration enforcement officers in public—activities that are protected by the First Amendment.
That’s why Common Cause and Michael Khalili are suing these agencies, standing up for ordinary people who exercise their constitutional rights to observe public immigration enforcement.
This includes observing federal immigration enforcement operations from public places, recording what they see, and sharing that information with others.
For more than 50 years, Common Cause has worked to make government more open and accountable, to empower people to participate in civic like.
Common Cause is challenging the government’s retaliation against constitutional observers in court to protect our constitutional right to peacefully observe federal immigration enforcement.
text:
Across the country, constitutional observers have been watching, photographing and recording federal immigration enforcement officers in public—activities that are protected by the First Amendment. And several federal agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Department of Justice (DOJ), and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), are actively intimidating or retaliating against these observers.

That’s why Common Cause and Michael Khalili are suing these agencies, standing up for ordinary people who exercise their constitutional rights to observe public immigration enforcement.

What is a constitutional observer?

Constitutional observers are ordinary people who watch and document government activity in their communities. This includes observing federal immigration enforcement operations from public places, recording what they see, and sharing that information with others.

Our lawsuit argues that people have a First Amendment right to peacefully observe and record law enforcement officers carrying out their duties in public, as long as observers do not interfere with those duties. Constitutional observers help create a record of government activities, providing their communities with information that might otherwise never become public.

One of those observers is Michael Khalili, who documented the actions of federal immigration officers. He has worked with his neighbors to track, document, and share information about immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis, Minnesota. In March, a federal immigration agent photographed his vehicle and his face. The next day, his Global Entry was revoked. Less than two months later, he was pulled over by an ICE agent and threatened with arrest if he continued to exercise his right to observe law enforcement in public.

“The truth about the federal government’s actions in Minnesota only came to public attention because of the efforts of countless regular citizens who acted as constitutional observers in my community,” Khalili said. “While I consider my personal contribution to have been small, I was photographed more times than I can count and have been the subject of government retaliation Und threats simply for exercising my constitutional rights.”

Common Cause and Michael Khalili File Lawsuit Challenging Federal Policy of Intimidation and Retaliation

With Michael Khalili, Common Cause has now filed a lawsuit against several federal agencies, arguing that they have adopted a policy of intimidating and retaliating against constitutional observers. This policy includes:

Photographing or recording observers’ faces and license plates.

Using facial recognition technology and other databases to identify observers.

Adding observers’ personal data to government databases, including domestic terrorist watchlists.

Threatening observers with arrest or other legal consequences.

Following or confronting observers.

Using force against people engaging in constitutional observation.

These actions are designed to discourage people from observing and document immigration enforcement. People should not risk government retaliation for exercising their First Amendment rights.

You can read our complaint here.

What is Common Cause asking the court to do?

Common Cause and Michael Khalili filed the lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. The case is currently pending.

We are asking the federal district court to declare that these retaliatory actions by federal agencies violate the First Amendment, and bar the government from enacting them going forward.

Why This Matters

People should be able to observe their government without being threatened into silence.

For more than 50 years, Common Cause has worked to make government more open and accountable, to empower people to participate in civic like. That work depends on people being able to speak out, organize with their communities, and hold their government officials accountable.

The right to observe government action is part of that accountability. When people are afraid to document what they see, the public loses an important source of information about what the government is doing in their community.

Common Cause is challenging the government’s retaliation against constitutional observers in court to protect our constitutional right to peacefully observe federal immigration enforcement.

text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Rep. Summer Lee is living in a different political world than the one she entered almost four years ago when she became the first Black woman elected to Congress from Pennsylvania.

Lee, 38, came to Washington in 2023 as the number of Black lawmakers continued to grow, thanks, in part, to the Voting Rights Act, landmark legislation born out of the civil rights movement that made it harder to carve up minority communities into majority-white congressional districts.

But the U.S. Supreme Court’s April decision in Callais v. Louisiana severely weakened that part of the 60-year-old law — a law that had already been curtailed in 2013 after the justices threw out the provision that required the federal government to approve voting changes in places with a history of discrimination before the changes could take effect.

After Callais, some Republican-led Southern states moved swiftly to enact new district maps ahead of the midterm elections in November, part of a larger effort to offset potential Democratic gains in other areas of the country through an unprecedented wave of mid-decade redistricting.

Jonathan D. Salant

Fight over noncitizen voting — which is extremely rare — signals potential battle over 2024 election results

“We're at a place that I won't say is predictable, but I would say is not incredibly shocking,” said Lee, D-Swissvale, who focused on civil rights and social justice while getting her degree at Howard University’s law school, became a labor organizer, and then won a state legislative seat before being elected to the U.S. House.

The bottom line is that the current generation of Black leaders suddenly faces some of the same battles for representation that their parents and grandparents once did.

“I think James Baldwin said it best — young people are never good at listening to their elders, but they never fail to imitate them,” said U.S. Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J. “I think what's important right now is to do like our ancestors did when they faced assaults on voting rights: Show your conviction, your determination, your will and your work in righting these wrongs.”

A half-century of impacts

The impact of the Voting Rights Act has been felt for more than a half-century. The number of Black members of Congress rose from six in 1965, when the legislation was passed, to a record 66 in the current Congress, including Lee. Five are Republicans — four in the House and one in the Senate — but all four House GOP members are either retiring or seeking higher office.

The voting rights law has long enjoyed bipartisan support; the law last was renewed for 25 years in 2006 by votes of 98-0 in the Senate and 390-33 in the House.

One of the aye votes was cast by the late Rep. John Lewis, D-Ga., whose skull was fractured in 1965 by an Alabama law enforcement officer when he and other peaceful protesters attempted to cross the Edmund Pettis Bridge in Selma en route to Montgomery to demand the right to vote. The national outrage that followed the violence pressured Congress to act and pass the law.

In recent years, as Supreme Court decisions have chipped away at the law, some lawmakers — mostly Democrats — have tried to undo parts of the rulings, including with the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act, which would revive the federal government’s oversight of voting laws in areas of the country with a history of discrimination, one of the most controversial parts of the original voting rights act.

Jonathan D. Salant

In response to Trump, Summer Lee offers a different state of the union

“We are fighting the same fight, and we're going to win it in the same way,” said Democratic Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, the first Black woman elected to Congress from New Jersey. “I never thought that we'd have to have this experience again, never.”

The Supreme Court ruling in Callais said that those challenging new district lines had to prove that they were drawn to specifically discriminate against minority voters, rather than improving one party’s chances over the other. In Louisiana’s case, the conservative majority ruled that the challengers hadn’t cleared that bar.

“None of the historical evidence presented by plaintiffs came close to showing an objective likelihood that the state’s challenged map was the result of intentional racial discrimination,” Justice Samuel Alito wrote in the majority opinion.

He said Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act “was designed to enforce the Constitution — not collide with it,” but lower court decisions have forced states “to engage in the very race-based discrimination that the Constitution forbids.”

In parts of the country, especially in the South, race and party affiliation are often intertwined, lawmakers said. The result: Reducing the number of congressional districts held by Democrats means reducing the number of congressional districts represented by people of color.

“This idea that you could completely disaggregate race and the ongoing struggles around race from the question of partisan gerrymandering in the South is deeply dishonest,” said U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., senior pastor of the Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta, where Martin Luther King Jr. used to preach.

“As the father of a 10-year-old and a 7-year-old, it saddens me that my children live in a world where they have fewer protections with their voting rights than I did when I was their age,” Warnock said.

Refighting the voting rights battles

Following the court’s decision earlier this year, four Southern states rushed to eliminate majority-minority districts before the 2026 midterms.

Lawmakers said they wanted to increase the number of Republican members of Congress. The redrawn lines turned Black majority districts in Louisiana and Tennessee that were represented by Democrats into what the Cook Political Report now rates as solid Republican.

With the new lines in place, analysts predict that a half-dozen or more Black representatives could lose their House seats in November — with potentially more losses in years to come as other states move to redraw their maps.

Lee said the impact goes beyond a loss of Black representation. Issues such as environmental justice, gun safety, expanded health care and education are also going to be affected.

It could also lead to fewer discussions about issues such as police reform and housing discrimination, said Sierra Dunn, executive director of Gov. Josh Shapiro’s Advisory Commission on African American Affairs.

“Our history has taught us a lot that when we don't have diversity in our legislature or in any level of government, even in the executive branch, the impact can be detrimental to some of those communities,” Dunn said.

The court decision, along with efforts by President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans to pass legislation imposing new requirements for registering and voting, has sparked another round of queries to the state commission.

“We get more questions about just what are we doing, how can we understand this political climate, how we navigate, how can we get our voices,” Dunn said. “You see elected officials. You see people wanting to take the lead. You see, also, the younger generation getting more involved in our political space as well.”

That younger generation brings a “fresh set of eyes and ears” on the issue, Democratic strategist Antjuan Seawright said.

“I like to think about it through the lens of tag team wrestling,” Seawright said. “When you're starting to get tired or worn down, you can make your way slowly or quickly, depending on who you are and how worn down you are, to your partner and you tag them in to help pick up the fight. This generation is experiencing tag team wrestling.”

Old techniques and new technology

They also bring new weapons — technology that didn’t exist during the civil rights battles of earlier generations.

“You're marrying sort of the old principles around organizing, which was very much boots on the ground, with this new technology, social media, these powerful platforms,” Butler said.

“People coming of age now have platforms that our forefathers didn't have. So now you're going to get a much more, to be frank, educated, more sophisticated, more nuanced way of organizing and fighting, but it's going to be organizing and fighting just the same.”

Those efforts to organize have gotten a new focus since the Supreme Court rulings and redrawn districts, said Lee, who was born more than two decades after President Lyndon Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act.

“To those of us who were looking forward to a better society, a more equitable society, a society that was more embracing of diversity, it’s a reminder to us that it's our responsibility to still fight for that,” Lee said. “This is the wake-up call.”
