text:
SAN FRANCISCO (KGO) -- San Francisco educators are accompanying students' families to immigration court hearings and other immigration-related appointments as immigration enforcement operations ramp up nationwide.

Several times a week, educators step out of the classroom to accompany parents to appointments, including hearings at 630 Sansome Street, where many San Francisco immigration court hearings take place.

"Parents and family members feel a giant relief from feeling supported and not going to these intimidating meetings by themselves," said Daniel Gatica, a Spanish teacher with the San Francisco Unified School District.

The Deportation Data Project at UC Berkeley found that ICE arrests in the San Francisco Bay Area are up nearly 70% from 2025. Gatica, who teaches at June Jordan School for Equity, said he has noticed the impact immigration tensions can have on students.

"When the brain is in fight or flight, their brain is incapable of retaining information," Gatica said.

MORE: Bay Area families on edge as schools respond to ICE activity in communities

Gatica is part of a group of San Francisco educators who have been accompanying parents to immigration court hearings for the past two years. The nonprofit Faith in Action trains the educators.

"We have educators from over 20 schools that have accompanied students to ICE appointments, immigration court and other immigration related appointments. We've trained many more than that. So there's probably 150 or so that have been involved," said Matt Alexander, Faith in Action co-director and community organizer.

Since January, Faith in Action said educators have accompanied parents or unaccompanied minors to more than 130 immigration appointments or court hearings.

"We really are there for emotional moral support with our families, to make them feel less isolated and alone," said Geri Almanza, treasurer of United Educators of San Francisco.

SFUSD does not track students' legal status. Last year, nearly 13,000 students were enrolled in English learner classes. Bill Hing, a professor of law and migration studies at the University of San Francisco, said having someone accompany families can make a difference.

MORE: Supreme Court rules Trump administration can continue rapidly deporting migrants to 3rd countries

"I actually do think it makes a difference when an immigration judge or the government attorney or the government investigators sees that there's someone that brought them here," Hing said.

For Gatica, the work outside the classroom has become an important part of supporting students and their families.

"The most fulfilling work and the most impactful work for students in the end," Gatica said.

Faith in Action said educators have also served as translators at 630 Sansome when Spanish-speaking families do not understand what to do next.

text:
Demonstrators marched through Boise on Sunday, October 18, protesting immigration enforcement and bringing attention back to the federal raid in Wilder nearly one year ago.

The march brought community members together to raise concerns about immigration policies and the impact of enforcement operations on Idaho families.

In October 2025, federal authorities conducted a raid at a horse racing event in Wilder as part of an illegal gambling investigation. "Officers violently detained more than 400 people, including children.

Many of those people were injured at the hands of agents. On that October afternoon, a normal family outing turned into a nightmare." Said Emily Croston staff attorney at the ACLU during an interview before the protest. According to authorities, the operation resulted in five gambling-related arrests and 105 immigration-related arrests.

"The families were not allowed to eat. Ivan Saon had just bought lunch when officers ordered him to throw it away. Detainees were also denied consistent access to bathrooms and water.

When Ivan's 10-year-old daughter urgently needed to use the bathroom, officers refused to let her go, forcing her to relieve herself in the middle of the crowded track." Said Rosseli Guerrero, ACLU communications and narrative specialist, as she shared stories from people who experienced the events in Wilder firsthand.

During Sunday’s demonstration, speakers discussed the psychological effects they say children and families have experienced since the raid, including fear and emotional distress. "Fear uncertainty helplessness and the constant question. Who will be next." Said Lucia Venegas mental health specialist.

Among those participating in the march was Lucas, a puppet wearing a lucha libre mask. Organizers say Lucas represents children who were present during the Wilder raid and symbolizes the emotional impact they say some continue to experience.

The ACLU of Idaho has also filed a lawsuit challenging how law enforcement carried out the operation, alleging civil rights violations.

The march began at Ann Morrison Park and continued toward the Idaho State Capitol, with demonstrators calling for accountability and changes to immigration enforcement practices.

Organizers say they hope the protest brings continued attention to their concerns about the Wilder raid and immigration enforcement across Idaho.

text:
A federal judge has ordered the Donald Trump administration to reopen America’s Green Card Lottery, reviving a pathway to permanent residency that attracted more than 20 million entries in its last completed registration cycle. The ruling comes as federal statistics show Florida has overtaken California as the nation’s leading state for new green card holders.

U.S. District Judge Jinsook Ohta in San Diego issued a preliminary injunction Wednesday, Oct. 14, directing Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the State Department to proceed with the Diversity Visa Lottery for fiscal year 2027. Under a revised court timetable, officials must announce registration details by Oct. 29 and open applications by Nov. 1. Registration must remain open for 30 days, with selected applicants notified no later than Dec. 3.

The ruling follows months of uncertainty surrounding a program Congress established in 1990. The State Department postponed registration for the 2027 Lottery while implementing changes to the application process. Immigration attorneys challenged the delay, arguing that the administration could not effectively suspend a program mandated by federal law. The administration could appeal the decision.

Florida has become the nation’s leading state for new green card holders. According to the Department of Homeland Security’s 2024 statistics, 219,470 people obtained lawful permanent resident status in Florida during fiscal year 2024, surpassing California’s 217,420. Florida’s total increased 41% from 155,500 in 2023 and accounted for more than 16% of the 1.36 million people granted permanent residency nationwide.

The increase was substantial even compared with previous years. In 2022, Florida recorded 113,650 new permanent residents. Within two years, that figure had nearly doubled. California, meanwhile, saw a considerably smaller increase, from 205,040 in 2023 to 217,420 in 2024.

The figures include immigrants arriving from abroad as well as people already living in the United States who obtained permanent residency through a change in immigration status. They cover family sponsorship, employment-based immigration, humanitarian categories and the Diversity Visa program. Federal statistics do not provide a readily available state-by-state breakdown of how many Lottery recipients settled specifically in Florida.

Unlike most American immigration pathways, the Diversity Visa program does not require applicants to have an American employer or qualifying family sponsor. Instead, it offers people from countries with historically low immigration rates a chance to obtain permanent residency through random selection.

The program has a statutory allocation of 55,000 immigrant visas annually, although legislative deductions reduced the available number to approximately 51,850 for fiscal year 2026. The State Department recorded 20,822,624 qualified entries for that Lottery. Selection does not guarantee permanent residency. Applicants must satisfy education or work-experience requirements and pass immigration and security screening.

The Trump administration has raised national security concerns about the program. Diversity Visa issuance was initially suspended in December 2025 following a deadly shooting at Brown University and the killing of an MIT professor. The original suspension ended Aug. 28 under a federal court order, but the State Department immediately imposed a new pause, citing a review of screening and vetting procedures.

Under that guidance, applicants may still submit visa applications and attend interviews, but no Diversity Visas are being issued, with no exceptions. The latest court order requires the government to reopen Lottery registration but does not itself lift the separate suspension of visa issuance.

text:
Former President Barack Obama issued a rare statement Sunday rebuking the Trump administration for targeting the president’s political enemies, namely for launching a federal investigation into Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.

“It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say,” Obama said in a lengthy statement shared on social media. “But that’s exactly what the Trump Administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.”

The remarks come after federal agents raided Omar’s Washington D.C., home last week, confiscating her laptop, cellphone and passport, as well as other notebooks and documents related to her and her family’s immigration.

“To understand why this is so appalling, it’s important to know the facts. Congresswoman Omar came to this country with her father when she was 12 years old,” Obama said, noting that both she and her father became naturalized citizens five years after arriving from Somalia.

In diatribes against Democrats, President Donald Trump has repeatedly singled out Omar, whom Obama described as “one of the Trump Administration’s fiercest critics.”

Trump has called Omar “garbage” and broadly condemned Somalis. Vice President JD Vance has also joined in, at one point claiming in March, without evidence, that Omar “definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America.”

U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said last week that her office is investigating potential improprieties related to Omar’s financial disclosures, but the search warrant that authorized agents to seize Omar’s belongings listed potential violations related to immigration, not finances.

More articles

Lawyers for Omar have demanded the immediate return of all of her property.

Omar has not been charged with a crime and has denied wrongdoing, accusing the Trump administration of “political intimidation.”

“Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone — all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case,” Obama wrote on Sunday. “Think about that. The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president.”

The search came just weeks ahead of the pivotal midterm elections. Obama weighed in as he prepared to take his star power to Michigan next weekend to campaign for Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson.

The former president added that “the fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar’s political views. Because if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her — or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.”

title: Cuban left homeless after leaving an ICE facility and sues the agency for holding his documents
description:

In July 2025, ICE revoked his supervised release and took him into custody again to carry out the deportation.

text:
Cuban Rolando Ramírez Fuentes, 57 years old and living in Tampa, Florida, became homeless after spending nine months detained by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), according to a federal lawsuit that accuses the agency of withholding his driver's license and Social Security card even after he was released.

Ramírez, who arrived in the United States from Cuba in 1980 at the age of just 11, is one of seven immigrants who filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against ICE and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on October 13 in a federal court in Washington, D.C.

According to the lawsuit backed by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), the Cuban was arrested by immigration agents in July 2025 while he was outside of his workplace.

He remained in custody until April 28, 2026, when a federal judge ordered his release after granting him a writ of habeas corpus.

However, after regaining his freedom, the ICE did not return his Florida driver's license or his Social Security card, two documents that, according to his lawyers, he needs to find employment and handle daily tasks.

The lawsuit claims that Ramírez requested the return of his belongings, but the agency did not respond favorably nor provided an explanation justifying their retention. His lawyers assert that he also did not receive copies of the documents.

According to the court filing, the lack of documentation has prevented him from finding work, which in turn has limited his access to medical care for a heart condition.

Without sufficient income to pay for accommodation, he ended up homeless, a situation that persisted when the lawsuit was filed, more than five months after his release.

A deportation order dating back to 2004

According to a court ruling issued in Florida on April 28, 2026, the Cuban received a deportation order on February 12, 2004, following a drug-related conviction in 2003.

Despite that order, he/she remained in the United States under immigration supervision for years, although he/she went through other periods of detention.

In July 2025, ICE revoked his supervised release and took him into custody again to carry out the deportation.

His defense then went to a federal court to challenge the extension of the arrest.

Judge John E. Steele of the Middle District of Florida concluded that there was not a significant likelihood that Ramírez Fuentes would be deported in the reasonably foreseeable future.

For that reason, he ordered that he be released within 24 hours, although he would remain subject to the conditions of immigration supervision.

The court ruling did not overturn his deportation order nor did it grant him a new immigration status. What it determined was that he could not be held indefinitely under those circumstances.

Seven immigrants report a practice by ICE

The case of Ramírez Fuentes is part of a broader legal action filed under the name Gonzalez v. Department of Homeland Security.

The seven plaintiffs argue that ICE maintains a practice of unjustly retaining documents and belongings after releasing individuals detained for immigration reasons.

Among the items being claimed are passports, work permits, driver's licenses, Social Security cards, cell phones, money, clothing, and even items of sentimental value.

One of those affected is Vladimir Izmailov, a Russian citizen who applied for asylum in the United States and, according to the ACLU, has been unable to secure stable employment because the agency has not returned his work authorization.

Izmailov is also claiming his wedding ring, while his family has had to resort to loans to pay the rent.

Another claimant, the Salvadoran Joel Vigil Rodríguez, states that he has been trying for months to recover his phone, his keys, and other items confiscated when he was arrested.

Lawyers believe that these cases demonstrate consequences that go beyond the material loss of belongings: they affect the ability to work, maintain housing, receive medical care, and establish identity with authorities.

What do immigrants demand from the justice system?

The lawsuit claims that ICE violates the Fourth Amendment of the United States Constitution, which protects individuals from unreasonable searches and seizures.

Lawyers argue that, although immigration authorities may hold belongings during a detention, they should not continue to keep them after release if there is no legal justification for doing so.

They also question the compliance with the agency's own administrative regulations regarding the conservation and return of personal property.

The plaintiffs request that the court recognize the case as a class action, order the return of the documents and belongings that were unjustifiably withheld, and establish safeguards to prevent similar situations from occurring in the future.

The ACLU explained in a statement that the economic consequences of these detentions can last for months after immigrants regain their freedom.

Michael Perloff, the organization's attorney, argued that the Fourth Amendment exists precisely to prevent government agents from seizing and retaining personal property without a legitimate reason.

For the moment, the accusations are pending judicial resolution. The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comments made by the newspaper El País, which reported on the case of the Cuban citizen on October 16.

text:
Protests are sweeping France as anger over conditions in schools meets frustration with high living costs and a government accused of doing little to address problems facing people.

About 550,000 people demonstrated nationwide on Saturday, according to the Interior Ministry. Most marched peacefully, while a small minority attacked buildings, looted shops and clashed with police, who fired tear gas and charged protesters.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said 1,200 people were arrested and 150 police officers were injured. Behind the confrontations lies a political crisis, fuelled by anger at deteriorating services and overstretched household budgets, and compounded by a sense that France’s political institutions offer little hope of change.

Here is how school blockades became a nationwide movement – and what that means for President Emmanuel Macron.

How have the protests spread, what are protesters demanding?

The movement began last month in high schools in Paris’ working-class northern suburbs, where students protested against teacher shortages and poor facilities. School blockades and demonstrations later spread to cities including Bordeaux, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon, Lille and Marseille.

Saturday brought together students and trade unions, alongside supporters of the “yellow vest” movement that emerged in 2018 to challenge rising living costs and economic inequality.

Emile Chabal, a professor of contemporary history at the University of Edinburgh, told Al Jazeera the demonstrations were “the logical outcome of a series of protests” stretching back to the yellow vests.

That movement was driven by financial pressures and resentment at “the French presidential system”, he told Al Jazeera, alluding to a structure which often leads to the election of a centrist candidate, such as President Emmanuel Macron.

Saturday combined those longstanding grievances with students’ anger at deteriorating state schools. The yellow vests had demanded better public services.

Bringing students’ grievances together with wider social demands, therefore, represented “the worst possible outcome for the French government”, Chabal said.

Students’ immediate demands concern conditions in France’s lycees (public high schools), which generally educate pupils aged 15 to 18. They want smaller classes, enough teachers, better buildings and less exhausting timetables. Their complaints also reflect broader concerns about whether the state can provide the education and opportunities young people need.

But for workers, including school staff, the dispute also concerns wages and the resources available to deliver public services.

The school protests coincided with a nationwide public sector strike against the government’s budget plans. Bringing all these concerns together under one umbrella represented “the worst possible outcome for the French government”, Chabal said.

It comes as the proposed 2027 budget includes a 54 billion euro ($60.8bn) package of cost-cutting and tax measures, which the government says is necessary to reduce France’s deficit. The proposals include freezing the pay scale used to calculate civil servants’ basic salaries, which unions say would be the fourth consecutive annual freeze.

Donatella della Porta, a sociologist and political scientist, said students were inspiring wider mobilisation around inequality, cuts to public investment and democratic rights, with demands for social welfare spending rather than militarisation.

“They do not want to fight wars; they want a different future,” she told Al Jazeera.

She also linked the movement to young people’s mobilisation over Gaza, with Palestinian flags appearing at demonstrations across several European countries.

How has the government responded?

The government has focused its immediate response on public order, with President Macron saying those responsible for violence would be “prosecuted and punished”.

His comments came as a fire largely destroyed the historic town hall in the city of Limoges, while public buildings and shops were attacked elsewhere.

But those involved in violence represent only a small minority of the much larger mobilisation. Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the left-wing France Unbowed party, has accused the government of repressing school students and allowing the confrontation to intensify.

His argument reflects a wider political dispute about whether the government treats the protests chiefly as a security problem or addresses the grievances that have brought different groups together.

Experts say France’s problems extend beyond disagreement over individual budget measures and reflect deeper discontent. Emile Chabal, from the University of Edinburgh, said political paralysis since the 2024 parliamentary elections, which left no bloc with an outright majority, had created “an environment in which no political party or movement is able to channel social discontent”.

That fragmentation makes it difficult to build a durable agreement on spending, taxation or public services. It also leaves protesters questioning whether changing governments produces meaningful changes in policy.

The protests are also “a tough blow for Macron”, Chabal said, whose promises of youthful energy and a reformed, dynamic France have been undermined by “his inability to articulate his political project and his deeply unempathetic persona”.

Chabal added that the unrest included violence sometimes seen on the fringes of French demonstrations, with direct-action tactics associated with the yellow vests. Targets included shops and, more unusually, public buildings. He described the destruction of Limoges’ town hall as particularly significant because of its place in France’s civic history.

Other researchers emphasise the role of policing. Guya Accornero, a specialist in social movements at Lisbon’s University Institute, said previous confrontations had created lasting tensions between protesters and police.

During the current protests, a 15-year-old lost a hand to a police stun grenade, while a 14-year-old suffered a shattered jaw after being struck by a tear gas canister fired at close range, according to Human Rights Watch. The organisation condemned excessive force against children, saying the demonstrations had been overwhelmingly peaceful.

“Young people have been violently repressed also when using non-disruptive tactics,” she told Al Jazeera.

Who could benefit politically?

There is no clear answer from the experts who spoke to Al Jazeera. Paul Smith, an associate professor in French history and politics at the University of Nottingham, believes far-right leader Marine Le Pen stands to gain.

“I see only one beneficiary and that’s Le Pen,” he told Al Jazeera, suggesting the unrest could also damage Melenchon’s presidential prospects.

Chabal cautioned against assuming a far-right gain, but he said fear of disorder had historically benefited conservative or centrist parties in France, including after the 1968 protests.

Le Pen has not entirely dismissed the protesters’ grievances, describing them on X on Saturday as “legitimate social demands”, while claiming they had been “held hostage by the far left”.

The far-right may seek to reap the rewards of public discontent, but experts say it is more likely to channel that anger towards immigration and the scapegoating of migrants, rather than blaming the structures of neoliberalism and capitalism for the protesters’ woes, as Melenchon has suggested.

With a presidential election due in April 2027, candidates face competing pressures, demonstrating that they can restore order while convincing voters they will address the conditions behind the mobilisation.

The challenge, Chabal said, is how to create change in “an environment in which no political party or movement is able to channel social discontent”.

text:
On Sunday morning, scraped and bruised, Ricardo Gonzalez put his arm in a sling to go to the park to watch his son’s soccer game. The day before, he sustained those injuries after being assaulted by federal agents during an immigration enforcement operation.

“He’s just in pain. He can’t really sit down, it hurts when he gets up,” Leslie Gonzalez, his daughter, told the Watchdog in an interview Sunday. “He’s just trying to get out of the house and move around. He didn’t just want to sit in the house and dwell all day.”

Gonzalez was riding an e-bike near Elm Avenue and 56th Street in North Long Beach when federal agents struck him with their unmarked vehicle, according to Leslie. Agents then tased him twice.

“My Dad is one of the hardest working men out there. Because of him, I have a roof over my head and I have all the opportunities around me,” Leslie wrote on a GoFundMe she set up to support her dad. “Our family is everything because of him. We ask for your support and prayers during this awful time.”

Video taken by Sherman Austin, founder of stopice.net, shows agents handcuffing Ricardo while he lays face down in the gutter yelling that his arm is broken.

In a separate video posted by @gustavo.gonzalez890 on TikTok, an ICE agent can be seen going through Ricardo’s wallet. The agent said he was looking for an ID, which was still in Ricardo’s pocket. Leslie told the Watchdog that her dad’s ID and Meta glasses were not returned to him.

Leslie organized the GoFundMe to raise money to cover the cost of Ricardo’s hospital bills as well as any legal expenses that may arise as a result of the incident. As of noon Sunday, the campaign had received $8,100 in donations, exceeding its initial goal of $6,500.

“As his madrina (godmother), Ricardo is not just my godchild; he is part of my spiritual family, someone I love, care for, and feel a deep responsibility to protect and support,” Wendy Rodriguez wrote in a post on Instagram. “Seeing him go through something like this is heartbreaking.”

Gonzalez, 40, is a U.S. citizen born in Hanford, CA, according to Leslie. For the past eight or so years, Gonzalez worked for the city of Long Beach — first in the health department and then the utilities department, a position he left in September, Leslie said.

Outside of work, Leslie said Gonzalez enjoys watching TV, playing video games on his Playstation and repairing the family’s cars, a skill he picked up from his father, a Mexican immigrant.

“He loves riding his e-bike,” Leslie said. “He loves to take the time to be out and take his little rides by himself.”

Leslie added that her dad is a people person, who loves making new connections wherever he goes.

“My dad just gives off that vibe that he’s super nice,” she said.

In another video recorded by Austin, masked agents can be seen handcuffing a woman and placing her in the back of an unmarked vehicle. A man, who identified himself as her husband, is shouting at the agents that she is a U.S. citizen.

Long Beach Police Department officers can be seen interjecting themselves between the agents and the man in an apparent attempt to deescalate the situation. In a video posted @oc_inside on Instagram, a large crowd surrounded the agents’ vehicle and demanded they release the woman. At one point, she can be seen running down the street and an agent opts not to immediately pursue her.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not respond to requests for comment.

Numerous videos show LBPD vehicles blocking streets, with numerous people asking why the police department is assisting in a federal immigration operation, which is against city and state law.

The department, for its part, released a statement clarifying its presence, saying ICE personnel “requested emergency assistance from LBPD and LBFD due to vehicle vandalism taking place and a subject in need of medical aid.”

According to the LBPD, an officer located Ricardo, handcuffed, bleeding and detained. Fire department personnel were unable to reach the scene due to trash cans — placed there by residents to obstruct federal vehicles, videos show — blocking the street, so LBPD officers transported Ricardo to a nearby fire station, where they removed the handcuffs.

LBFD personnel then took Ricardo to a local hospital.

“LBPD left the area and some ICE agents followed LBPD personnel to a secure parking lot in the police station,” the department continued. “The ICE agents were subsequently directed to leave the station. They were later advised that if they wanted to file a vandalism report, they could contact the City of Long Beach Communications Center and an LBPD officer would respond to their location to take a report.”

The department said it made no arrests and added that, while it does not assist in immigration enforcement, it also “cannot legally obstruct or interfere with federal enforcement operations.”

Hours after the incident, multiple Long Beach officials condemned the operation, including Mayor Rex Richardson, who said “our residents shouldn’t have to be put in these situations, families shouldn’t have to live in fear in their own neighborhoods.”

“To our immigrant communities, you’re a part of this city,” Richardson said in a video posted to social media. “You belong here and you belong to feel safe here.”

Richardson went on to note the timing of this latest push for immigration enforcement in Long Beach and across the state as potential voter intimidation. He said the city is coordinating with election officials to ensure safe access to the polls.

Councilwoman Tunua Thrash-Ntuk, who represents the 8th District where the incident took place, also commented, saying agents need to keep their “hands off our people!”

“In a free country, no one should be riding their bike in their own neighborhood only to be subjected to an unprovoked assault by a government agent,” Thrash-Ntuk wrote in a statement, adding that Ricardo is an American citizen and a former employee of the city.

“ICE has no place terrorizing our streets or subjecting our residents to random stops and harassment simply because of the color of their skin,” Thrash-Ntuk continued. This lawless chaos demands our universal condemnation.”

In the aftermath of the attack, Leslie said she couldn’t believe how many organizations and people reached out to her family. The support at the scene of the incident as well as everything that has come after has been overwhelming and the family is thankful, she said.

“I wouldn’t have believed in a million years that this would ever happen to my family,” Leslie said. “But that’s just a bad mindset to put yourself in because it could happen to anyone.”

text:
More than 105,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan will keep their deportation protections that were set to end Monday, the Department of Homeland Security announced Sunday.

The move keeps those immigrants under the temporary protected status, which allows them to live and work in the U.S. Although that status was set to end Monday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin did not issue an official decision to terminate TPS for Ukraine and Sudan.

DHS issued the same statement for both countries Sunday, saying that an announcement would be made at an appropriate time and Ukrainians and Sudanese people in the country under TPS would retain protection.

The announcement comes after DHS left immigrants from El Salvador in the same state of limbo after the designation expired for the Central American country last month. But the Trump administration, with the backing of the Supreme Court, has moved to wipe the temporary protection designations for most of the countries that had them, including by targeting Haitians who sought refuge in the U.S. after their protections ended in July.

Trending

Congress established TPS in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries deemed too unsafe because of armed conflict, natural disasters or other humanitarian crises.

Approximately 103,700 Ukrainians and 1,900 Sudanese people are beneficiaries of the program, according to DHS. The Biden administration granted TPS for Ukraine in 2022 because of the war with Russia, and Sudanese immigrants have had the status for nearly 30 years because of the ongoing armed conflict, displacement of millions inside the country and famine.

A bipartisan group of Senators had introduced a bill in September extending TPS for Ukrainians.

“The reality is that it is simply not safe for them to return to Ukraine,” Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said in a statement announcing the legislation. “We should not force Ukrainians who we allowed into the U.S. and who are here legally and contributing to our communities back into an active war zone.”

text:
Immigrants from Ukraine and Sudan enrolled in the Temporary Protected Status policy will be able to live and work in the U.S. without fear of deportation for the time being, even though their protections were set to expire soon, the Department of Homeland Security told CBS News on Sunday.

The TPS protections of tens of thousands of Ukrainians and hundreds of Sudanese immigrants were officially slated to terminate on Monday.

But in statements on Sunday, DHS said final decisions on the fate of the humanitarian immigration programs will "be made at the appropriate time."

Until such decisions are announced, DHS added, nationals of Ukraine and Sudan enrolled in the TPS program will "retain protection."

The decisions to keep the deportation protections in place, albeit not final, stand in sharp contrast to the Trump administration's broader posture toward TPS programs.

Trump administration officials have routinely denounced TPS as a de facto amnesty policy abused by the Biden administration that encourages illegal immigration and that has been extended too often, despite its temporary nature.

Over the past year and a half, the Trump administration, as part of its aggressive immigration crackdown, has revoked the TPS protections of more than 1 million immigrants from over a dozen countries, including Afghanistan, Haiti and Venezuela.

The programs for Ukrainian and Sudanese nationals are among a handful of TPS policies that have remained in place nearly two years into President Trump's second term, alongside the protections for tens of thousands of immigrants from El Salvador. Their TPS program was also set to lapse last month, but DHS retained their protections, pending a final announcement.

Created in 1990 by Congress, TPS allows the U.S. government to offer a temporary deportation reprieve and work permits to immigrants, illegal and legal alike, who hail from countries facing armed conflict, an environmental disaster or another crisis that makes their return there unsafe.

The TPS policy for Ukrainians was first announced by the Biden administration in the spring of 2022, soon after Russia launched its full-blown invasion of Ukraine. As of March 2025, there were more than 100,000 Ukrainians enrolled in TPS, including those allowed into the U.S. under a Biden-era sponsorship policy.

title: Trump 'border czar' says Ilhan Omar could be 'of course' denaturalized and deported
description:
Tom Homan, Donald Trump’s “border czar”, has said that the Republican presidential administration could “of course” strip Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar of her citizenship and deport her.
The investigation was launched only weeks before the November midterm elections, in which Omar is on the ballot.

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar also wrote.
text:
Tom Homan, Donald Trump’s “border czar”, has said that the Republican presidential administration could “of course” strip Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar of her citizenship and deport her.

Homan’s comments during a Saturday appearance on Fox News were the first remarks explicitly mentioning denaturalization and deportation in connection with Omar that were attributed by name to a top Trump administration official since federal agents raided the Minnesota US House representative’s home on 12 October.

The search of Omar’s home sparked major backlash and accusations that the Trump administration was weaponizing the federal government to target a political rival whom the president and his supporters have openly fantasized about denaturalizing and deporting.

The federal government’s investigation into the most prominent Somali American in the US is to see whether Omar or her family violated any laws when obtaining her citizenship. The investigation was launched only weeks before the November midterm elections, in which Omar is on the ballot.

When asked on Saturday by a Fox News host whether the investigation into Omar could involve “denaturalizing and then deporting her”, Homan answered: “Of course”.

“If you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody,” Homan said. “We’ve done it before. It’s a long, tedious process, but it’s been done before.

“And certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen.”

Homan also seemed to imply during his Fox News appearance that the federal government is investigating Omar for other allegations – but refused to give details.

“I’m not going to go there,” Homan said. “I know things, but that’s a question for the FBI.”

Omar – a naturalized US citizen from Somalia – was a child when her father filled out the immigration paperwork which the federal government is evidently scrutinizing. Her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, died in June 2020.

In a letter after her home was searched, Omar’s attorneys accused the US justice department of potentially influencing an election in violation of longstanding internal policy.

The move to investigate Omar came amid a heightened offensive by the administration in pursuit of its aggressive anti-immigrant crackdown. In addition to funneling resources and deploying droves of officials to arrest, detain and deport undocumented immigrants throughout the country, the administration has also escalated its on offensive on legal migration.

The administration has been pursuing dozens of cases nationwide in which they are attempting to denaturalize Americans born outside of the US, who they claim fraudulently obtained their citizenship.

As Homan alluded to on Sunday, the lengthy denaturalization process requires a federal investigation and drawn-out court proceedings.

Nonetheless, as of April, the US justice department had reportedly identified nearly 400 foreign-born citizens that it sought to investigate.

The investigation into Omar follows unsubstantiated accusations by rightwing figures who support Trump that she obtained her citizenship fraudulently. Omar denies the accusations, which also include allegations that her ex-husband is her brother, whom she only married so he could obtain immigration status in the US.

The federal government reportedly seized Omar’s phone during the raid on her home and has issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including of Omar’s relatives.

Omar’s attorneys have demanded that the federal government return her property and preserve any audio or video taken during the search.

Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was eight and spent years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She and her family came to the US in the 1990s, and she became a naturalized US citizen in 2000, according to her lawyers.

There is “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”, said her attorneys’ letter, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

After the raid on her home, Omar posted on X that she was “ok”.

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar also wrote. She said: “Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns” for years – and “this is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”

“I will not be silenced,” Omar added.

title: Ilhan Omar: The US Democrat targeted by Donald Trump - DW.com
description:
"Ilhan Omar, whatever the hell her name is, with the little – with the little turban, I love her.
"Ilhan Omar is garbage.
These are just three of Donald Trump's many attacks on US Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar.
Who is Ilhan Omar?
Criticism of Israel and accusations of antisemitism Young, outspoken, female, Muslim, and a left-wing Democrat – politically, Ilhan Omar is almost the polar opposite of the 80-year-old Republican Trump.
text:
"Ilhan Omar, whatever the hell her name is, with the little – with the little turban, I love her. She comes in, does nothing but bitch."

"Ilhan Omar is garbage. She's garbage. Her friends are garbage. […] These aren't people that work. These aren't people that say, let's go. Come on, let's make this place great. These are people that do nothing but complain."

"She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other. And she comes into our country, and she says, 'I have a constitutional right.' She's telling us about the constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet."

These are just three of Donald Trump's many attacks on US Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar. Few people have been targeted as ferociously by the US president. But why has Trump singled her out for such hostility?

Who is Ilhan Omar?

Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, 44, was born in Mogadishu, the capital of Somalia. She fled the civil war in the country while still a child, and spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She finally came with her family to the US in 1995, at the age of 12, and became a US citizen in 2000. She joined the Democratic Party, and made a career as a politician on the party's left wing. Since January 2019, she has served as representative for the state of Minnesota and one of the first two Muslim women to enter the US Congress.

Ilhan Omar is a practising Muslim who wears a hijab, and Congress altered a 180-year-old rule for her that prohibited head coverings in the chamber of the House of Representatives. Politically and socially, Omar champions progressive values, and often makes a connection between her faith and her commitment to social justice, human rights, and the protection of minorities.

Omar campaigns on issues such as universal health insurance, increasing the minimum wage, climate protection, and the cancellation of student debt. She is also one of Donald Trump's most prominent and outspoken critics, repeatedly accusing him of racism and systematically fomenting hatred against minorities, immigrants, and Muslims. She has frequently condemned raids by the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE), which she describes as a "militarized campaign of fear." She has also accused the president of corruption in office.

Criticism of Israel and accusations of antisemitism

Young, outspoken, female, Muslim, and a left-wing Democrat – politically, Ilhan Omar is almost the polar opposite of the 80-year-old Republican Trump. But she is also a controversial figure within her own party.

Omar is one of the fiercest critics of Israel in US politics, and has repeatedly called Washington's support for the country into question. She has been accused of antisemitism, and of supporting the movement BDS (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions), which encourages people to boycott Israeli businesses. Omar has defended BDS as a legitimate form of non-violent protest and freedom of expression. In 2019, she even introduced a resolution in the US Congress that aimed to strengthen the right of Americans to boycott, with a view to countering laws that restrict what the BDS movement can do.

In early 2023, Republicans removed her from the House Foreign Affairs Committee over a number of controversial tweets, including a comment she made in 2021 that seemed to equate the actions of the US and Israel with those of the Taliban in Afghanistan, and the Palestinian group Hamas. The latter is classified as a terrorist organization by the US and many other countries around the world.

Accusations of embezzlement and immigration fraud

Her critics also tried to link Omar to a corruption scandal in her home state of Minnesota. During the COVID-19 pandemic, around $250 million (€220 million) were misappropriated from a government-funded food program for children. Omar had previously called for the rules of the program to be eased.

Many of those convicted were from the state's Somali community, something that political opponents, including Trump, seized on to claim Omar was involved. No law enforcement authorities have ever accused her of any wrongdoing.

The most recent accusation against Omar concerns her immigration to the US. For years, her opponents have claimed that she made false statements during the procedure, even alleging that she entered into a fraudulent marriage with her biological brother to help him secure a US visa. On October 12, federal officials ordered a search of Omar's home, investigating allegations that Omar's father lied about her age on her immigration application.

Controversial house search

Omar has repeatedly denied the accusations, describing them as part of a "campaign of political intimidation" and "an attempt to target political enemies." Several leading Democratic politicians have come to her defense, accusing the Trump administration of weaponizing the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security against its political opponents.

Former immigration officials told the Reuters news agency that it is extremely unusual for a house search to be conducted as part of such an investigation, as the government should already have all the relevant immigration documents.

Many see a raid on the home of a sitting member of Congress over a formality from 26 years ago as excessive, and have been especially critical of the timing of the raid, just three weeks before the Congressional elections in which Omar is standing for re-election.

The long-standing, unwritten "60-Day Rule" holds that authorities do not take any public action against political candidates in the two months before an election, so as not to influence the outcome. Critics see the fact that this practice has been ignored in Omar's case as amounting to election interference.

Other Muslim politicians also targeted

With the midterm electionslooming, Trump is battling with plummeting approval ratings, and Omar is not the only Muslim politician the president has been attacking. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate in the Senate election in Michigan, is another.

At a rally last Saturday in Tennessee, Trump said of El-Sayed: "I call him Mohammed. Somebody said, 'His name isn't Mohammed, it's Abdul.' I said, 'To me, it's Mohammed.' I'm the president. I can call him whatever the hell I want. To me, he's Mohammed, and he's a radical jihadist."

There is no intelligence whatsoever to suggest that El-Sayed has any extremist connections. The 41-year-old epidemiologist was born and brought up in Michigan. He went to university there, then won a Rhodes scholarship to Oxford, where he gained a doctorate in public health. For many years, he was the health director of the city of Detroit. Like Omar, he too belongs to the progressive left wing of the US Democratic Party.

During the election campaign, El-Sayed has repeatedly emphasized that he is not the one responsible for the rise in food prices, the expensive rents, and other political grievances. He has placed the blame squarely on what he describes as the failed policies of the administration in Washington.

text:
A 56-year-old Mexican man held at a federal immigration facility in Laredo was found dead in his cell Saturday morning, his daughter and U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Laredo, confirmed to The Texas Tribune.

Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias was found unresponsive by staff at the Rio Grande Processing Center during a security check at around 10 a.m. Saturday, Cuellar said. Staff performed CPR and called emergency services.

Andrade-Covarrubias is the seventh person to die while detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Texas this year — the first being Geraldo Lunas Campos, whose death was ruled a homicide by the El Paso Medical Examiner’s office in January.

He’s also the second to die in an ICE facility in Laredo this year. Felix Alcorta-Rodriguez, a 63-year-old Mexican who was being held at Webb County Detention Center, died on June 19 after being found unresponsive, according to the agency.

GEO Group and officials with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent Sunday.

Andrade-Covarrubias’ daughter, Estefani Andrade, told the Tribune that her family has not yet been contacted by federal agencies. Instead, she said, they heard about his death on Saturday through the Webb County Medical Examiner, which is performing his autopsy.

Estefani Andrade, 29 and a U.S. citizen, said the family is going to visit the detention facility on Monday to get his belongings.

Andrade-Covarrubias lived in Dallas for decades, had three adult children who were all born in the country and worked as a contractor painting apartments and townhomes, his daughter said. He wanted to eventually return to Mexico and had been travelling back and forth to build a house there, his daughter added.

She said her dad was detained in June at the border after coming back from Mexico by bus. She added that during his months in detention, “he lost weight because he didn’t look the same as when we were doing, like, the video calls with him.”

Cuellar said he planned to visit the facility Sunday afternoon.

“I’ll ask the basic questions: What happened?” he said. “What were the conditions? [Was] there medical? Is there anybody ill? I’m gonna talk to the medical folks there.”

Estefani Andrade said her dad had a heart condition, along with diabetes and high blood pressure. He had medicine with him when he was detained, but she said staff at the center wouldn’t “give him his medications.”

She also said her dad was sick at the detention facility. He had a cough — which she said was concerning since he was hospitalized for COVID-19 in 2021 and that took a lasting toll on his health — and told her that he wasn’t feeling good. He sought help from the facility’s medical staff but he told her that “they would just ignore him.”

She said her dad told her that he felt like medical staff at the center was brushing off his concerns, even when he told the staff that he was having trouble breathing and feeling tightness in his chest.

Estefani Andrade said she is now trying to be strong for her mom, who is devastated.

“When she got the news, she wasn’t all there,” she said. ”It’s hitting her really hard.”

title: Op ed: Performing refugeehood - How will Sudanese navigate Egypt's incoming asylum system?
description:
These leave one wondering: how will Sudanese navigate an asylum service run by the persecutor?
Violence, and the subsequent victimisation one felt afterwards, are crucial to convincing the UNHCR officer that one does indeed need protection.
Between UNHCR and the Egyptian state Navigating Egyptian bureaucracy is a lengthy, frustrating process for many Sudanese.
Despite relentless pressure by the Egyptian state, solidarity “makes you feel powerful,” one interviewee told me.
Sudanese may have to curate new narratives as the asylum service shifts hands to a state which is actively targeting them.
text:
By Joseph A. Owens for Radio Dabanga

Egypt has slowly whittled down its commitments to the 1951 Refugee Convention. And now we wait for the final nail in the coffin: the implementation of Asylum Law No. 164, which gives the government the authority to decide who will be protected from violence and deportation.

For Sudanese in Egypt before 2023, registering with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and the subsequent wait, often years in limbo, for an interview to determine one’s refugee status, is an all-too familiar and exhausting process.

Under new regulations, decisions on refugee matters will shift from UNHCR. Commentators have warned that this risks the state arbitrarily denying or withdrawing asylum amid a history of documented human rights abuses against Sudanese.

Escalating deportations, police patrols, and a recent violent raid on gold miners in the Aswan and Red Sea Governorates have only sowed further distrust. These leave one wondering: how will Sudanese navigate an asylum service run by the persecutor?

UNHCR’s position in Egypt

UNHCR Egypt is often likened to a ‘surrogate state,’ an organisation fulfilling the basic duties of a government by providing meagre cash assistance, endorsement for residency, and referrals for medical assistance. It attempts to make life liveable in Egypt. Most importantly, UNHCR offers supposed safety from deportation and violence.

Yet this protection must be earned, defying the logic that it is a right enshrined in the Refugee Convention. I spoke to multiple Sudanese who felt they had to embellish their stories during their interactions with UNHCR officers. “You just call them and play the role of victim,” Eltahir told me. He recalled speaking with them thirteen times to find a solution to repeated arbitrary detentions he faced and violence on the street from those acting on behalf of the Government of Sudan, receiving one callback to advise him to move areas.

‘Performing for the UN’

For Sudanese, the most important interaction is the Refugee Status Determination (RSD) interview: a showdown between the UNHCR-appointed officer and one seeking protection. This interview will decide whether one can legally reside in Egypt based on a well-founded fear of persecution.

Before fleeing Sudan, Abdelrahman had written down all violent events he faced in Sudan and Egypt so he would remember them clearly. This is a common practice, often suggested by refugee-led organisations and community members throughout Cairo and Giza.

Others undergo mock interviews with fellow Sudanese or share their experiences through WhatsApp channels, warning other asylum-seekers of what to expect, such as how to navigate difficult interviewers.

While these are normal practices, the way applicants tell their story is critical. Interviewees are expected to recall violent incidents in chronological order, focusing on specific details, such as the colour of a torturer’s shirt or how many people were in a prison cell. Violence, and the subsequent victimisation one felt afterwards, are crucial to convincing the UNHCR officer that one does indeed need protection.

“The other reasons [for leaving Sudan], I did not mention. These are about personal wellbeing, doing a master’s degree and finding a good job. These are not reasons which will convince their claim … they would say, ‘We are not a charity.’ I focused on the conflict, the casualties, the people who were killed in my family, the safety of my life and the persecution,” Hassan, from North Darfur, said, describing his RSD interview in detail.

I asked him how he felt about this, but he said he had no option. “I should play that role well and just make sure that I send the message across well. If they think I really am a victim, then I can get some assistance.”

Despite his best efforts, Banda, “fresh from the trauma in Sudan,” could not continue his interview: “I know there are times you test if someone is consistent or not, but you feel they’re quite intense. It reminded me of my detention experiences.”

Banda was subsequently rejected. He believed he was not passive enough and “too articulate” to be considered a true victim. In the eyes of UNHCR, “some people are expected to suffer, to look poor, illiterate, not educated … they should be that way.” Upon appeal, with a more scrupulous officer, he was finally recognised.

Much has been written about the optics of refugeehood: how one should look or present oneself to receive assistance, or what Didier Fassin calls ‘humanitarian reason’. There is no hierarchy of suffering in the 1951 Refugee Convention, but it is often a determining factor in ‘earning’ the right to be recognised as one who genuinely has faced persecution.

UNHCR officers often begin from a place of suspicion. While fraud does exist, the parameters of what is ‘true’ and what is ‘not’ often depend on the temperament and ability of the interviewer and their supervisor. Abdelrahman was rejected due to credibility concerns regarding his Fur identity. He felt this was because of the interviewer’s lack of knowledge of Darfur and her scepticism of his confident understanding of refugee law; he was simply ‘too’ educated. It took an appeal with another officer who had researched his hometown more thoroughly to be recognised.

Demanding justice

Performing victimhood can be a tactic to secure residency, yet many have forced UNHCR to recognise their claims to justice. Hassan was deported from Jordan along with hundreds of other Sudanese after a sit-in outside UNHCR offices demanding protection and working rights. Despite the threat of removal, at the time he insisted that “we’re gonna fight.” He and others lay blame directly on UNHCR for not addressing their concerns, nor intervening in their forced removal back to Sudan.

Hassan was detained, released, and subsequently travelled to Egypt, meeting other deportees. He then confronted an officer at UNHCR Cairo, pointing to his document from Jordan which assured the organisation would protect him. Acquiescing, the officer agreed that what had happened was a violation of his human rights. “You have to hold them accountable,” he advised me.

Likewise, upon rejection, Abdelrahman explained in detail to the UNHCR officer conducting his appeal exactly how little knowledge the previous officer had about Darfur, besides quoting the Refugee Convention. Playing this game of victimhood while still affirming his rights, remained crucial not just for recognition, but for dignity and ownership over his own story.

More formalised resistance in Egypt is limited, as the social contract with UNHCR and promises of protection have remained fragile. Many Sudanese remember the fatal Mustafa Mahmoud sit-in of 2005 outside of their office and blame the agency for not acting quick enough to secure a solution to Sudanese’s protection issues before Egyptian police opened fire on protesters.

Between UNHCR and the Egyptian state

Navigating Egyptian bureaucracy is a lengthy, frustrating process for many Sudanese. Residency appointments, facilitated by UNHCR, now stretch months into the future and require multiple visits. Obtaining a birth certificate often requires the intervention of Egyptian lawyers. Requesting medical or police reports sometimes requires a bribe.

UNHCR has tried to make these processes easier by partnering with hospitals, referring people to local law firms, and negotiating with immigration officials in *Abbassia. Yet getting UNHCR’s attention is exhausting. This often means calling for hours or travelling to their office in 6th of October City before sunrise to secure a place in line. This is the reality for many of the almost 900,000 of Sudanese registered with the agency. In turn, UNHCR often decries the limited funding from resource-rich countries, while European money is increasingly being spent on policing migration.

Convincing Europe and Egypt

The European Union remains the architect behind Asylum Law No. 164. This is just one agreement among others with North African countries aimed to hold asylum-seekers and refugees in place, preventing their arrival in Europe in exchange for billions of euros. To create conditions for ‘local integration’, the EU has required Egypt to offer (through the new asylum law) pathways to citizenship, freedom to leave and return to the country, and unrestricted access to the labour market. These measures could theoretically lift Sudanese out of the precarious labour that is rife throughout the country.

Through this new asylum architecture, Sudanese will have to curate their own stories to convince a state which actively brutalises them to provide protection. The hierarchy of suffering and need to victimise oneself will intensify. Given the EU’s desire to stop migration from countries of origin, including through its funding of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces to police migrant routes through and out of Darfur and closing maritime routes off the coast of Egypt, there is little reason to believe deportations will cease.

Community-based initiatives and information sharing among networks on how to navigate the new asylum service will need greater support. Demanding justice amid this hostility may require buying into the language of the Egyptian state, as demonstrated by Hassan and Abdelrahman toward UNHCR.

Living otherwise

Despite this repression, Sudanese have created a sense of place in Egypt. Established communities dating back decades were later joined by South Sudanese and, after 2003, by Darfuris and Nuba. Organisations run by Sudanese proliferate throughout Cairo and Giza, with mutual-aid networks providing support and basic safety nets which UNHCR and the Egyptian state do not.

Beyond these networks, many simply show up for each other. During phone calls with interviewees, some were interrupted by community members with requests to join an aid distribution meeting, or to go meet new arrivals to the country. This is the kind of solidarity which has travelled with those displaced. Despite relentless pressure by the Egyptian state, solidarity “makes you feel powerful,” one interviewee told me.

Sudanese may have to curate new narratives as the asylum service shifts hands to a state which is actively targeting them. However, these solidarity and mutual-aid networks will continue to foster a sense of place.

*The state’s administrative hub for General Department of Passports, Immigration and Nationality located in Cairo.

text:
The race is on to get out the vote in the final stretch of the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.

President Donald Trump continued his campaign travel blitz on Saturday with a rally in Kentucky aimed at boosting Republican turnout.

Meanwhile, organizers planned hundreds of "No Kings" rallies across the country this weekend. Many attendees held signs opposing Trump's policies, but organizers framed the events as a nonpartisan effort to encourage early voting. The national movement is also mobilizing to prepare for "mass nonviolent action in rapid response to election disruption or subversion if needed."

The rallies come amid an escalating legal battle in California, where the Trump administration is asking a judge to pause the counting of mail-in ballots from suspected noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed as part of a broader effort to prevent fraud.

California's Secretary of State Shirley Weber says the federal government hasn't provided evidence to support its allegations and warns that these "unprecedented measures" could threaten voting rights.

The Justice Department upped the stakes, warning in a letter addressed to the Los Angeles County Counsel’s office that local election officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters may be at risk of prosecution.

"They will all go to jail for a long period of time," Trump said on social media.

Meanwhile, Democratic Senators Alex Padilla, Dick Durbin and Sheldon Whitehouse are urging the Justice Department in a letter to reaffirm that it won't interfere in the election and rule out any attempt to seize ballots before the midterm results are certified.

The DOJ didn't immediately respond to requests for comment on the letter.

title: US workers facing deadly heat borrow from tomato pickers to win key protections
description:
Miami-based WeCount is among the labor groups that are now adopting the fair food program model for other hot, low-wage jobs.
The state-level protection route For years, WeCount advocated for heat protections for workers at the state level.
In 2021, the organization, along with labor partners across the state, launched the “que calor” campaign, meaning “how hot”, with the goal of securing heat protections for workers.
“We believe every worker deserves these protections.” WeCount has also advocated for federal heat protections for workers through proposed Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha) standards written under the Biden administration.
Proposed legislation introduced last November by Indiana representative Mark Messmer would block Osha from implementing the heat protections.
text:
“It’s the kind of heat that makes you feel like you’re being dehydrated, like your skin is drying out,” said Lucas Benitez, after harvesting watermelons with his sons and wife this summer. “The heat that we had 30 years ago is not nearly the heat that we have today.”

This summer was the hottest on record in the US, and most workers in fields, greenhouses and unconditioned indoor facilities still do not have heat protections on the job, putting their health at risk as the climate crisis is expected to make extreme heat more frequent and intense.

Benitez began working in tomato fields in Immokalee, Florida when he was just 16, and in the early 1990s went on to help found the Coalition of Immokalee Workers (CIW), named after the major tomato growing region in south-west Florida. Today, CIW’s fair food program has some of the strongest heat protections for workers in the country, and its approach is being emulated by other groups – in the US and beyond – as federal, state and local efforts to protect people from extreme heat stall.

The program’s protections were hard won after years of boycotts, hunger strikes and protests against food corporations. The model, described as “market-based enforcement” by academics, works by targeting the reputation of the known brand-name of a company – say a fast-food retailer – to improve conditions rather than smaller entities in the supply chain.

Retailers agree to pay a small premium to buy from farms that comply with a worker-protection code of conduct. Farms that violate the code can lose their preferred status, giving workers a powerful way to enforce protections without relying on government regulators.

Miami-based WeCount is among the labor groups that are now adopting the fair food program model for other hot, low-wage jobs. Worker organizations in dairy production in Vermont, construction in Minnesota, sugarcane production in India, and banana production in Ecuador have created similar human rights initiatives.

Florida produces about 70% of all indoor plants sold in the US. The workers who grow these plants were exposed to temperatures over 100F (37.8C) this summer and reported heat-related symptoms and dehydration, said Oscar Londoño, the co-executive director of WeCount, a human rights organization led by immigrant workers and families in south Florida.

“Workers feel like they’re on the verge of fainting,” Londoño said. “We have, unfortunately, far too many stories of heatstroke.”

Extreme heat put other workers in danger this summer too. In September, 24-year-old Obed Azahel Hernandez Perez died from extreme heat exposure while harvesting sweet potatoes in Chickasaw county, Mississippi. And, last year, 47-year-old Marco Antonio Hernandez Guevera died after collapsing from the heat on his first day in the field at a tomato farm in Immokalee.

In Texas, hospitals are seeing an increasing number of cases of kidney disease among outdoor workers, which research suggests could be linked to prolonged exposure to extreme heat.

The state-level protection route

For years, WeCount advocated for heat protections for workers at the state level. Despite largely being symbolic (it did not include enforcement or penalty measures), the legislation died in committee every year, Londoño said. In 2021, the organization, along with labor partners across the state, launched the “que calor” campaign, meaning “how hot”, with the goal of securing heat protections for workers. Two years later, WeCount set its sights on passing a local ordinance.

Unlike the drafted state legislation, the county bill had strong enforcement in the form of monetary penalties to make sure there was industry-wide compliance, Londoño said. The 19-page local ordinance included provisions when the heat index hit 90F (32.2C) for paid rest breaks, access to clean drinking water, and first aid procedures. In 2023, a five-member committee of Miami-Dade county commissioners voted 4-1 in favor of the ordinance and the full county commission passed the bill unanimously through first reading.

But before the county commission’s final vote on the bill, the Florida state legislature blocked the local worker heat protection ordinance with a pre-emptive law banning local efforts to require heat protections for outdoor workers throughout the state. “It was devastating to see the legislature pre-empt commonsense protections,” Londoño said. “We believe every worker deserves these protections.”

WeCount has also advocated for federal heat protections for workers through proposed Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha) standards written under the Biden administration. “Unfortunately it looks like that heat standard is stalled. Workers can’t depend on that,” Londoño said. Proposed legislation introduced last November by Indiana representative Mark Messmer would block Osha from implementing the heat protections.

Without federal heat standards, many people remain unprotected, said Roy McAllister, director of occupational safety and health at the United Food and Commercial Workers International Union (UFCW), which represents 1.2 million workers. Few slaughterhouses at meatpacking and poultry plants are air-conditioned, and workers are exposed to heat from lack of ventilation, hot steam, meat carcasses, salt tanks, steriliser tanks, and ovens, he said. In warehouses and in grocery store receiving areas, some people work their shifts in areas that are hot, stuffy, and lack adequate air circulation.

“As we just saw, this is the hottest summer on record that we’ve ever had.” McAllister said. “It continues to get hotter every year. We’re starting to see more and more people exposed to high temperatures and there’s no federal protective measures to keep employers accountable.”

A long fight for better conditions

With today’s extreme heat, the Coalition of Immokalee Workers decided it was necessary for the tens of thousands of people in their program to have access to electrolytes on participating farms year-round. This summer, the CIW’s fair food program added the new requirement to its heat protection standards in a matter of weeks, which already required participating growers to provide shade, cool drinking water, paid rest breaks, heat illness training for workers and supervisors, and the ability for workers to seek medical attention without fear of retaliation.

But to get to this point – with 14 major participating food retailers, including Walmart, McDonald’s, Whole Foods and Trader Joe’s – workers in the fair food program put pressure on retailers through protests and hunger strikes around the country. Benitez was among a group of Coalition of Immokalee Workers who held a hunger strike outside of Taco Bell’s headquarters in Irvine, California, in 2003 in an effort to get the chain to agree to only buy tomatoes from farms that pay their pickers a living wage.

“Taco Bell has a policy that it will not buy food from contractors that mistreat animals,” Benitez told the Guardian during his hunger strike in 2003. “All we are asking is that they have the same policy for humans.”

At the same time, student-led organizations boycotted Taco Bell over the working conditions of tomato pickers, getting some of their universities to cut ties with the franchise. After three years of boycotts, Taco Bell agreed to the coalition’s demands in 2005. Later, the coalition took on McDonald’s, which agreed to pay more for tomatoes to increase the wages of pickers in 2007.

WeCount is now in this phase of the strategy with its planting justice program and has set its sights on Costa Farms, one of the world’s largest indoor plant growers. The day after Labor Day, WeCount coordinated actions at Costa locations in Florida, South Carolina, and Virginia.

Costa Farms told the Guardian that the company has received requests to join WeCount’s planting justice program. “We take the underlying issues seriously, but the WeCount program’s core workplace protections are already part of Costa Farms’ existing systems and practices, including paid heat-prevention training, a comprehensive heat illness prevention plan, audited payroll and employee-controlled timekeeping systems, complaint-resolution processes and onsite medical support,” the company said in a written statement.

“For more than six decades, Costa Farms has invested in the safety, training and development of our team members, and that commitment continues to shape how we care for and support our workforce today.”

“We believe if Costa Farms becomes part of a new gold standard it will set a precedent for others to do the same while signaling to the major retailers that growers are ready to adopt this program,” Londoño said. “If we can transform Florida we can transform the entire industry.”
