text:
Minnesota's Senate candidates offered sharply different positions on federal policy during their October 16 debate, with questions about political independence, government accountability and the cost of living dominating the discussion.

MINNEAPOLIS, MN (October 16, 2026). Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan and Republican Michele Tafoya confronted each other Friday over Minnesota's welfare-fraud scandals, President Donald Trump's policies, immigration enforcement and the rising cost of health care during an hourlong U.S. Senate debate that gave voters their most extensive side-by-side examination of the candidates ahead of the November 3 election.

The debate, moderated by MPR News politics editor Brian Bakst, covered a broad range of domestic and international issues, including the war in Iran, U.S. relations with Israel and Russia, tariffs, Social Security, reproductive rights, Supreme Court appointments and artificial intelligence. Although both candidates acknowledged the need to address rising costs and protect public programs, they disagreed sharply about the government's responsibilities and the policies Minnesota's next senator should support.

Flanagan repeatedly challenged Tafoya's independence from Trump, who endorsed the Republican candidate earlier in the week. Tafoya countered by questioning Flanagan's record as lieutenant governor and arguing that Minnesota's current administration had failed to adequately protect taxpayer dollars, improve educational outcomes and maintain public safety.

The contest will determine who succeeds retiring Democratic Sen. Tina Smith. With early voting underway, the debate provided an opportunity for Minnesotans to assess how the candidates would approach federal legislation and whether their campaign arguments were supported by specific policy commitments.

Trump's Endorsement Becomes an Early Point of Contention

The debate opened with a question about Trump's recently announced agreement involving diesel purchases from Russia. Tafoya said she opposed the arrangement because she did not believe it would meaningfully reduce fuel prices for Minnesota consumers and feared it would benefit Russian President Vladimir Putin.

She described the decision as one of several issues on which she was willing to disagree with Trump.

Flanagan challenged that position, pointing to Tafoya's acceptance of Trump's endorsement and suggesting that the Republican candidate was attempting to present herself differently as the election approached.

Tafoya responded that she wanted support from voters across the political spectrum, including Republicans, Democrats and independents. She said her campaign was focused on Minnesota rather than any national political figure.

The president's influence resurfaced throughout the discussion. Flanagan linked Tafoya to Trump's positions on tariffs, health care, immigration and the war in Iran. Tafoya maintained that she would evaluate issues independently and work with members of both parties.

Near the end of the debate, Bakst asked whether Tafoya would appear alongside Trump if the president visited Minnesota during the campaign's closing weeks. She did not answer directly, instead saying she welcomed voters regardless of their political affiliations.

Flanagan faced a similar question about campaigning with Gov. Tim Walz. She emphasized that the Senate campaign was her own and described the extensive travel she had undertaken to meet voters across Minnesota.

Welfare Fraud and the Walz Administration

Minnesota's welfare-fraud scandals produced some of the debate's most contentious exchanges.

Tafoya argued that Flanagan should accept responsibility for failures in the administration in which she has served as lieutenant governor. She repeatedly cited allegations of extensive fraud involving public programs and accused state leaders of failing to prevent taxpayer money from being misused.

Flanagan acknowledged that Minnesota's response had fallen short.

She said fraud was unacceptable and agreed with Walz's acknowledgment that the administration should have acted sooner. She cited her support for an independent inspector general and stronger penalties for people convicted of fraud.

When Bakst asked what responsibility she personally accepted, Flanagan said the governor had taken responsibility for executive oversight. She distinguished that responsibility from her own work on paid family and medical leave, child tax credits and school meals.

Tafoya rejected the distinction, arguing that Flanagan had publicly identified herself with the administration's accomplishments and should also answer for its failures.

During the exchange, Tafoya cited a figure of up to $9 billion in fraud. That figure was presented as a campaign assertion, not as a verified total established during the debate. The amount of confirmed losses, alleged fraud and estimated exposure requires careful distinction.

Flanagan questioned whether Tafoya applied the same standards to the Trump administration. She criticized the president's removal of federal inspectors general and his pardons involving people convicted of financial crimes.

The discussion exposed a significant political challenge for Flanagan. Her experience in state government is central to her qualifications for the Senate, but that experience also places her under scrutiny for administrative failures during the past eight years.

Tafoya, meanwhile, was pressed on whether her proposed federal enforcement measures would protect legitimate service providers and beneficiaries from losing funding because of misconduct committed by others.

Immigration Enforcement and Operation Metro Surge

The candidates offered sharply different assessments of federal immigration enforcement in Minnesota, particularly Operation Metro Surge and the conduct of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.

Flanagan reiterated her position that ICE should be dismantled and replaced with an immigration system that maintains border security while protecting due process and providing a pathway to citizenship for qualifying immigrants.

She criticized the federal operation's effect on Minnesota communities and challenged Tafoya over her earlier support for the enforcement initiative.

Tafoya said she supported immigration enforcement but believed the operation had been poorly managed. She argued that the country must maintain secure borders while preserving opportunities for lawful immigration.

Drawing on her family's immigration history and her experience as an adoptive mother, Tafoya said immigration and public safety should be treated as complementary responsibilities.

She also criticized Minnesota's state leadership, arguing that local law enforcement should have played a more active role in protecting residents, demonstrators and federal officers.

Flanagan rejected that account and accused Tafoya of minimizing the consequences of aggressive federal enforcement.

The candidates disputed how to characterize confrontations involving officers and protesters. Tafoya cited violence directed at law enforcement personnel, while Flanagan emphasized the rights of residents and the disruption caused by federal operations.

Tafoya also proposed tougher consequences for fraud committed by noncitizens, including removal from the country and restrictions on returning. Flanagan raised concerns about due process, arguing that accusations alone should not determine whether someone is deported.

The debate did not establish how Tafoya's proposal would distinguish between allegations and convictions or how federal agencies would implement those consequences within existing legal protections.

Public Safety and Gang Violence

Public safety was another area in which the candidates disputed both the seriousness of particular problems and the appropriate government response.

Bakst noted that violent crime had declined nationally and in Minnesota according to government statistics, then asked what additional federal action would be necessary.

Tafoya emphasized stronger enforcement against violent offenders and closer cooperation among federal, state and local agencies.

Flanagan pointed to investments in law enforcement resources, crime prevention and services for victims.

The discussion turned to gang violence involving young people of Somali descent and Trump's public comments about Minnesota's Somali community.

Tafoya said the president's language about the community had been inappropriate. She nevertheless argued that officials should identify specific criminal activity rather than avoid discussing it out of concern about political sensitivity.

She suggested that the FBI, U.S. Marshals Service and local law enforcement agencies could work together more closely, including on criminal activity organized or promoted through social media.

Flanagan acknowledged the seriousness of gang violence but warned against treating an entire community as responsible for the actions of individuals.

She cited coordination through the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension and state investments in local public safety.

The candidates also disputed their relationships with law enforcement organizations. Tafoya cited endorsements from police groups, while Flanagan pointed to public safety funding and her work with communities across the state.

Those competing claims concern different measures of support and effectiveness. Endorsements alone do not establish the success or failure of a public safety policy.

Iran War and Congressional Oversight

Foreign policy occupied a substantial portion of the debate, beginning with U.S. relations with Russia and continuing through the war in Iran.

Tafoya said the conflict with Iran needed to end quickly and argued that no president should be permitted to wage war indefinitely without congressional authorization and public accountability.

She also maintained that Iran must not acquire nuclear weapons and called for a withdrawal strategy that would protect international security and commerce.

Flanagan said she had opposed the war from its beginning. She accused Tafoya of supporting the operation until its political and economic consequences became difficult to defend.

Flanagan cited military casualties, federal spending and rising fuel prices as evidence of the conflict's consequences for American families.

Tafoya disputed Flanagan's characterization of her earlier position. She said she would review classified intelligence and support ending the war if it continued after she took office.

Both candidates expressed opposition to an indefinite conflict, but they disagreed about responsibility for the war and how Congress should respond.

Asked about a proposed $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget, Flanagan said the military should receive necessary resources but opposed additional funding for the Iran war.

Tafoya emphasized the national debt and the need for cooperation between parties on federal spending. She did not directly endorse the proposed defense budget.

The candidates also discussed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Flanagan gave his performance a failing assessment and supported impeachment. Tafoya said his performance remained incomplete and required further evaluation.

Israel, Gaza and American Military Assistance

The candidates expressed substantially different views on Israel's military operations in Gaza.

Flanagan condemned Hamas's October 7 attacks while criticizing the destruction and civilian suffering that followed Israel's military response.

She said she would oppose additional offensive weapons and military assistance to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government and supported a two-state solution.

Tafoya defended Israel as an American ally and rejected Flanagan's description of Israel's actions as genocide.

She said that characterization had deeply troubled Jewish Minnesotans with whom she had spoken and emphasized her support for Israel and the Jewish community.

The disagreement concerned both the language used to describe the conflict and the conditions under which American military assistance should continue.

Neither candidate's statements, by themselves, establish a legal determination concerning allegations of genocide.

Russia, Ukraine and Energy Costs

Tafoya criticized Trump's diesel purchase agreement with Russia, saying the arrangement would provide little relief at Minnesota gas stations while strengthening Putin's position.

Flanagan also opposed the agreement and criticized Trump's approach to Russia.

On Ukraine, Flanagan said the United States should continue treating the country as an ally.

The debate did not produce a detailed proposal from Tafoya concerning future American financial or military assistance to Ukraine.

Both candidates connected foreign policy decisions to Minnesota's economy, particularly the cost of diesel fuel for farmers and transportation-dependent businesses.

Those costs became a recurring subject as the debate turned toward tariffs and international trade.

Tariffs, Agriculture and Trade Policy

Flanagan criticized Trump's tariffs, arguing that they had increased costs and damaged relationships with important trading partners.

She pointed to the difficulties facing Minnesota farmers, particularly producers of corn and soybeans, and argued that trade disputes had created uncertainty in markets already affected by high operating expenses.

Flanagan acknowledged that some targeted tariffs, including those involving steel, could be justified. She nevertheless called for Congress to exercise greater authority over trade policy.

Tafoya defended the use of tariffs as a negotiating tool.

She argued that American producers had operated under unequal trading conditions and that temporary tariffs could encourage other countries to negotiate more favorable agreements.

Tafoya said she would have preferred a different approach from Trump in some instances, particularly in dealing with major trading partners.

The candidates also cited agricultural endorsements. Tafoya pointed to support from the Minnesota Farm Bureau, while Flanagan cited the Minnesota Farmers Union.

Their differences centered on the consequences of tariffs for Minnesota producers and whether the potential benefits of renegotiated trade agreements justified the immediate costs.

Neither presented a detailed economic analysis of individual tariffs during the debate.

Federal Taxes and Government Spending

The candidates disagreed over the federal government's approach to taxation, spending and assistance for working families.

Tafoya supported tax relief involving tips, overtime earnings, Social Security benefits and an expanded child tax credit.

She argued that lower taxes would allow Minnesotans to retain more of their earnings and make decisions without additional government involvement.

Flanagan said she supported certain tax provisions benefiting working people, including relief for tips and overtime.

She challenged Tafoya's suggestion that she opposed all elements of the federal tax legislation and criticized provisions she said would reduce access to health care and food assistance.

Flanagan also argued that federal tax policy had provided disproportionate benefits to wealthy households.

Tafoya repeatedly raised concerns about the national debt and argued that reducing federal spending would require cooperation across party lines.

The debate did not include comprehensive tax plans from either candidate, leaving questions about how their proposals would affect federal revenue, deficits and different income groups.

Social Security: Different Levels of Policy Detail

Social Security produced one of the debate's clearest differences in the specificity of the candidates' proposals.

Bakst asked how they would address the approaching depletion of the program's retirement trust fund.

Flanagan supported raising the amount of earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes, referring to income of $250,000 or more.

She also endorsed the Social Security Expansion Act and argued that the proposal would strengthen the program's finances for decades.

Tafoya acknowledged the seriousness of the problem but declined to commit to a specific financing mechanism.

When asked whether she would support higher taxes or an increase in the retirement age, she said the issue required careful consideration and bipartisan negotiations.

She argued that a responsible solution could not be developed during a brief debate exchange.

Flanagan criticized Tafoya for not presenting a specific plan.

Tafoya maintained that effective legislation would require senators willing to negotiate rather than insist on predetermined answers.

The candidates therefore differed not only over their preferred approach but also over how much detail they believed voters should expect before the election.

Flanagan identified a proposed revenue mechanism. Tafoya emphasized negotiation without specifying which changes she would support.

The financial effect of Flanagan's proposal would require independent actuarial analysis, while Tafoya's position leaves voters without a clear indication of how she would vote on potential changes to taxes, benefits or retirement eligibility.

Health Care and Medicare for All

Health care produced another substantial disagreement.

Flanagan endorsed Medicare for All, arguing that Minnesota families face unaffordable premiums, deductibles and treatment costs.

She described conversations with residents whose annual deductibles reached $16,000 and $18,000.

Flanagan also called for eliminating prior authorization requirements that can delay medical treatment.

She criticized decisions made by insurance administrators and automated systems that interfere with care recommended by medical professionals.

Tafoya rejected Medicare for All as financially unrealistic, arguing that the proposal would require enormous federal spending and expand government control over health care.

She instead called for reforms addressing hospital prices, pharmaceutical costs and insurance-industry practices.

Tafoya said she would work with lawmakers from both parties to address those problems.

Both candidates acknowledged that health care costs are too high. Their disagreement concerned whether the country should pursue a substantially different insurance system or focus on reforming existing arrangements.

The debate did not establish the projected cost of Medicare for All or the potential savings from the candidates' respective proposals.

Supreme Court Appointments and Judicial Reform

The possibility of future Supreme Court vacancies prompted questions about how each candidate would exercise the Senate's confirmation authority.

Flanagan supported expanding the number of Supreme Court justices, considering staggered terms and strengthening judicial ethics requirements.

She criticized Trump's judicial appointments and said she could not presently envision supporting one of his nominees, although she also described evaluating nominees individually.

Tafoya opposed expanding the court.

She said she favored judges who interpret the Constitution according to its text and rejected judicial activism.

Tafoya argued that increasing the number of justices for political purposes would undermine the Court's independence.

Flanagan viewed structural changes as necessary to address concerns about ethics and public confidence in the judiciary.

Their positions matter because the Senate has the authority to confirm Supreme Court justices and other federal judges, making judicial appointments a direct responsibility of the office they are seeking.

Abortion Rights and Federal Legislation

Tafoya described herself as a pro-choice Republican and said she did not intend to change Minnesota's existing abortion protections.

She argued that the Supreme Court's reversal of Roe v. Wade had returned significant authority over abortion policy to the states.

Flanagan challenged whether Tafoya's position was consistent with a letter she had signed addressing Republican delegates and her support for conservative judicial nominees.

Tafoya said she had faced criticism within her party for her position on abortion.

Bakst pressed Tafoya to explain what she meant by reasonable access during the first three months of pregnancy and whether she would support federal restrictions after that period.

She did not identify a specific federal legislative standard.

Flanagan argued that abortion access remained a federal issue because Congress and the courts could affect protections nationwide.

Tafoya's description of herself as pro-choice and her support for preserving Minnesota law did not establish how she would vote on a proposed nationwide abortion restriction.

That question remained unanswered at the conclusion of the exchange.

Artificial Intelligence and Data Centers

Artificial intelligence received attention during the debate's closing portion.

Tafoya emphasized technological innovation and local authority over data-center development.

She argued that communities should decide whether to permit large facilities and negotiate arrangements that serve local interests.

She opposed broad federal mandates governing those local decisions.

Flanagan also emphasized the interests of affected communities but called for stronger federal oversight of artificial intelligence companies.

She proposed establishing an independent regulatory body and placing inspectors within companies to monitor potential risks.

Flanagan argued that AI development presented serious concerns requiring government intervention.

Neither candidate outlined detailed legislation, but their responses indicated different priorities.

Tafoya concentrated on innovation and local decision-making. Flanagan favored a more active federal regulatory role.

Bipartisanship and Political Independence

Tafoya repeatedly challenged Flanagan to identify occasions when she had disagreed with Democratic leaders.

Flanagan cited work with Republicans during her career in child advocacy and in the Minnesota Legislature.

She also identified support for year-round E15 biofuel sales as an issue on which she differed from some members of her party.

Tafoya described herself as willing to work with Democrats and Republicans, particularly on fiscal policy and Social Security.

Both candidates presented bipartisan cooperation as an important qualification for the Senate.

The debate offered examples of their stated intentions and past political relationships, but it did not independently establish how effectively either would negotiate legislation in Washington.

Town Halls and Congressional Term Limits

Bakst asked whether the candidates would commit to holding regular in-person town halls.

Flanagan said she intended to continue traveling throughout Minnesota and meeting constituents, citing the statewide tours she had conducted during the campaign.

Tafoya also committed to town halls and said she would hold as many as constituents wanted.

Neither established a minimum number.

On congressional term limits, Tafoya expressed support for limiting service to two or three terms.

Flanagan opposed term limits, arguing that voters should determine how long elected officials remain in office.

The responses provided a clear difference in how the candidates viewed congressional tenure.

Closing Arguments Focus on Their Opponents' Records

Tafoya closed by arguing that Flanagan's years in Minnesota government had produced insufficient results.

She cited fraud, education, public safety and state finances, telling voters that Flanagan should be held accountable rather than promoted to federal office.

Tafoya promised lower taxes, stronger crime enforcement and greater government accountability.

Flanagan concluded by emphasizing affordability, Medicare for All, universal child care, higher wages and opposition to the Iran war.

She returned to Trump's endorsement of Tafoya and argued that the Republican candidate would support the president's policies in Washington.

Both candidates used their final statements to reinforce arguments they had made throughout the debate rather than introduce new proposals.

What Minnesota Voters Learned

Friday's debate clarified several important policy differences.

Flanagan supports Medicare for All, expanding the Supreme Court, raising Social Security payroll-tax contributions from higher earners, stronger federal regulation of artificial intelligence and replacing ICE with a restructured immigration system.

Tafoya opposes Medicare for All and Supreme Court expansion, supports targeted health care cost reforms, favors using tariffs as a negotiating tool, emphasizes local control of data centers and proposes stronger consequences for fraud.

Both candidates said the war in Iran should end and that Social Security must be protected. Both also supported stronger action against fraud, although they disagreed over enforcement methods and political responsibility.

Some questions remained unresolved.

Tafoya did not identify a specific Social Security financing plan or a clear position on federal abortion restrictions. Flanagan did not provide detailed financing or implementation proposals for Medicare for All or her proposed restructuring of immigration enforcement.

The candidates also presented competing claims about the scale of Minnesota fraud, the effects of federal tax legislation, crime trends, military spending and the costs of their policy proposals.

Those assertions require examination against government records, court documents, independent financial analyses and other evidence. Their appearance in a debate does not make them established facts.

The Final Weeks Before Election Day

With the November 3 election approaching, Minnesota voters have limited time to assess the candidates' records and proposals.

Tafoya faces questions about how her stated independence from Trump would translate into Senate votes, particularly on judicial appointments, immigration enforcement and federal spending.

Flanagan faces continued scrutiny over her role in the Walz administration and whether her federal policy proposals can be implemented within existing budgetary and political constraints.

The debate provided substantial information about their priorities, but it also demonstrated the limits of campaign exchanges as a substitute for detailed policy plans.

Minnesota's next U.S. senator will serve a six-year term and participate in decisions involving federal spending, health care, immigration, foreign policy and judicial appointments.

Friday's debate gave voters a clearer understanding of the candidates' differences. The remaining task is to examine the evidence behind their claims and determine which approach they believe would best serve Minnesota.

text:
On a bright, chilly autumnal morning in Seattle, lawyer Janet Gwilym is taking her two young clients Manon, 10, and her brother EJ, eight, to an immigration appointment at an imposing building.

Later, at her office, the siblings place items into the backpack of a cuddly soft toy – a bunny with fluffy ears, which they are preparing for his court appearance. Manon and EJ are intent on the task at hand – placing slime in the backpack so bunny has something to play with during the long hearing, along with a plastic card, which outlines the children’s rights. The idea is to help the children understand what to expect, so their actual court appearance is less stressful. Later, Janet shows the siblings a model courtroom, with plastic figures representing the immigration judge and the government lawyer. “What’s a hearing?” Manon asks. “Good question,” says Janet, explaining that it is a chance for Manon to have her case heard in front of a judge, who can decide if she may stay in America.

Mount Rainier, the highest peak in Washington state and a symbol of the enormity of the American West, looms large on the horizon above the US citizenship and immigration building. Manon and EJ are not the children’s real names – we used pseudonyms to protect their identities in our report for Noosphere, the independent journalism platform. Both children face the threat of deportation back to Haiti, a country that is so unsafe that the US State Department advises American not to go there – citing gang violence and the threat of kidnapping.

Manon and EJ crossed the border into America by themselves. Their mother left Haiti, fleeing the siblings’ abusive father, and while crossing the notorious Darién Gap – a remote, 60-mile stretch of rainforest, swamp and mountainous terrain between south and north America – she and their older sister disappeared, and are presumed dead. Manon and EJ completed the treacherous journey to America without a parent. Having legal representation can be a matter of life and death for children like Manon and EJ, Janet told me when I interviewed her for Noosphere. Migrant children without lawyers have a less than 1 per cent chance of staying in America.

Donald Trump returned to the White House promising to carry out the largest ever mass deportation campaign – and he pledged to target violent criminals and gang members. Yet, of late, the administration has been speeding up the deportation of an entirely different and less threatening group: unaccompanied migrant children. The number of deportation orders for unaccompanied children rose from 2,000 in January 2025 to 7,300 this July, according the Vera Institute of Justice, a non-profit research group. The question is why this particular group of migrants has become a focus for the White House.

The US Senator Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon, has accused the Trump administration of violating children’s rights and flouting federal law to hit quotas and satisfy their ideological crusade against immigrants. Reporting suggests it is Stephen Miller, the deputy chief of staff at the White House known to be focused on immigration policy, who is leading this drive to accelerate the removal of undocumented immigrant children. “The cruelty is the intent of this,” one source told The Guardian. The Trump administration says it is merely clearing up the mess created by President Joe Biden, who relaxed the pandemic-era rules on children crossing the border, which led to hundreds of thousands of unaccompanied migrant children arriving in America.

In July, after a long-running dispute with the contract provider, the Trump administration cut the federal funding that pays for children like Manon and EJ to have legal representation. Janet, the siblings’ lawyer, is the legal services director for the International Rescue Committee (IRC) in Washington state. She and her colleagues are currently representing 185 unaccompanied migrant children, despite having lost their federal funding. The IRC, founded at the call of the physicist and refugee Albert Einstein, is committed to ensuring these children are represented, for as long as possible. But other groups that lost funding in July have had to stop doing this work – and the Trump administration is now saying government lawyers will represent unaccompanied migrant children. Critics say that’s a clear conflict of interest – children will be in immigration court represented by the government that wants to deport them.

There are more than 24,000 unaccompanied migrant children like Manon and EJ in America who are facing immigration proceedings. The US Congress requires the federal government to provide legal representation for these children, because they are vulnerable and they’re too young to know their rights. But it’s not an absolute legal right – Congress asks the government to represent them “to the greatest extent practicable”. That ambiguity has enabled the Trump administration to cut funding for the network of lawyers like Janet who have years of experience representing these children, give contracts to inexperienced providers, and now come up with the idea of government representation for them. When pressed, the administration says it’s committed to providing legal representation for all “eligible unaccompanied children”.

In addition to the funding cuts for legal representation, court hearings have been sped up – more than 100 children were scheduled to appear in Seattle’s immigration court in a single day recently. Across America, there are reports of unaccompanied children appearing in front of immigration judges without lawyers. It’s a chaotic situation. Many immigration courts don’t allow cameras or reporters, so the true picture is unclear. News organisations have resorted to sending court artists into these immigration courts, who draw images of small children slumped into chairs in front of a judge. Janet says she is afraid that a real humanitarian crisis is coming. “It is already happening,” she told me for Noosphere, “but we will see some horrible outcomes from this if kids do not receive the representation that they need, if we do not follow due process and the rules and laws that we have set up to protect these children.” Janet fears that children will die if they are deported back to unsafe countries.

Where is the outcry, you might ask? The Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement policies and the images of masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents carrying out raids have become so common that migrant children facing deportation is just another headline. The Republican-controlled Congress has chosen to look the other way. Democrats are asking questions but have no powers of oversight, unless they win the House of Representatives in November’s midterm elections – which they are on track to do.

Trump was elected with a mandate to carry out a mass deportation campaign, and he and his top adviser, Miller, are interpreting that to include children who crossed into the US without parents. The Department of Homeland Security is now offering children aged 14 and above $3,000 (£2,250) to self-deport. The administration claims that many children who crossed the border alone during the Biden years were placed with sponsors who were smugglers and sex traffickers, and the aim now is to reunite children with their families. Critics say this is a smokescreen, obscuring the real agenda of deporting vulnerable children as a deterrent to families who might otherwise risk sending their children to the US.

Against this complicated backdrop, Manon and EJ are hoping to be allowed to stay in America. Both children told me how much they enjoyed school, and how about their hopes for the future. Manon wants to be a fashion designer and EJ dreams of being a football player.

Their session on what to expect in immigration court at an end, the children finish packing the bunny’s backpack and put him away, eager to head back to school. The classroom is one of the few places of safety in their uncertain world.

title: Mamdani welcomes court ruling rejecting Trump administration challenge to NYC sanctuary laws
description:
NEW YORK, CMC – New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has welcomed a federal district court’s ruling dismissing a lawsuit brought by the Trump administration challenging the city’s sanctuary laws for Caribbean and other immigrants.
Our local laws make New York City safer.
We will continue to uphold our local laws and use every tool at our disposal to protect New Yorkers from ICE’s abuses.
At a time when federal immigration enforcement is destabilising and separating families and putting communities across the five boroughs at risk, defending these protections has never been more important.
“Today’s ruling is a win for New York City and immigrant New Yorkers.
text:
NEW YORK, CMC – New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has welcomed a federal district court’s ruling dismissing a lawsuit brought by the Trump administration challenging the city’s sanctuary laws for Caribbean and other immigrants.

In his ruling, Judge Ramón Reyes Jr, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, wrote that the Trump administration lacks standing to bring its 2025 lawsuit claiming New York City’s sanctuary laws are pre-empted by federal law.

“This is a victory for New Yorkers and a rebuke to ICE’s (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency) deportation agenda,” Mamdani said.

“The federal government came to court seeking to force New York City to turn its public servants into deportation agents and divert our resources towards carrying out ICE’s cruel agenda. Today, they lost.

“The court made clear that the federal government has no standing to bring this case and cannot commandeer our city workers to do its bidding. Our local laws make New York City safer. They allow us to focus our resources on protecting and serving our communities and ensuring that every New Yorker can turn to their city government without fear that asking for help will make them a target for deportation,” he said.

The mayor said that the federal government wanted to use fear to divide the city, adding: “We will not let them. We will continue to uphold our local laws and use every tool at our disposal to protect New Yorkers from ICE’s abuses.

“Our city belongs to all of us, and we will not abandon our neighbours to satisfy an inhumane, xenophobic agenda,” he said.

New York City Mayor’s Office of Immigrant Affairs Commissioner Faiza N. Ali said that, for decades, New York City’s sanctuary laws have helped build trust between immigrant New Yorkers and their local government.

“These local laws are essential to ensuring that all New Yorkers can access critical public services, including healthcare, housing and public education, without fear. At a time when federal immigration enforcement is destabilising and separating families and putting communities across the five boroughs at risk, defending these protections has never been more important.

“Today’s ruling is a win for New York City and immigrant New Yorkers. It affirms our right to determine how to best use resources to serve and protect our communities. The federal government’s attempt to undermine our laws has been rejected, and we will not back down from our commitment to protecting our immigrant neighbours.”

She said her office would “keep working to ensure immigrant New Yorkers know their rights, can access trusted support and have the opportunity to live with safety and dignity”.

President and Chief Executive Officer of the New York Immigration Coalition (NYIC), Murad Awawdeh, whose organisation represents more than 200 immigrant and refugee groups in New York, hailed Judge Reyes for “upholding our constitutional rights and the state’s rights to pass laws that keep our communities safe”.

Awawdeh said Trump’s lawsuit was “a last-ditch attempt to make an end run around the Tenth Amendment”.

He said neither New York City nor New York State would be bullied by the federal government into giving up their rights and protections.

In his ruling, Judge Reyes wrote that “even if the United States has standing — and it does not — its pre-emption claims fail.

“All of the United States’ pre-emption claims — express, conflict and field — fail because the relevant federal statutes do not regulate private actors,” he said, adding that “there is nothing within federal law that obligates states to participate in federal immigration enforcement or compels states to comply therewith.

“The United States’ pre-emption arguments amount to nothing more than a backdoor around the Tenth Amendment and rest on a false distinction between (a) compelling local governments’ participation in federal immigration enforcement and (b) prohibiting local governments from dictating how their personnel and other resources may be utilised towards federal immigration enforcement,” the judge said.

LOS ANGELES (CNS) -- Thousands of demonstrators are expected to gather in downtown Los Angeles Saturday for a "No Kings" rally and march protesting President Donald Trump's administration, federal immigration enforcement policies and what organizers describe as threats to voting rights ahead of the November midterm elections.

The demonstration is scheduled to begin at 1 p.m. Saturday at Gloria Molina Grand Park, near Los Angeles City Hall at 200 N. Spring St., as part of a nationwide day of protests organized under the No Kings banner.

Organizers expect the march to begin around 2 p.m., with participants following a roughly 1.5-mile route beginning on Spring Street before returning to City Hall. The event is scheduled to conclude around 5 p.m.

The rally, organized by 50501 SoCal in partnership with more than 30 organizations, is among thousands of demonstrations planned across the country Saturday.

Organizers said the Los Angeles event will focus on opposition to federal immigration enforcement actions, concerns about potential election interference and efforts to encourage eligible voters to participate in the upcoming midterm elections.

Scheduled speakers include Assemblyman Isaac Bryan, D-Los Angeles; Jillian Burgos of Housing for All; Ernesto Ayala; Shannon Rivers; Cliff Pinkerton of California Ranked Choice Voting; and Paul Ramirez, founder of Valley Defensa.

A news release also lists Melina Abdullah among the planned speakers and says representatives of Black Lives Matter Grassroots LA are expected to address the crowd.

Musical performances by Izzy T and Shelton, along with a DJ set by Swage, are also planned.

Demonstrators are expected to carry handmade signs and two large balloons depicting Trump, including a 20-foot-tall balloon showing him wearing a diaper and a 15-foot-tall balloon depicting him in a Russian military uniform.

Organizers also plan a land blessing and drum circle by representatives of local Indigenous communities.

"The same administration that invaded our city is now threatening to interfere with our right to vote," Aztlan Tenochtitlan, a spokesperson for 50501 SoCal, said in a statement.

Organizers said the demonstration is intended to build on protests that followed federal immigration raids in Los Angeles and the deployment of National Guard troops and Marines to the region in June 2025.

The rally will also feature voter outreach aimed at helping eligible participants understand their voting options and make plans to cast ballots.

Among the organizations participating in the Los Angeles demonstration are the American Civil Liberties Union of Southern California, Oxfam America, Black Lives Matter Grassroots LA, Public Citizen, Democratic Socialists of America-Los Angeles, Working Families Party and several local immigrant-rights and community groups.

A separate No Kings demonstration is scheduled from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Colorado Boulevard and Fair Oaks Avenue in Pasadena.

Organized by San Gabriel Foothills Indivisible, the Pasadena gathering will also emphasize early voting and opposition to what organizers characterize as authoritarian actions by the Trump administration.

Rep. Judy Chu, D-Pasadena, Sen. Sasha Renee Perez, D-Pasadena and Pasadena City Councilman Rick Cole have been invited to speak at the gathering, according to organizers.

The Pasadena event is also expected to feature homemade signs, costumed performers and short voting-related skits.

Organizers of both demonstrations said they are committed to nonviolent protests.

More information about the downtown Los Angeles event is available at mobilize.us/mobilize/event/900835, while information about the Pasadena gathering is available at sangabrielfoothillsindivisible.org.

Voters are encouraged to register before California's Oct. 19 deadline.

A complete list of events nationally, with further details, can be found at nokings.org.

text:
In two weeks, Donald Trump faces his moment of truth; transformational midterm elections that will drastically influence the rest of his presidency, for better or for worse.

Assuming that he cannot find a way around the constitutional ban on him running for a third time in 2028, he now has a limited time left to make sure he leaves office the most consequential president ever. Again, for better, or worse.

Motivated deeply by fame, that could make for an (even more) volatile ride than we’ve seen so far as his administration enters its final stages.

Whatever happens in the House and Senate elections, he remains commander in chief of the US armed forces with the power to unleash conflict, perhaps with even less restraint than he’s shown in his intemperate and economically reckless decision to go to war against Iran.

So, if in many ways this era has resembled reality TV, the finale is yet to come, and Trump is all about attention grabbing climaxes that both rate and divert attention from his failures.

His administration’s threats to livestream an execution – plans he’s now had to walk back – to shift the focus from Iran, and his betrayal of Ukraine while doing deals with Russia is a new low.

Such barbaric politically motivated “entertainment”, usually confined to the most gruesome of autocracies, announced by former Fox News host, now Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, may be a sign of things to come.

During Trump’s second term, although arguably better organised and deliberate than the first, there have been few limits on his behaviour, surrounded as he has been by yes people.

Having increased his vote in 2024, winning the trifecta of the White House, with majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate, the president has been truly off the leash.

The 3 November midterms, in which all 435 seats in the House and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election, represent a likely turning point.

As in Australia, the issues motivating voters are predominantly hip pocket; cost of living and inflation, along with immigration, datacentres and AI.

And unlike his last presidency, when Trump’s economic performance was viewed positively at a similar point in the term, this time, voters blame his tariffs and war in Iran for high fuel prices and cost of living.

All of this means that the House is highly likely to swing to the Democrats in what may be less a “blue wave” than a “red undertow” and the Senate, while more borderline, may be lost as well. This is less an endorsement of the Democrats than a referendum on Trump, with his popularity at historic lows.

Should it play out that way, Trump will be faced with the prospect of spending his final two years of ultimate power with both hands tied behind his back.

When Obama lost the House amid economic woes in 2010, in what he described as a “shellacking”, and only narrowly held the Senate, it sharply limited his agenda for the rest of his term.

There was legislative gridlock that led to increased use of executive orders that in turn led to a deep split between Congress and the White House with threats of legal action over executive overreach.

Much the same happened after the 2018 midterms when Republicans lost control of the house in the largest Democrat gain since the 1970s but held the Senate.

Having followed Obama’s agenda of hope with his own agenda of disruption, Trump will strongly resist his final years in the White House being thwarted in the same way. And theoretically with no chance of a third term, there’s a high likelihood he will simply bulldoze his way through it with a sense of impunity.

Democrats will need to resist the urge to martyr him a second time with legal action and impeachment if, or when, he starts further stretching the system.

Meanwhile, these changed dynamics have implications for Australia and the rest of the world.

For years, everyone has been dancing around Trump’s unpredictability, his bullying and his threats.

Tariffs have been used as a weapon, war has breached international law, humanitarian aid has been decimated, inclusion and equality have been called “woke”, immigration has been weaponised, human rights have been eroded, and national sovereignty has been ignored.

Australia’s moves to regulate the US tech firms, to take back some control of our own information landscape, are a perfect case study, with concerns that asserting our own data sovereignty could lead to trade retaliation.

Here is an opportunity to reassert our values.

If Trump is a lame duck, surely we can say what we really think?

Since he was first elected in 2016, boundaries have shifted, and that’s enabled some scary behaviour that’s seeped into communities, communication and politics around the world.

Even here, where we have had longstanding bipartisan agreement against the death penalty, the ascendant One Nation supports bringing it back.

Only we can reset the boundaries of political populism.

Perhaps threatening to livestream an execution in front of a firing squad is a red line, or maybe we’ve already crossed it.

text:
A federal officer slammed a vehicle into a Houston construction worker and broke his leg, believing him to be a man who apparently died years ago, the dead man’s family said on Friday, further calling into question the account given by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The worker, 48-year-old Miguel Parra Hernandez of Mexico, remains hospitalized with multiple leg fractures and needs reconstructive ankle surgery, according to FIEL, a Houston-based immigration advocacy group. At a news conference on Friday, the group said the alleged suspect’s family had shared documentation proving his death.

After the episode on 10 October, ICE said in a statement that officers had observed a suspect they were targeting, identified as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, enter a vehicle with Parra Hernandez.

But on Friday, Rafael Lemaitre, spokesperson with the Harris county district attorney’s office, told the Associated Press that Mendoza-Cervantes was not in that vehicle.

ICE did not respond to requests for comment on Friday.

“ICE is lying,” said Cesar Espinosa, FIEL’s executive director. “Either somebody is not telling the truth or all of a sudden these two ICE agents have developed a sixth sense and are able to see dead people.”

ICE released a photo of a man it identified as Mendoza-Cervantes. But the man in the photo is actually Jose Hector Jimenez, who died years ago while being pursued by federal immigration authorities as he was trying to re-enter the US, according to FIEL.

The man’s daughter provided his death certificate from the Mexican government, which has been turned over to the district attorney, Espinosa told the AP. US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) did not respond to a request for comment.

Jimenez’s daughter, Jamie Jimenez, did not respond to requests for comment from the AP. Her husband, Andres Rendon, confirmed to the AP that Jimenez was his wife’s deceased father.

Criminal charges against the ICE officer who drove the vehicle are being considered by Harris county district attorney Sean Teare, who has said surveillance footage contradicts ICE’s claim that Parra Hernandez stepped in front of the vehicle.

The video shows a black SUV speeding over a median and driving toward a man who is running away. The video does not show the car hitting him – that view is blocked by another vehicle – but it shows the SUV inches from the fleeing man. The video then shows him on the ground.

US House member Sylvia Garcia, a Democrat who represents Houston, said that ICE appears to be lying about what happened.

“If ICE was pursuing a man who died years ago, it raises serious questions about how these operations are being carried out and whether agents are even verifying who they’re looking for before putting people’s lives at risk,” Garcia said in a statement to the AP. “It’s outrageous – but frankly, not surprising.”

ICE has been met with nationwide criticism throughout Donald Trump’s second presidency for its aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics.

Just in 2026, the second year since Trump returned to the White House, more than 30 people have died during interactions with immigration officials, the Guardian reported in late September.

Parra Hernandez’s attorney, Kim Bruno, told reporters that her client was suffering from depression in federal custody, especially after learning that he was not the target of the operation.

“This never should have happened in the first place,” Bruno said.

Miguel’s brother, Roberto Parra, said the two would work construction all day together and he just wants his brother treated with humanity. He said Parra Hernandez has a family to support, and his only crime was coming to a country out of necessity.

FIEL is seeking Parra Hernandez’s release before he is moved from a hospital to a federal detention center.

Nidia Delfín, the sister of Luis Enrique Delfín, who was detained in the ICE vehicle that hit Parra Hernandez, called for her brother’s release from federal custody so he could serve as a witness.

“He’s still very concerned, still very afraid,” she said. “He’s not the same guy that was out” before Parra Hernandez was struck on 10 October.

Guardian staff contributed

title: Federal court dismisses suit against New York's sanctuary laws in a loss for Trump administration

Sanctuary laws limit cooperation between local officials and the federal government when it comes to civil immigration enforcement.
New York City has recently been facing increased scrutiny over its sanctuary laws.
The Democratic congressional candidate said the police’s conduct violated “the spirit, if not the letter” of the city’s sanctuary laws.
Still, local immigration advocates are relieved that the federal court stepped in to protect the city’s sanctuary laws.
text:
A federal court dismissed a lawsuit filed by the Trump administration against New York City’s sanctuary laws on Thursday as the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, heralded the loss, saying he would not allow the government to “use fear to divide our city”.

The ruling marks the latest defeat for the federal government, as it sues cities and states over legal protections for immigrants. Federal courts in Los Angeles, Chicago and Minnesota have thrown out similar lawsuits over the last two years.

The US district judge Ramón E Reyes Jr affirmed in Thursday’s ruling that “there is nothing within federal law that obligates states to participate in federal immigration enforcement or compels states to comply”. He argued that the city’s agencies couldn’t be forced into using their resources to enforce civil immigration laws, and rejected the Trump administration’s argument that local officials were illegally obstructing its immigration agenda.

Sanctuary laws limit cooperation between local officials and the federal government when it comes to civil immigration enforcement. In New York City, there are limits on the police department’s ability to hold immigrants for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) through detainer requests, and on general information sharing between the agencies.

Mamdani celebrated the ruling. “The federal government came to court seeking to force New York City to turn its public servants into deportation agents and divert our resources toward carrying out ICE’s cruel agenda,” he said in a statement. “The court made clear that the federal government has no standing to bring this case and cannot commandeer our city workers to do its bidding. Our city belongs to all of us, and we will not abandon our neighbors to satisfy an inhumane, xenophobic agenda.”

The justice department did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but had said in its initial complaint that the New York’s sanctuary policies resulted in criminals being released into the city who should have been held for immigration removal.

New York City has recently been facing increased scrutiny over its sanctuary laws. Earlier this month, an agent with ICE shot 28-year-old Oscar Belgal while he had his child in the back of his car, before the agency detained him.

The NYPD eventually arrived on the scene and was criticized for its heavy-handed response to protests, which included shoving Darializa Avila Chevalier. The Democratic congressional candidate said the police’s conduct violated “the spirit, if not the letter” of the city’s sanctuary laws.

Jessica Tisch, the New York City police commissioner, said during a Thursday press conference that the NYPD was not involved in the federal immigration operation prior to the shooting. Tisch said officers arrived for the purpose of preserving evidence.

While the federal government lost its case in New York City, it has been successfully pushing a major expansion of a program that formalizes relationships between federal immigration enforcement and local police departments. These 287 (g) contracts, as they are known, deputize local officers to enforce federal immigration law. New York City does not have such a contract but the ACLU has tracked the rapid expansion of the program across the country during the second Trump administration.

Still, local immigration advocates are relieved that the federal court stepped in to protect the city’s sanctuary laws. They had explained in an amicus brief in the case that the city’s sanctuary laws serve a key “trust-building function” and encourage immigrants to apply for public benefits, visit hospitals and seek assistance from police without fear of arrest.

They wrote: “The city’s decision not to participate in federal civil immigration enforcement efforts has particular gravity during this administration, which has pursued immigration enforcement on a massive scale in an often lawless, violent and gratuitously cruel manner.”

text:
ICE detainees are asking a federal judge to intervene at the agency's largest detention camp, citing sworn accounts alleging that guards beat people who resisted removal to Mexico and that masked personnel allegedly beat others and ordered them to cross the southern border.

The motion for a preliminary injunction, filed Thursday in federal court in El Paso, Texas, concerns Camp East Montana, a sprawling immigration detention facility at Fort Bliss. The request is backed by declarations from 43 people, including current or former detainees and relatives or friends of those who died, 29 medical records, four government oversight reports and two expert declarations. Plaintiffs argue the conditions amount to unconstitutional punishment under the Fifth Amendment.

One Cuban detainee claimed that guards slammed his head against a wall repeatedly and crushed his testicles after he refused removal to Mexico. Another detainee alleged they were taken toward the southern border, told to “jump over into Mexico," and that masked personnel beat some who refused.

Read More on News

The allegations have not been established by a court. The preliminary-injunction motion presents the plaintiffs' evidence and arguments, and the judge has not ruled that the accusations are true.

An ICE Office of Detention Oversight inspection found a 37.5 percent failure rate in February, including deficiencies involving use of force and restraints, security, sexual abuse and assault prevention, and tuberculosis protocols. Despite that, the inspection gave the facility an "Acceptable/Adequate" rating, according to the filing.

An unannounced follow-up inspection in May found that overall deficiencies had increased from 49 to 52, while "Priority Component Deficiencies" rose from three to 12, according to the motion. Eight were repeat deficiencies. The report listed zero corrective actions, plaintiffs said.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has maintained that allegations concerning the conditions at Camp East Montana are "categorically false," a "smear campaign" and "fearmongering clickbait."

Newsweek has contacted DHS and ICE for comment via email.

Among the supporting evidence filed Thursday is a collection of declarations from detainees, many identified by pseudonyms.

"Isaac," a 43-year-old Cuban man, alleged guards confronted him in September 2025 after he refused removal to Mexico, returning with about 30 others.

"Outside in the hallway, the guards started beating on me," Isaac said in his sworn declaration.

He said guards slammed his head against a wall about 10 times, twisted his ankles and crushed his testicles, leaving him with severe pain that lasted about a month.

When they reached what Isaac understood to be the Mexican side of the border, he said approximately 15 to 20 masked people were there. A guard allegedly told the detainees that because their own countries would not accept them, Mexico was a good option, and that those who refused could instead be sent to "a jail cell in El Salvador or to Africa."

Isaac said he refused and was allowed back on the bus. He said only a Nicaraguan man and another Cuban man returned on the bus with him, while "the rest went to Mexico."

The exhibit also contains an anatomical diagram on which Isaac marked areas where he said guards injured him.

A second Cuban detainee, "Abel," similarly alleged guards beat him after he refused to be cuffed and taken to Mexico. He said he was subsequently transported with about 13 others to the border near Santa Teresa, where masked people were present, and detainees were directed toward a bus bound for Mexico. Abel said only four people returned with him.

Told to ‘Jump’ Into Mexico

Another declaration, from a Cuban detainee identified as "Eduardo," goes further.

Eduardo alleged that on two occasions people working at the facility attempted to remove him to Mexico, despite his being Cuban and never having been there.

He said that during one trip around October 23, 2025, he was transported with 10 Cubans and two Nicaraguans to Santa Teresa. The people who transported the group worked at the detention center, Eduardo said, while masked people were present near the border wall along with one unmasked ICE representative.

"When the guards took us out of the truck, they replaced the metal cuffs with plastic ones and then told us to jump over into Mexico," Eduardo said in the declaration.

He alleged that detained people were warned they could face federal charges and remain in detention if they refused.

"The masked people sometimes beat on people to get them to jump the wall even if they don't want to," Eduardo alleged. "I have seen other people get beaten up and forced to jump."

Eduardo said he refused to cross, although he claimed that "a lot of people" did. The filing does not identify the masked personnel Eduardo described, and his allegation does not by itself establish their agency or employer.

The filings describe alleged beatings extending beyond the Mexico removals. "Eduardo" said guards beat him multiple times after he sought medication, including an October 2025 incident in which he alleged six or seven guards stomped on him while he was cuffed until he lost consciousness. He said another beating after his release from solitary left him bruised and bloody and required a second ambulance trip to a hospital.

"Samuel," a 19-year-old Venezuelan, alleged officers body-slammed and beat him after he turned off a light, breaking a tooth, crushing his testicles, and injuring his ear. He said he lost consciousness and was taken by ambulance to a hospital, and later reported continuing hearing loss and receiving a $1,140 medical bill related to the emergency visit.

The preliminary-injunction motion alleges excessive force was systemic and cites ICE oversight findings that staff lacked training in de-escalation and use-of-force techniques and failed to document uses of force, preserve video and audio evidence, and conduct appropriate after-action reviews.

The motion also cites a detainee death that the El Paso Medical Examiner ruled a homicide caused by"asphyxia due to neck and torso compression," and says government oversight material found evidence connected to the death "was missing or destroyed."

Separately, plaintiffs allege guards fractured named plaintiff Gerald Akari Angye's wrist and spine while he was shackled and not resisting.

"Urgent protection is desperately needed at Camp East Montana," Gerald Akari Angye said in a statement shared with Newsweek, alleging that detainees continue to lack adequate food, water, medicine and recreation. Angye said he would "never be the same" after the violence he alleges he experienced at the hands of guards.

"The inhumane conditions at Camp East Montana seem to be getting worse. No one of good conscience can support what is happening there. I plead with the court to give relief to people held in the horrible Camp East Montana."

text:
LOS ANGELES (CNS) -- Thousands of demonstrators gathered in downtown Los Angeles Saturday for a "No Kings" rally and march protesting President Donald Trump's administration, federal immigration enforcement policies and what organizers describe as threats to voting rights ahead of the November midterm elections.

The demonstration began at around 1 p.m. Saturday at Gloria Molina Grand Park, near Los Angeles City Hall at 200 N. Spring St., as part of a nationwide day of protests organized under the No Kings banner.

A march began about an hour later, with participants following a roughly 1.5-mile route beginning on Spring Street before returning to City Hall. The event is scheduled to conclude around 5 p.m.

The rally, organized by 50501 SoCal in partnership with more than 30 organizations, is among thousands of demonstrations planned across the country Saturday.

Organizers said the Los Angeles event will focus on opposition to federal immigration enforcement actions, concerns about potential election interference and efforts to encourage eligible voters to participate in the upcoming midterm elections.

Scheduled speakers include Assemblyman Isaac Bryan, D-Los Angeles; Jillian Burgos of Housing for All; Ernesto Ayala; Shannon Rivers; Cliff Pinkerton of California Ranked Choice Voting; and Paul Ramirez, founder of Valley Defensa.

A news release also lists Melina Abdullah among the planned speakers and says representatives of Black Lives Matter Grassroots LA are expected to address the crowd.

Musical performances by Izzy T and Shelton, along with a DJ set by Swage, are also planned.

Demonstrators are expected to carry handmade signs and two large balloons depicting Trump, including a 20-foot-tall balloon showing him wearing a diaper and a 15-foot-tall balloon depicting him in a Russian military uniform.

Organizers also plan a land blessing and drum circle by representatives of local Indigenous communities.

"The same administration that invaded our city is now threatening to interfere with our right to vote," Aztlan Tenochtitlan, a spokesperson for 50501 SoCal, said in a statement.

Organizers said the demonstration is intended to build on protests that followed federal immigration raids in Los Angeles and the deployment of National Guard troops and Marines to the region in June 2025.

The rally will also feature voter outreach aimed at helping eligible participants understand their voting options and make plans to cast ballots.

Among the organizations participating in the Los Angeles demonstration are the American Civil Liberties Union of Southern California, Oxfam America, Black Lives Matter Grassroots LA, Public Citizen, Democratic Socialists of America-Los Angeles, Working Families Party and several local immigrant-rights and community groups.

A separate No Kings demonstration is scheduled from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Colorado Boulevard and Fair Oaks Avenue in Pasadena.

Organized by San Gabriel Foothills Indivisible, the Pasadena gathering will also emphasize early voting and opposition to what organizers characterize as authoritarian actions by the Trump administration.

Rep. Judy Chu, D-Pasadena, Sen. Sasha Renee Perez, D-Pasadena and Pasadena City Councilman Rick Cole have been invited to speak at the gathering, according to organizers.

The Pasadena event is also expected to feature homemade signs, costumed performers and short voting-related skits.

Organizers of both demonstrations said they are committed to nonviolent protests.

title: They free immigrants from ICE in hours. S.F. says wait a year. - Mission Local
description:
The delay means Bay Area immigrants will languish in detention because the network cannot meet demand.
The Bay Area Habeas Network, which consists of nine Bay Area legal nonprofits and public defenders’ offices, aims to file emergency habeas corpus petitions for every immigration arrest in the area.
The Bay Area Habeas Network, which has freed at least 49 Bay Area residents arrested by ICE in the last five months, asked San Francisco for $250,000 in August to contribute to this work.
“ICE is weaponizing geography against immigrants,” said Jordan Weiner, an immigration attorney at La Raza Centro Legal and one of the founding members of the Bay Area Habeas Network.
The network has filed 49 petitions total for 57 Bay Area residents since the network began on May 1.
text:
The Bay Area’s network of pro-bono immigration lawyers won’t receive needed city funding to release people from detention until late next year, according to Hillary Ronen, director of La Raza Centro Legal. The delay means Bay Area immigrants will languish in detention because the network cannot meet demand.

The Bay Area Habeas Network, which consists of nine Bay Area legal nonprofits and public defenders’ offices, aims to file emergency habeas corpus petitions for every immigration arrest in the area. Those petitions can quickly release someone from detention, often within hours.

On Tuesday in Santa Rosa, for example, three vehicles surrounded a Mexican-born father and tow-truck driver as he sat in his car in a parking lot. About half-a-dozen masked officers in vests marked “POLICE ICE” exited their cars, drew their guns, pulled him out and handcuffed him, according to his attorney and court filings.

The man was taken to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s San Francisco holding cells at 630 Sansome St., where a group of attorneys filed a habeas petition seeking his release.

A federal judge ordered his release the same day. He is now back home with his 18-year-old daughter and wife, a U.S. citizen.

But those petitions require a team of round-the-clock attorneys to interview immigrants in detention and write legal arguments. They monitor arrests and quickly step in to file petitions.

The Bay Area Habeas Network, which has freed at least 49 Bay Area residents arrested by ICE in the last five months, asked San Francisco for $250,000 in August to contribute to this work.

After inquiries from Mission Local, the mayor’s office said the request will be considered as part of next year’s budget process. But that funding would not arrive until September 2027, said Ronen, the former District 9 supervisor.

“The emergency is now,” she said. “We need to challenge every illegal arrest of our neighbors by ICE, today.”

The demand is significant: 116 habeas petitions have been filed in San Francisco’s Northern District court between the start of President Donald Trump’s term and July 1, 2026. But according to federal data from the U.C. Berkeley’s Deportation Data Project, 3,870 immigrants were arrested across 18 major Bay Area cities in that time, meaning thousands likely went without a petition to challenge their detention.

Santa Clara County has already committed $250,000 to hire one more attorney, according to the network. San Francisco’s contribution would also mean an additional lawyer.

San Francisco already funds several nonprofits that are members of the network directly, but not the network itself.

The request comes as immigration arrests surge in other parts of California. Though there has not been a surge locally, arrests across major Bay Area cities rose 81 percent between July 2025 and July 2026, according to a Mission Local analysis of federal data released by U.C. Berkeley.

How does the Habeas Network respond to arrests?

A habeas petition asks a federal judge to decide whether the government is holding someone lawfully. Attorneys argue that ICE arrested people without a warrant, for example, and subsequently win their release from detention.

While winning doesn’t end a person’s immigration case, it does let them fight from home instead of a detention center.

Speed is everything when it comes to filing habeas petitions: If a petition is not submitted quickly, ICE can move a detainee out of Northern California. Once that happens, a petition can no longer be filed in San Francisco’s federal court.

“ICE is weaponizing geography against immigrants,” said Jordan Weiner, an immigration attorney at La Raza Centro Legal and one of the founding members of the Bay Area Habeas Network.

One immigrant with pre-existing medical conditions was arrested near the Highland Hospital in Oakland, for example, and lawyers were unable to find him in the ICE locator before he was transferred to Texas and then deported.

When someone calls one of the regional Rapid Response Networks to report an arrest, the network sends an attorney to the San Francisco ICE field office. The attorney then interviews the detained person and gathers facts about their case.

Meredith Sullivan, an attorney with Centro Legal de La Raza in Oakland, spent last Tuesday on the sixth floor of that office sitting across a glass wall from her clients and interviewing them, including the tow-truck driver from Mexico.

“It’s very sobering, and it’s extremely unfair. You’re trying to get as much info as possible with a time crunch,” she said.

Sullivan then shared those facts with the network of attorneys, who wrote up a habeas petition with a legal argument pushing for release. Once the petition is filed, a federal judge reviews it and, if they accept it, orders the immigrant released, usually within hours.

The network has filed 49 petitions total for 57 Bay Area residents since the network began on May 1. Over 90 percent of them were ordered immediately released, according to materials shared by the creators of the network.

“If we didn’t get to these individuals, then they would be in a detention center in the middle of a desert, or deported to a third country,” Ronen said.

The network says it needs more funding

Ali Saidi, who leads immigration work at the Contra Costa County Public Defender’s Office, said the network does not have the lawyers to meet demand. The attorneys writing habeas petitions need to be “cranking out a complex legal motion” and cannot also be at the court gathering facts.

“We’re not able to cover them all,” said Jennifer Noris, an immigration defense attorney in the same office.

Ronen said she met with Supervisor Jackie Fielder’s office, the Office of Civic Engagement and Immigrant Affairs and Mayor Daniel Lurie’s office on Aug. 26 to make the request.

Ronen said the city’s contribution would likely come as a budget supplemental, a one-time bucket of funding that must be approved by the Board of Supervisors.

City staff was receptive, Ronen said, but she heard nothing until Oct. 15, after Mission Local inquired about the funding. The mayor’s office then said it would consider it, but only next year.

What the network truly needs, said Shira Levine, co-founder of the network and former immigration judge, is a regional response. Santa Clara has funding through June 2027 at least, and San Mateo has almost finalized its own contract. Napa and Sonoma counties both made “soft commitments,” according to the network.

But “were there to be greater levels of enforcement,” as threatened last year during President Trump’s aborted immigration surge in October, the network would be critical, Levine said.

“It’s impossible to flip a switch” and quickly hire the needed lawyers, she added.

text:
BATAVIA, N.Y. — The son of a SUNY Brockport IT worker spoke out after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents took his father into custody Tuesday morning.

German Machado, an IT tech at SUNY Brockport, was arrested by ICE after officials said he overstayed his visa, which allowed him to stay in the United States from August 2016 until February 2017. His son Eduardo Machado told News10NBC’s Erin Mahon that the family came from Venezuela and is seeking political asylum after his mother received threats for her work as a journalist.

“The process takes a very long time. And in that time, you are provided with a work authorization card to legally work and live while the process is ongoing,” Eduardo said.

Eduardo said he and his brother now hold the same work permit as their father and both have entered the workforce. “It’s nothing different from an American. I, they asked me for my social security number, which I have. They ask for a document from the federal government that states that you are allowed to work with — which is that work authorization card. And then your background check. Just like any other American,” Eduardo said.

Eduardo said the family is afraid but believes they deserve due process. “Because we are doing the legal process. We came the right way. We came legally. We are here legally, with documents from USCIS, the federal government that allow us to be here while our case is in process,” Eduardo said.

Eduardo’s brother Sam said the family filed their asylum and withholding removal application in September 2016, before their initial visas expired the following February. Since then, their application status remained pending, and they had not yet received a hearing date. ICE officials said that work authorization or a pending application does not confer legal status.

“We’ve been following every recommendation,” Sam said. “We’re grateful to the United States for the opportunity to seek asylum, and still trust the legal process while waiting for a determination,” he continued.

The family said they have only heard from German once since his arrest, during a brief phone call just after 9 a.m. Tuesday when he arrived at the detention facility. He called his wife to confirm that ICE arrested him, and that he was taken to the detention center in Batavia. The family has not received updates regarding the next step in his legal proceedings.

In the last year, ICE arrested five other SUNY employees and a University of Buffalo researcher. SUNY employees included Yan Vazquez Hidalgo, Alex Ramirez Gonzalez, Mohamed Fofana, Dane Ka and Ibrahim Halil Topkaya. All of the SUNY employees, with the exception of Topkaya, and the UB researcher, Dr. Shovgi Huseynov, were released.

News10NBC will continue to follow developments in this case.
