text:
EL PASO, Texas – Legal organizations filed a motion for preliminary injunction demanding ICE provide adequate healthcare and improve conditions for people detained at Camp East Montana, the nation’s largest immigration detention facility located on the Fort Bliss military base in El Paso, Texas. The motion comes as ICE is on track to have its deadliest fiscal year on record, as deaths in detention have nearly doubled since last fall, including three deaths at Camp East Montana alone.

The motion, which was supported by more than 40 declarations from people currently or formerly detained at Camp East Montana, loved ones of people who have died, and correctional and medical experts, describes the government's systemic failure to provide adequate medical care and humane living conditions. The conditions reported include medical neglect, unsanitary and unsafe conditions, confinement to windowless tents for 23 to 24 hours a day, barriers to legal counsel, and such little food that people experience substantial weight loss and other serious medical conditions. People detained at the facility also describe being physically beaten by guards and confined in extreme isolation as punishment for seeking help.

“The conditions reported in those declarations shock the conscience,” Dean Williams, a former state prison director who evaluated the conditions in Camp East Montana, wrote in support of the motion. “People describe degrading, unsafe, and unsanitary conditions, abuse by guards, and extreme restrictions and harsh treatment far beyond those of the most secure prisons I have overseen.”

In May of 2026, the American Civil Liberties Union, ACLU of Texas, Texas Civil Rights Project, and Farella Braun + Martel LLP filed their lawsuit against ICE after the federal government began detaining thousands of people in a tent encampment on the Fort Bliss military base in the El Paso desert. The facility has repeatedly come under fire since its opening in August 2025 following rampant reports of abusive, inhumane, and deadly conditions.

Quotes from named plaintiffs in the lawsuit are as follows:

“Urgent protection is desperately needed at Camp East Montana,” said named plaintiff Gerald Akari Angye. “Today, people are still being detained in this windowless camp with inadequate food, water, medicine, and recreation. People with health issues do not receive the care they need. This case remains important to me because I am a voice for those harmed by this regime. I will never be the same after the violence I experienced by guards at Camp East Montana. Many others are still being held in those horrible conditions. The United States preaches democracy and human rights, but it is separating families and torturing people who are seeking safety. The world is watching. The inhumane conditions at Camp East Montana seem to be getting worse. No one of good conscience can support what is happening there. I plead with the court to give relief to people held in the horrible Camp East Montana.”

“It’s hard for outside observers to understand what people go through at Camp East Montana,” said named plaintiff Navdeep. “That’s why we are sharing our stories. I don’t want people to continue suffering and experiencing the terrible conditions I experienced there. We need the court to take action to immediately improve conditions at Camp East Montana and to prevent additional suffering.”

“Camp East Montana is not built to accommodate the basic needs of people,” said named plaintiff ZOR. “If the court fails to intervene, things may get even worse. If nothing is done, I worry it will be a signal that it is okay that for the law to continue being ignored at Camp East Montana. I believe the conditions at Camp East Montana are meant to break people down emotionally and to punish them so they become desperate to leave. It is unbearable to be mistreated every day and trapped in a dirty room with up to 72 people. Many of us are only able to endure it because of the strength we get from the thought of our families.”

Additional quotes from co-counsel are as follows:

“We cannot wait any longer,” said Rita Lomio, Senior Counsel at the ACLU’s National Prison Project. “ICE and the Department of Defense have long known of the cruel and deadly conditions at the tent encampment on the Fort Bliss military base. They have demonstrated time and again that they cannot or will not act to end the abuse. Former prison and jail directors have found that conditions at Camp East Montana are unprecedented and make all who live and work at the encampment unsafe. While litigation continues, a preliminary injunction is needed to end the most egregious abuses before more people needlessly suffer and die.”

"The need for court-ordered relief is urgent," said Savannah Kumar, staff attorney at the ACLU of Texas. “For the past year, the government has disappeared thousands of people into its desert camp that has been the site of beatings by guards, death, disease, and hunger. The situation has continued to deteriorate. People held inside tents describe the denial of desperately needed medical care, environmental hazards, and filthy conditions. These unbearable conditions violate U.S. law and erode the moral fabric of our country. A preliminary injunction is necessary to prevent additional death and abuses at the largest immigration detention camp in the country. All of us, no matter where we were born, are created equal and are entitled to dignity that is being systematically denied at this horrific tent camp.”

“State-sanctioned violence is occurring in and outside of facilities like Camp East Montana, and the blatant disregard for human life and access to basic health care should shock the conscience of every American,” said Rochelle Garza, President of the Texas Civil Rights Project. “If we, as a society, say nothing and go along with the notion that certain lives matter less than others, the government’s abuse and neglect will continue to be normalized. Our preliminary injunction is an effort to stop ICE, and the harm that has seeped into the walls of their detention facilities, from going unchecked.”

“Detention does not strip individuals of their fundamental rights to safety, dignity, and necessary medical care,” said Cynthia Castillo, partner at Farella Braun + Martel LLP. “The record in this case shows deeply troubling medical neglect, dangerous living conditions, and mistreatment that demand immediate action. A preliminary injunction is essential to prevent further irreparable harm and to ensure that individuals detained at Camp East Montana are treated humanely while their legal claims are heard.”

description:

text:
AMY GOODMAN: U.S. immigration officials are facing new accusations of misleading local authorities about their activities in New Jersey. Earlier this week, ICE confirmed it had secretly used a federal government warehouse in Roxbury, New Jersey, to stage and process detained individuals in September. The Trump administration says the processing was done in the warehouse parking lot, but not inside the building. This was despite an order from a judge barring the site’s use for immigration enforcement action until an environmental study was finished.

Early this year, the Department of Homeland Security spent nearly a billion dollars to purchase the Roxbury warehouse and 10 others, with plans to convert them into ICE jails. After DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin replaced Kristi Noem and pledged a lower-profile style of enforcement, DHS announced it would sell several of the warehouses, but not the one in Roxbury. Roxbury is located about 35 miles northwest of the notorious ICE jail Delaney Hall in Newark, which has been the site of months of protests.

We go now to New Jersey to speak with Democratic Congresswoman Analilia Mejía.

Congressmember Mejía, thank you so much for being with us. You have exposed this story. What exactly is going on?

REP. ANALILIA MEJÍA: Well, thank you. Thank you. And first, let me say my heart breaks for the families mourning their children to such senseless violence in Oregon. It is heartbreaking and yet another reason why commonsense gun control is needed across our country. And hopefully, new momentum will take shape in the 120th.

Now, I’ll say, you know, this is not surprising to catch ICE and DHS essentially trying to skirt or cherry-pick which laws they actually adhere to. What is surprising is that they would finally tell on themselves. For some time, there has been escalated activity, ICE activity, terrorizing communities across my district, across New Jersey, across the country. Many activists, organizers, community members noted that they saw, they believed that there was activity happening at Roxbury despite a court order, and, thankfully, engaged with my office, other members of the New Jersey delegation, and we have persisted in trying to uncover the truth. We’re going to continue, because, again, ICE and this administration cherry-picks which laws it adheres to, and then breaks due process and equal protection for the many.

AMY GOODMAN: Can you explain more in detail what the laws are that are broken here and the significance of the amount of money that DHS spent buying this warehouse in Roxbury, New Jersey, as well as others around the country, and what they’re doing with them now?

REP. ANALILIA MEJÍA: Well, in the late spring, after ICE disclosed that they — their intention around this warehouse facility, New Jersey stepped in. And a court deemed, a court upheld a — issued an order stating that ICE may not use the facility at Roxbury as a detention center. They may not process individuals there. They may not house individuals there. And apparently, what has happened, on at least two occasions, ICE agents did go to this site, did take individuals there. They say that they processed several individuals on those two occasions. And then, when a Newark field office director found out that they were, in effect, in violation of the law, told them that they had to cease and desist.

But again, what this points to is an inability by ICE to adhere to court orders, an inability by ICE to be transparent, because community members and the state and my office, on multiple occasions, asked whether or not this site was being utilized. Finally, they have confessed that they are — they have been using this site. But again, the trust is broken with this agency, and it is exactly why we need to abolish and replace ICE. We need comprehensive immigration reform. The American people do not want chaos and violence, which is what this administration has brought to our streets.

AMY GOODMAN: Can you also talk about Delaney Hall in New Jersey, in Newark? You confronted DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin in June about Delaney Hall, describing what you called medical abuse, which included sporadic insulin, abuse of pregnant women, withholding blood pressure and other medication. Can you talk about what he said and what information you’ve gathered at this point?

REP. ANALILIA MEJÍA: Well, sadly, sadly, we gained very little information, because, again, this administration and across the board have been stonewalling both members of Congress, community members, refusing to answer questions about how, actually — how are they upholding, one, international law, our own Constitution, making sure that people who are in their custody are in fact kept healthy and safe.

We have to remember that this administration, in many ways, moved the goalpost. They took individuals who had temporary protective status and moved them from legal to illegal. They have slowed down the DACA process, again moving people from on the right side of the law, putting them on the other side of the law. And then, when you’re captured, even when you are trying to adhere to the law and follow the process for an asylum application or an immigration court, what we are finding is that these agents are violently taking people, turning their guns on people, and then housing them in prison-like conditions.

I have gone to Delaney Hall and the Elizabeth Detention Center on multiple occasions. And on multiple occasions — in fact, on every single occasion, I have encountered people who have complained that they have chronic health conditions, but they’re not receiving the medication that they’re required to take, that they have been prescribed by their doctors, that upon entering the facilities, their medications are often changed, or they’re given a handful of pills that they can’t identify. I’ve met individuals who, as you said, are pregnant and not receiving prenatal care that is required, including people with preexisting conditions and pregnancy, which, combined, make their pregnancies more vulnerable, are not given the care that they deserve.

Again, these are individuals that are not the worst of the worst, as Donald Trump tried to portray. These are gardeners and grandmothers. These are young people and women, mothers, fathers, individuals who have been trying to adhere to the law, who would like to be able to have due process and their day in court. But, unfortunately, this administration is just moving with a level of impunity and cruelty that, frankly, should shock every single American.

AMY GOODMAN: You have, as we wrap up, the New Jersey Attorney General’s Office saying it’s carefully reviewing reports of ICE activity at the Roxbury warehouse. Have you received an update on this? And GEO Group’s CEO told investors about the bed and facility expansion on an earnings call, not to Congress, not to the public. Can you talk about the significance of this being exposed by a private company —

REP. ANALILIA MEJÍA: Exactly.

AMY GOODMAN: — and not by the Department of Homeland Security?

REP. ANALILIA MEJÍA: Exactly. Now, this exposes what is actually underneath Trump’s ramp-up on immigration enforcement. Many Americans may not know that, essentially, two corporations own the majority or oversee the majority of detention centers in this country: CoreCivic and GEO Group. This is a massive, multimillion-dollar, if not billion-dollar, industry. In fact, GEO Group had a massive contract with our government in order to house as many undocumented people or process as many people as possible. I believe that this is the reason why you have individuals who, even when they’ve signed their own self-deportation orders, are held for months, because, again, every bed that is filled is an increase to that stock price and to someone’s bottom dollar.

But we have two corporations profiting from cruelty, and an administration that is willing, obviously, to take — to have this insider game in order to benefit those who are closely connected to this administration, at the expense of everyone. Again, the American people need to remember that it is your tax dollars that are paying CoreCivic and GEO Group to, in effect, mistreat people.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to thank you for being with us, Democratic Congressmember Analilia Mejía, representing New Jersey’s 11th Congressional District.

Coming up, Estrella: Bittersweet Freedom for a “Bad Mexican.” We’ll speak with Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Maria Hinojosa, out with a new documentary tracking the story of a trans woman who was jailed for almost a decade in Texas in a men’s prison, then deported. Stay with us.

title: Advocacy groups accuse Trump administration of fast-tracking migrant children's asylum cases
description:
Immigrant advocacy groups representing migrant children have sued the Trump administration to stop what they call a “cruel and unlawful scheme” to fast-track migrant children’s asylum cases.
The groups said unaccompanied children are facing rushed hearings, difficulty finding lawyers, and accelerated removal orders, including in cases involving alleged human trafficking and threats of violence.
The suit comes two days after the Department of Homeland Security announced it was offering unaccompanied migrant children $3,000 to self-deport, a $500 increase over last year’s incentive.
Earlier this month, the federal government quietly assembled a team of government attorneys to represent migrant children in court after the administration cut ties with a number of immigration advocacy groups that had previously provided those services.

text:
Immigrant advocacy groups representing migrant children have sued the Trump administration to stop what they call a “cruel and unlawful scheme” to fast-track migrant children’s asylum cases.

In a complaint filed Thursday night, the groups allege that new government policies have transformed the asylum process for migrant children into a “deportation assembly line depriving them of their rights.”

The lawsuit comes as immigration attorneys and advocates say unaccompanied migrant children are being rushed through the immigration system and that their deportations have been accelerated as part of the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown.

“A system that moves faster and that is by design made so that children are unable to access lawyers and are railroaded into deportation orders is not justice. It’s assembly line deportation of the most vulnerable among us,” said Lindsay Toczylowski, co-founder of the Immigrant Defenders Law Center, during a press call.

The groups said unaccompanied children are facing rushed hearings, difficulty finding lawyers, and accelerated removal orders, including in cases involving alleged human trafficking and threats of violence.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News.

In the suit, the groups said that U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has changed practices through a series of recent policy shifts that include reducing notice times for asylum interviews — in some cases proving less than 24 hours’ notice.

In the complaint, the groups also said that the Department of Justice has instructed immigration judges to complete all removal proceedings for detained unaccompanied children by Jan. 31, 2027. To meet the deadline, the groups allege that immigration judges are refusing to grant continuances of longer than three weeks.

“This push isn’t coming from just one agency. It’s a coordinated whole-of-government operation that abandons due process and child safety in service of faster removals,” said Jason Boyd, vice president for federal policy at the advocacy group Kids in Need of Defense.

The suit comes two days after the Department of Homeland Security announced it was offering unaccompanied migrant children $3,000 to self-deport, a $500 increase over last year’s incentive.

Earlier this month, the federal government quietly assembled a team of government attorneys to represent migrant children in court after the administration cut ties with a number of immigration advocacy groups that had previously provided those services.

Immigration advocacy groups have raised concerns about the initiative, arguing that the same government seeking to deport the minors should not be representing them in court.

title: Chicago-Area Cops Helped HSI Spy on Minnesota Anti-ICE Activists | WIRED
description:
The task force was made up of 14 law enforcement officers—six local cops and eight HSI Chicago agents.
Since Operation Midway Blitz in Illinois last autumn, residents in Chicago and surrounding communities have pressed elected officials for answers about cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE.
While Illinois state law prevents local law enforcement from participating in immigration enforcement operations, criminal investigations by HSI appear to fall outside those restrictions because they pertain to ICE’s other law enforcement functions.
The HSI Chicago surveillance team logged 219 vehicles parked in the vicinity of Co-Prosperity.
All information obtained during the April investigation in Chicago was shared with HSI St. Paul/Minnesota, according to the agency’s report.
text:
Chicago-area law enforcement officers took part in an undercover probe by Immigration and Customs Enforcement into Minneapolis mutual aid networks last spring as part of the feds’ conspiracy investigation into 15 Twin Cities activists facing federal felony charges for resisting Operation Metro Surge, according to newly released documents reviewed by WIRED.

An April report by ICE’s investigations wing, Homeland Security Investigations, titled “Antifa Roadshow,” details in-person and electronic surveillance by a joint task force of an April 2 talk. The task force was made up of 14 law enforcement officers—six local cops and eight HSI Chicago agents. The talk included self-described anarchists in Minnesota who spoke about their organizing experiences during the three-month immigration surge, which resulted in the killings of two US citizens.

The document, released by the 15 Minnesota activists’ defense team as part of the ongoing federal case against them, exposes close cooperation between local police, sheriffs, and HSI agents on a prosecution that critics say crosses the line into political repression. The Chicago HSI task force, which included officers from Chicago, Aurora, Downer’s Grove, Cook County, and Kane County, used two undercover agents, unspecified electronic surveillance, audio recordings, license-plate-reader data, and surveillance cameras from Chicago’s sprawling CCTV network to identify the April 2 event’s attendees and build connections to other anti-ICE protests in Illinois and other states.

Records produced by the Kane County Sheriff’s office show the unit in question is the Chicago-area Homeland Security Investigations Task Force. Local cops who join the unit are accepted on either a full- or part-time basis for two years, with the sign-off of their superiors.

Since Operation Midway Blitz in Illinois last autumn, residents in Chicago and surrounding communities have pressed elected officials for answers about cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE. While Illinois state law prevents local law enforcement from participating in immigration enforcement operations, criminal investigations by HSI appear to fall outside those restrictions because they pertain to ICE’s other law enforcement functions.

Chicago police have substantial approval requirements for surveilling and infiltrating protests or public gatherings, per a 2017 departmental order. It is unclear how these regulations apply to Chicago Police Department agents participating in joint task forces with federal agencies.

In response to questions from WIRED, the CPD claims that no First Amendment notifications to CPD’s chain of command or the department’s general counsel were made for the April 2 investigation, and says its work with HSI is permitted under Illinois law because it pertained to criminal enforcement, not immigration. A source with knowledge of the matter stated that CPD believed the early April surveillance operation was in service of a federal racketeering investigation. The only financial element mentioned in the report is a GoFundMe account to support the Crimethinc speaking tour. There is no mention of funds solicited or received at the April 2 event.

The Chicago Mayor’s Office did not provide comment ahead of publication. In response to queries from WIRED, ICE would neither confirm nor deny details of past or present investigations and said individual agents are not authorized to speak to the media.

HSI is also emerging as the point agency for Trump’s war on internal dissent and opposition politicians: Its agents, not the FBI, conducted the Minnesota 15 investigation and served a search warrant earlier this month on congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.

The targeted April 2 event was held at Co-Prosperity, a Leftist gallery in the Southside Chicago neighborhood of Bridgeport. Several speakers from the Twin Cities area attended the event to share information about resisting federal immigration surges. This was part of a national tour last spring that was organized by the longtime anarchist collective Crimethinc, whose meetings have been infiltrated by federal informants repeatedly over the decades and contributed to the convictions of Eric McDavid, as well as 2008 Republican National Convention protester Matthew DePalma.

Per the four-page HSI report, a plainclothes cop from suburban Aurora was dropped off at the Co-Prosperity event by Officer Mike Xu from the wealthy village of Downers Grove; HSI undercover agent #9147 walked in five minutes later, once the undercover cop from Aurora confirmed no security checks were done at the door.

The undercover HSI agent transmitted a live recording of the event to the rest of the surveillance team for an hour, until transmission was lost. The recordings of the incident were uploaded and shared with HSI agent Kenneth Popovits, a financial crimes investigations supervisor who was working on a temporary assignment in Minneapolis.

Remarks by defendant Callum Robinet from the April 2 talk in Bridgeport about building rapid-response networks are included in the federal conspiracy indictment brought against the Minnesota 15, implicating the Chicagoland law enforcement that participated in surveillance in the controversial prosecution.

The Aurora Police Department, Downer’s Grove Police Department, and Kane County Sheriff did not respond to requests for comment.

The HSI Chicago surveillance team logged 219 vehicles parked in the vicinity of Co-Prosperity. Several subjects already under investigation, including some of the speakers on the tour, were identified by ICE. Ryan Wasson, a Kane County Sheriff’s deputy, spotted a hooded, masked man outside the venue removing an object from his trunk. Running the license plate, Wasson identified the man as the subject of an October 4 arrest during Operation Midway Blitz whose prosecution had been declined by assistant US attorney Christopher Veatch.

Outside the venue, agents Joel Sullivan and Michael Finerty spotted an unnamed subject already under investigation for running “an anti-ICE Signal chat and group called ‘ICE Cream Patrol’” and noted an orange Hyundai had been documented near two March 2026 protests outside the ICE detention center in Broadview, Illinois. The surveillance lasted for roughly two hours until 8:30 pm local time on April 2.

Nick Nunez, a veteran Chicago Police detective detailed to the joint task force, filed a request to obtain surveillance footage from a CPD camera outside the venue; the request would take a week to complete, and it is unclear whether he received footage. All information obtained during the April investigation in Chicago was shared with HSI St. Paul/Minnesota, according to the agency’s report.

Ed Yohnka, a spokesman for the American Civil Liberties Union of Illinois, calls the surveillance of the Bridgeport gathering “very troubling,” adding that local law enforcement should make a full accounting of their role in the incident and participation in joint task forces with federal agencies.

“No one should be subjected to surveillance and infiltration by law enforcement simply for engaging in constitutionally protected activity, including the ability to gather together and express dissatisfaction with public policy,” Yohnka says. “It is also a moment for local law enforcement to reexamine their participation in task forces with the Trump administration, especially any group focused on combatting ‘terrorism.’”

The April 2 meeting in Bridgeport is not the only out-of-state gathering spied upon by HSI during the Minnesota 15 investigation. Reports obtained by defense attorneys through discovery show that events on the same Crimethinc tour in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and Seattle, Washington, were monitored in person by local HSI agents, who reported the speech’s contents back to their colleagues in Minneapolis.

text:
Seven recommendations were proposed to CBP and ICE on body-worn camera program management

DHS backed six of the recommendations but rejected automated camera activation at ICE

CBP had about 11,500 cameras in use as of June 2026, while ICE had about 4,800 as of April

The Government Accountability Office has issued seven recommendations calling on U.S. Customs and Border Protection and Immigration and Customs Enforcement to refresh outdated plans for their body-worn camera programs, adopt metrics that gauge results and give field offices clear rules on when to record.

The Department of Homeland Security concurred with six of the recommendations but declined to adopt automated camera activation at ICE. GAO stood by the proposal, saying extra safeguards would bolster compliance with ICE rules.

The watchdog’s recommendations come as DHS continues to assess its technology capabilities. The Potomac Officers Club’s 2026 Homeland Security Summit on Nov. 10 will bring DHS leaders and industry together to discuss the department’s strategic priorities. Register today to hear from agency decision-makers through keynotes, panels and Q&A sessions.

Why Do CBP and ICE Need New Camera Program Plans?

CBP started fielding cameras in fiscal 2021, and ICE followed in fiscal 2024. As of June 2026, CBP had roughly 11,500 devices in use, nearly all with Border Patrol. ICE had about 4,800 as of April, split almost equally between Enforcement and Removal Operations and Homeland Security Investigations.

Both agencies drafted initial plans with core program management elements, but CBP has not revised its version since 2022 and ICE since 2024. Auditors said the documents miss major shifts, including larger deployment targets and a 2025 halt on further rollouts. GAO wants the plans aligned with current cost and schedule requirements and backed by contingencies for present risks.

Why Does GAO Want Body-Worn Camera Performance Measures?

CBP and ICE cite aims such as improving public trust, transparency, accountability and officer safety, and each tracks some data on device availability and reliability. Neither has set results-oriented goals to show whether the programs deliver on those aims. GAO said possible metrics could examine how footage factors into use-of-force investigations.

What Gaps Did GAO Find in Camera Oversight and Field Guidance?

Both agencies maintain policies on camera use and footage handling, supported by supervisory checks and monthly reviews that verify recordings are labeled correctly. GAO said controls such as triggering cameras automatically when emergency lights switch on would better ensure ICE officers record as required.

Most CBP and ICE offices also lack instructions tailored to their missions, which auditors said raises the risk of improper camera use. GAO directed CBP to ensure Border Patrol, the Office of Field Operations, Air and Marine Operations and the Office of Professional Responsibility each issue such guidance.

text:
Democratic incumbent U.S. Rep. Veronica Escobar is seeking a fifth term this November, facing Republican challenger Adam Bauman, a Navy veteran and former Border Patrol agent.

Escobar, 57, was unopposed in the March Democratic primary, while Bauman, 50, defeated former district court Judge Manuel J. Barraza in the Republican primary runoffs in May.

In his first run for public office, Bauman was among seven candidates who sought the GOP nomination for the congressional seat that represents most of El Paso County – with the exception of some portions of the Lower Valley and East Montana that fall under District 23.

A Republican has been elected only once to the congressional district – Ed Foreman in 1962.

Adam Bauman

Bauman didn’t respond to requests for an interview with El Paso Matters and did not submit a candidate questionnaire to the news organization.

On a podcast last year, he said he was born in Phoenix and came to El Paso in 2001 when he was stationed here with the Border Patrol.

In an interview with KTSM Channel 9 this week, Bauman cited lowering property taxes as one of his priorities, acknowledging that those are set by local governments and not under the purview of Congress. He said, however, that he’d ensure federal dollars allocated to local entities are “appropriated correctly.”

Bauman on his campaign website or social media pages has not offered specific plans on how we would address rising property taxes.

ELECTION 2026 VOTER GUIDE: Everything you need to know about the Nov. 3 general elections in El Paso

On immigration, Bauman told KTSM that while there’s a need for legal immigration, the federal government’s current deportation methods are merely “enforcing the laws that are on the books.” He said Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents are doing “the best they can to deal with the criminal illegal aliens that are present currently” and should be commended for doing their jobs.

The federal government is facing numerous lawsuits challenging the Trump administration’s immigration policies, many arguing some such as prolonged detention without a bond hearing violate the constitution.

Bauman has said he’d support three-term limits for members of Congress, who don’t currently have any term restrictions.

U.S. representatives serve two-year terms and are paid $174,000 a year.

Veronica Escobar

A former English teacher and county judge, Escobar was first elected to Congress in 2018.

She cites affordability as one of her top priorities, saying the economy is “working against too many Americans and in favor of the wealthiest individuals and corporations.”

She said the federal tax code needs to be reformed so the wealthy pay their fair share and loopholes that allow corporations, including data centers, to benefit from massive tax breaks should be closed.

The focus in Congress, she said, should be on investing in programs families depend on, including expanded healthcare access, universal prekindergarten, child care subsidies, increased Pell grants, student loan forgiveness and protections for Social Security and Medicare.

“We also need to clean up Washington and restore public trust,” she said, adding that the Trump administration’s corruption and the ethical concerns surrounding the president, his family and Cabinet officials have been deeply troubling.

Trump has retained extensive business interests while serving as president, raising questions about his family’s cryptocurrency ventures, foreign businesses and other financial dealings. Reported pledges to his proposed White House ballroom have also raised ethical concerns.

The administration has denied corruption allegations.

She said she would support Congress banning stock trading by its members — which she says she has never done.

SEE ALSO: Democrat Claudia Ordaz seeks third term as Republican Jesse Romero makes first run for Texas House

Escobar said one of the most divisive issues around the country – and during election season – continues to be immigration.

She said that while Democrats lost ground on the issue of immigration in 2024, she believes the tide has turned against the Trump administration’s hardline policies that have targeted not only people with criminal records but also those with legal status and valid documents.

“The expansive nature of his mass deportation efforts has really shocked the conscience of most Americans,” she said.

But, she added, Democrats also need to avoid swinging too far in the other direction. The previous administration under President Joe Biden saw record numbers of border crossings that strained communities like El Paso and created difficult conditions for migrants and local residents alike, she said.

“There has to be a middle ground, and we cannot return to the policies that enraged Americans when we were seeing up to 10,000 people per day at the border,” she said. “The American people still want secure borders. They still want to make sure that immigrants with criminal histories are not given multiple chances and don’t continue to re-enter the country.”

Escobar introduced the bipartisan Dignity Act in 2023 and again in 2025 alongside Republican U.S. Rep. María Elvira Salazar of Florida. The act provides pathways to legal status for many undocumented immigrants, establishes a family reunification program and enhances border security.

She said she hopes there’s still bipartisan support for the legislation after the midterms, saying more than 100 organizations have signed up to support the bill.

“Families, mixed-status families are begging for action. Industry and corporations are begging for action. Communities and churches are begging for action. The hard part is done. The bill is written,” Escobar said.

SEE ALSO: Texas House District 77 pits incumbent Vince Perez against political newcomer Humberto Perez

Escobar touts several accomplishments in her years in office, including the designation of Castner Range as a national monument in 2023; securing funding for the new $700 million Veterans Affairs clinic under construction in East El Paso, slated to open in late 2028; moving forward planned renovations to the Bridge of the Americas, which are now out to bid; and stopping warehouses in the city of Socorro from being converted into a mega-immigration detention center by the Department of Homeland Security.

“So, every two years, essentially, I’m reapplying for my job, and many of these projects require strong oversight, accountability and transparency,” Escobar said.

She said she’s also helped secure more than $77 million in Community Project Funding

for various El Paso projects since the federal program began in fiscal year 2022, including for senior nutrition programs, water and wastewater infrastructure, the expansion of the Ysleta Port of Entry, and a border health center.

Republican swing and campaign finance

Republicans made some inroads in El Paso County during the 2024 election as part of a national trend of Hispanic voters swinging toward the GOP. Escobar for the first time in her congressional campaigns received less than 60% of the vote that year.

But recent polling of El Paso County adults suggests those gains may have been lost in the wake of President Donald Trump’s politics, particularly when it comes to controversial immigration enforcement tactics.

ANALYSIS: Poll suggests El Paso Republicans are shedding their 2024 gains

Local GOP candidates haven’t reported much in campaign fundraising, and Bauman until this week had not filed finance reports with the Federal Election Commission as he had not met the $5,000 threshold in contributions to file.

His Oct. 15 filing shows he raised about $5,330 in contributions, including $2,700 from his own pocket – among the lowest among major party candidates across the country seeking House seats. He has $2,500 cash on hand, his report shows. However, Bauman only accounts for about $520 of the more than $2,800 he’s spent, listing banners and yard signs as his expenditures.

Escobar reported raising just over $1.02 million in this election cycle and has about $256,600 left in her campaign coffers, according to her Oct. 15 FEC filing.

Her biggest individual donations in this election cycle are from community and business leaders who frequently contribute to local candidates, including $7,000 each from Richard Aguilar, Robert Bowling IV, Miguel Fernandez, Steve Fox, Rick Francis, Lane Gaddy, Patrick Gordon and Ted Houghton, as well as from philanthropist Melinda French Gates.

Among the top political action committees that donated to Escobar are L3Harris Technologies Inc. PAC, Honeywell International PAC, Deloitte PAC, American Federation of Teachers, AFL-CIO Committee on Political Education and Honeywell International PAC, with $10,000 in donations each. Each giving $7,500 were the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees People PAC, American Association for Justice PAC and Elect Democratic Women PAC.

The winner will be sworn into the 120th Congress in early January 2027.

Early voting for the Nov. 3 midterm begins Monday, Oct. 19, and runs through Oct. 30.

text:
Washington — Vice President JD Vance acknowledged Thursday that there are some federal immigration officers "who really screw up" and said the Trump administration has a responsibility to take action against those who do.

Vance sat down with "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil for a one-hour town hall in Michigan, which will air Saturday. Michigan is home to one of the closely watched Senate races between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.

During an exchange about immigration, Vance drew comparisons between law enforcement officers and members of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE.

"Most of them are amazing people who are patriots and they wanna do a good job protecting their country. Sometimes you have some people who make mistakes. Sometimes you have some people who really screw up," Vance said. "And obviously, we have a responsibility to prosecute, investigate when people do screw up."

Dokoupil pressed the vice president on some of those instances, noting that in some cases, "people talk about them before they're investigated," and he asked Vance about the biggest mistakes involving ICE's immigration actions. Vance declined to single out any incidents but said the Trump administration has responded when officers have been accused of misconduct.

"There are a number of cases where we've investigated and either provided further training, or sometimes even provided disciplinary situations within ICE," the vice president said. "We don't always advertise that stuff, as you know, Tony, because we believe that people have to be judged in a court of law and through a normal investigatory process."

Since the Trump administration has ramped up immigration enforcement actions as part of President Trump's immigration crackdown, officers with ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection have come under criticism for their use-of-force practices.

Two Americans, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were shot and killed by immigration authorities during protests in Minnesota earlier this year. The ICE officer who fatally shot Good, Jonathan Ross, was placed on administrative leave shortly after the shooting. In May, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul questioned whether Ross had been reassigned to her state. The Department of Homeland Security declined to say at the time where Ross was working.

No criminal charges have been filed in either case. The Justice Department opened an investigation into Pretti's shooting earlier this year.

There have since been a series of incidents involving immigration officers during targeted enforcement operations.

An ICE officer in May fatally shot a 25-year-old Colombian man in his car in Maine in July, and in September, an immigration officer shot a Venezuelan man in the back in Austin, Texas.

Earlier this month, ICE agents shot a man in New York during a targeted enforcement operation, striking him in the neck. The agents were trying to arrest the man, Oscar Belgal, who is from the Dominican Republic, with a 5-year-old boy in the back seat.

Then, a vehicle driven by ICE agents hit and injured a man near Houston.

Watch CBS News' "Things That Matter: A Town Hall With Vice President JD Vance" on Saturday, Oct. 17 at 8 p.m. ET/PT on the CBS Television Network or stream it on Paramount+. The one-hour special will also be available to watch afterward on CBSNews.com, YouTube and CBS News 24/7.

AUSTIN, TEXAS – On Thursday, October 15th, Congressman Greg Casar (D-Texas), alongside Representatives Bennie G. Thompson (D-Miss.), Ranking Member of the House Committee on Homeland Security, and Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), Ranking Member of the Judiciary Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement, and five other members of Congress held a field hearing to investigate the numerous ICE shootings across Texas, including the recent shooting of Wilber Garcés-Pérez.

Representatives Greg Casar, Bennie G. Thompson, and Pramila Jayapal were joined by Representatives Troy A. Carter, Sr. (LA-02), Lou Correa (CA-46), Lizzie Fletcher (TX-07), Sylvia Garcia (TX-29), and Al Green (TX-09).

The Members of Congress were joined by witnesses Ms. Rachel Reyes, mother of Ruben Ray Martinez, Kristin Etter, Director of Policy & Legal Services at the Texas Immigration Law Council, Carolina Rivera Nelson, Attorney at the ACLU of Texas, and Danny Woodward, Policy Attorney with Texas Civil Rights Project.

“Texas has become the epicenter of Trump’s deadly deportation machine, so we brought Members of Congress from across the country to Austin to see it firsthand,” said Congressman Greg Casar (D-Texas). “ICE shot Wilber Garcés-Pérez, a DoorDash driver and a father, in the back then denied him medical care. They even tried to deport him so he could never speak the truth. Donald Trump’s ICE isn’t going after the worst of the worst — it’s gone after people like Wilber, who have no criminal record. We will fight to hold the perpetrators in this administration accountable, and not provide another dime in funding to this rogue agency.”

“Democrats came to Austin today to demand justice and accountability for Wilber Garcés-Pérez and the others that have been shot by immigration agents in Texas. If Republicans refuse to conduct any oversight of the Trump administration, we must do so in their place,” added Congressman Bennie G. Thompson. “What we heard today was powerful and informative. Make no mistake: we will do everything possible to hold this administration accountable for what it is doing. This violence, lawlessness, and chaos in our communities must end.”

“Twenty-five days ago, ICE agents in Austin, Texas shot Wilber Garcés-Pérez in the back. Instead of taking him to the hospital, they locked him up in a detention center and did not allow him to have surgery for 11 days. This is not the most recent shooting by ICE, and is one of nearly a dozen that we know of since Trump returned to office,” said Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal. “ICE is a lawless, rogue agency that is causing generational trauma in communities across the country. House Democrats today are doing the oversight work that Republicans refuse to do — and we will continue to do everything possible to protect our communities from Trump’s mass deportation agenda.”

“The shooting and medical neglect of Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez follows the many other cases that have become synonymous with cities being swarmed with masked, armed federal agents and the nation’s dangerous descent into tyranny: Renée Nicole Good, Alex Pretti, Johan Sebastian Guerrero, and too many others. No life is meaningless, and each individual assaulted or killed by our immigration system is someone’s child, someone’s sibling, someone’s parent, and they all still belong here with us,” said Congressman Troy A. Carter, Sr. “Unless you’re Native American, we all come from somewhere else. The Trump immigration system is structured and staffed as a deportation machine that violates individuals’ constitutional rights. Democrats will fight for an immigration system that honors our history and sets forth a reasonable, compassionate path to citizenship.”

“President Trump got elected on the promise to go after the “worst of the worst.” Instead, since January, federal immigration agents have detained over 500 U.S. citizens and killed at least three. ICE is arresting people with no criminal record to hit political quotas while cutting training and lowering hiring standards,” said Congressman Lou Correa. “There is an urgent need for major reforms to keep our communities safe from violence. DHS was created to defend Americans against foreign terrorists. Instead, we have permanent residents and American citizens being shot by ICE agents in our streets.”

“In Texas, we have witnessed at least three ICE shootings since this administration began its aggressive, unprecedented enforcement actions,” said Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher. “People across our community in Houston are still reeling from the shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. Just last weekend, ICE agents ran over and gravely injured Miguel Parra Hernandez while pursuing someone else. ICE’s reckless and brutal actions are not only unprecedented, they’re unconstitutional. They are making us less safe, creating fear and danger for immigrants and citizens alike. This Republican-led Congress that has enabled this lawlessness has utterly failed Wilber Garcés-Pérez, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, Ruben Ray Martinez, and so many others. All Americans deserve better from our government, and that is why I joined Congressman Casar, Ranking Member Thompson, Congresswoman Jayapal, and my Democratic colleagues in Austin today to hear from some of the many people impacted, learn more, and demonstrate our commitment to bringing justice, accountability, and change.”

“Trump promised to go after the worst of the worst. But judging by what we’re seeing across Texas and the country, that sounds more like ICE’s recruitment strategy. People are being shot, injured, and killed by federal agents operating without basic law enforcement standards or accountability,” said Congresswoman Sylvia Garcia. “In Houston, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was killed on his way to work. One hundred days later, his family still has no answers. Instead they’ve been met with stonewalling and excuses. These families deserve the truth and justice, and we will not stop fighting until they get both.

“No President is above the law, and no federal agency should be allowed to serve as judge, jury, prosecutor, and executioner while operating with impunity,” said Congressman Al Green. “Under President Trump, ICE has been emboldened to use deadly force against people in our communities while the administration evades transparency and accountability, engaging in a cover-up. These shootings are not isolated incidents. They are part of a deeply troubling pattern of conduct that threatens the constitutional rights and lives of people in this country.”

text:
Oakland County commissioners won't vote on a proposed policy banning federal immigration civil enforcement on county property without a warrant.

A petition to bring a vote failed by 11-7 during the Oakland County Board of Commissioners meeting Thursday, Oct. 15.

The language in the draft specified that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers "shall not be permitted to enter, remain in, or conduct civil immigration enforcement activities" in Oakland County buildings or property like parking lots without a warrant. The policy would prohibit county employees from assisting or cooperating with civil immigration enforcement activities while on county property.

Charlie Cavell, a Democratic county commissioner who represents a south Oakland County district including Berkley and Ferndale, proposed a motion to bring the policy before the board.

“We have not passed legal aid for immigrants. We have not passed food aid to support immigrants … this is the least we can do,” said Cavell.

Bob Hoffman, a Republican commissioner who represents a district in north Oakland County including Holly and Brandon, also supported the discharge petition.

"Illegal immigration is not the cause. It’s the effect of a broken immigration system," Hoffman said. "If the local police departments did some of the things that ICE does, they’d be charged with excessive force and some would be charged with murder."

Several commissioners who are Democrats expressed concerns about the enforceability of the policy.

Tim O'Hara of Rochester who supported the policy banning ICE from operating on county property, admonished the Democratic majority on the board, saying the members "refused to consider the most basic protections for its most vulnerable constituents."

A similar policy banning immigration enforcement on county property had been adopted in nearby Washtenaw County. In August, a federal judge dismissed a federal government challenge to the policy.

title: Harris County DA says witness to ICE auto-pedestrian incident has been relocated by ICE
authors: Kyle McClenagan, Bianca Seward, www.houstonpublicmedia.org, kyle-mcclenagan, bianca-seward
description:
On Oct. 10, an ICE vehicle struck Parra Hernandez after he exited a vehicle following a pursuit on Clay Road in northwest Houston.
He was the passenger of the vehicle ICE had been pursuing, according to DHS.
FIEL Houston, a local civil rights organization, said Friday it had been contacted by the daughter of the man ICE was allegedly searching for the day Parra-Hernandez was struck by an ICE vehicle.
According to FIEL, the man ICE was looking for had been dead for nine years.
On Friday, Espinosa said Parra-Hernandez was still awaiting additional surgeries while he remained in ICE custody at a hospital.
text:
Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said his office has interviewed the man who was detained in the backseat of an unmarked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) vehicle when an agent struck Miguel Parra Hernandez in northwest Houston on Saturday.

"We were the only law enforcement that ever spoke to him." Teare said.

In an appearance on Hello Houston, Teare said ICE had already moved the witness more than 300 miles south to the Port Isabel detention center when his office requested an interview with the detainee. The DA's office immediately sent an investigator to interview the witness.

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

"We notified ICE the second we were made aware of them that this individual is a material witness [and] we need to speak to him," Teare said. "The interview for us ended at about 8 p.m. that night. He was on a plane sent to Mexico by 1 o’clock the next morning."

ICE nor the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) immediately responded to a request for comment regarding why the witness had been relocated to Port Isabel.

On Oct. 10, an ICE vehicle struck Parra Hernandez after he exited a vehicle following a pursuit on Clay Road in northwest Houston. Parra-Hernandez suffered a broken leg and is still receiving treatment as of Friday, according to his family. He was the passenger of the vehicle ICE had been pursuing, according to DHS.

According to a spokesperson for DHS, ICE agents were conducting a “targeted enforcement operation in Harris County to arrest Jose Mendoza-Cervantes,” who ICE claimed was driving the vehicle and fled the scene.

A DHS spokesperson said the incident is under an active internal investigation and, per standard practice, the officer involved has been suspended.

"Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are reckless and false," the spokesperson said. "The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct."

Teare said Parra Hernandez's case may be "even more egregious" than the Lorenzo Salgado-Araujo case. Salgado-Araujo was shot and killed by ICE agents in early July during another "targeted enforcement operation," of which Salgado-Araujo was not the intended target.

In the Parra-Hernandez case, Teare said his office has not yet seen the ICE agent's body camera footage and has not yet confirmed the cameras were turned on during the incident. They say sheriff's office body camera footage confirms the ICE agents were wearing body cameras.

FIEL Houston, a local civil rights organization, said Friday it had been contacted by the daughter of the man ICE was allegedly searching for the day Parra-Hernandez was struck by an ICE vehicle. According to FIEL, the man ICE was looking for had been dead for nine years.

"The biggest shock came on Wednesday afternoon when the daughter [of] alias Jose Cervantes Mendoza came forward, who we now know his name is Jose Hector Jimenez Mendoza," Caesar Espinosa, the executive director of FIEL, said at a press conference Friday. "She called our office sobbing because she saw her dad's picture all over the news, all over the ICE website and saying that they were looking for her dad."

On Thursday, the New York Times reported that this same daughter, Jamie Jimenez, provided a Mexican death certificate showing that Jimenez Mendoza died in Laredo in October 2017. Houston Public Media has not independently verified the reported death certificate.

Espinosa said Jimenez Mendoza died "at the hands of" U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) while attempting to cross into the U.S.

"So whether it's a government flaw, or whether it's irresponsibility, or whether they didn't fingerprint Mr. Jose Hector Jimenez when he passed, there had to have been a record that Jose Hector Jimenez was deceased nine years ago," Espinosa said. "We have all the verifying documentation to prove that, which we have turned over to the district attorney's office.

On Friday, Espinosa said Parra-Hernandez was still awaiting additional surgeries while he remained in ICE custody at a hospital.

"He still has multiple fractures on his right leg, still has to have reconstructive surgery on his ankle, and more importantly, his state of mind is slowly starting to deteriorate," Espinosa said. "This man is in his bed and around him 24-7 are armed ICE agents."

Houston Public Media’s Michael Adkison contributed to this article.

title: How ICE Continues to Wield Washington's Own Data - The Urbanist
description:
Officers often already know the name of the person they are detaining due to the state driver data they have accessed.
Therefore, it is impossible to be confident that ICE cannot use the data broker pathway to access Washington state driver data.
However, the primary way ICE appears to be accessing DMV data in Washington state at this time is through the Nlets queries.
Governor Bob Ferguson has said that his office’s actions of canceling ICE and DHS’s access to Nlets has resulted in blocking 100,000 attempts to use Nlets to access state data.
Godoy emphasized that being even more explicit about the need for a court warrant in order to access state driver data wouldn’t be sufficient.
text:
In the wake of accelerated immigration enforcement by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) across the country this summer and into fall, new data shows that Washington state driver data is still being used to enable and assist in these arrests.

The update comes from the University of Washington Center of Human Rights (UWCHR), which published an initial report at the beginning of the year showing how Washington state driver data was being accessed to assist in federal immigration enforcement. Now, nine months later, UWCHR has data showing this practice has continued unabated. Researchers have confirmed 356 arrest incidents between August 1, 2025 and October 13, 2026 that have resulted from federal agents receiving Washington State Department of Licensing (DOL) driver data through the interstate querying system Nlets.

“We know that 356 is likely only a small fraction of the total cases that are happening,” said UWCHR Director Angelina Godoy at a press conference on Tuesday. “Those are just the ones where we were able to confirm it with smoking gun evidence connecting a given plate search to a known immigration arrest.”

ICE continues to access this DOL data in spite of the 2019 Keep Washington Working Act and government officials being aware of this data access pathway since at least 2018, according to the report.

Federal agents’ general operating procedure is to travel to target-rich environments where they think they might find immigrants. They ask the state for data about certain license plates via Nlets, run the registered owner names they are given via Nlets through their own databases, and then decide whether to make an arrest.

Nilu Jenks, a candidate for the District 5 seat of the Seattle City Council, wants to add the Seattle Police Department’s use of Nlets to the Office of the Inspector General’s annual surveillance review while also calling for action from the state legislature and Governor Bob Ferguson.

“In District 5, ‘target rich’ is a polite way of saying racial profiling,” said Jenks. “It means agents deciding who looks deportable by the color of their skin and the work truck they drive: the roofer outside a hardware store on Aurora, the landscaping crew in Maple Leaf, the dad dropping his kids at school in Lake City. When a license plate becomes a name and home address in moments, every trip is a risk. Nobody should have to wonder whether it's safe to drive because of how they look, and no state database should help put a target on their backs.”

Godoy underlined that Washington state hasn’t been doing enough to address the increasing levels of violence and fear experienced by immigrant residents.

“This is a time of extraordinary pain and difficulty for immigrant communities in Washington and around our country, not only because we are experiencing unprecedented levels of immigration enforcement here in the region and around the country, but also because we're experiencing the use of increasingly violent tactics, which appear to involve overt racial profiling, often warrantless arrests, which challenge the Constitution,” Godoy said. “Multiple courts around the nation have found these practices to be unconstitutional, in fact, but here in Washington, this has been greeted thus far with relative silence, which I believe contributes to the invisibilization and isolation of immigrant communities in our midst.”

An escalating situation

Immigration enforcement has quietly increased across the country this summer, with ICE eschewing the more dramatic “surges” it conducted earlier in the year in Minneapolis, Chicago, and other cities. Washington state has been no exception to this swell, and Godoy said she expects to see the numbers continue to rise over time.

The Seattle Times reported that 74% of ICE arrests in Washington in June and July did not involve people with criminal convictions or pending charges.

Guillermo Rivera from Eastside for All, an equity advocacy organization, spoke about the detentions being observed on the Eastside at the press conference. “Most of these cases happen when people were driving, or close to their vehicles, or inside their vehicles, and this is not only happening in East King County, this is happening all around the state,” Rivera said. “The people are being detained when they are driving. People, we are afraid now to go into our cars, that they can stop us at any time. We're afraid to go to the supermarket, to take the kids to the doctor, to take our children to school.”

The UWHRC report described a common new technique being seen in ICE detentions known as “jump outs.” “Jump outs” involve multiple unmarked vehicles, sometimes lacking license plates, surrounding a target who is driving. Unidentified officers then jump out of their cars and violently detain their target. Officers often already know the name of the person they are detaining due to the state driver data they have accessed.

The “jump out” has become one of ICE’s key enforcement strategies since President Donald Trump began his second term.

19 of 22 shootings by immigration agents in Trump’s second term have taken place during these ICE traffic stops, an analysis this summer found, with the UWHRC identifying at least two additional ICE shootings during traffic stops since then.

The increasing brutality of immigration enforcement is also typified by two recent investments by ICE: up to $2 million on robot dogs and up to $20 million on gloves that deliver painful electric shocks.

Meanwhile, local lawmakers still don’t know if ICE is planning to buy the Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma, which could stymie state efforts to impose oversight on the facility. ICE’s current contract with the facility is set to expire on October 27.

The detention center has been receiving complaints about poor and dehumanizing conditions for years. Indeed, conditions there are so bad that Washington State Senator Yasmin Trudeau (D-Tacoma) refers to the facility as a concentration camp.

State data sharing also endangers U.S. citizens

UW researchers found evidence that in Minnesota, driver data queries were also being used to obtain information about community observers of ICE activity, which shows how similar tactics can be used to both increase immigration detentions and to surveil U.S. citizens without a warrant.

The UWHRC also found evidence that this practice is happening right here in King County.

The Urbanist is a nonprofit newsroom powered by reader support. Become a member, get perks, and support local journalism.

Become a Member

This past June, community member Tony Andrews saw a suspicious vehicle in a Fred Meyer parking lot in Bellevue. Andrews had attended a constitutional observer training through Indivisible Eastside, which allowed him to identify the vehicle as possibly belonging to ICE. Even though Andrews kept his distance, the suspicious vehicle circled tightly around Andrews’ car in the parking lot.

Andrews gave his vehicle information to the UW researchers who submitted a records request. The returned records showed that his license plate had been run through Nlets on the day and time that the incident with the suspicious vehicle took place.

“For me, this was just a violation of my privacy,” Andrews told The Urbanist. “For the immigrants, these violations are life-changing. For them, it can mean family separation.”

Handing data over to ICE

The UWHRC report detailed four different pathways by which ICE and other federal agents are able to get state driver data:

Direct access to state DMV databases

Access via Nlets queries

Access via data brokers

State and local agencies directly sharing the data

The report emphasized that all pathways must be addressed simultaneously; otherwise ICE will simply shift to a new means of accessing the data.

In Washington state, ICE had been accessing driver data via direct access to the state DMV databases as recently as last year, but for now, that pathway appears to be closed.

DOL sold its data to 14 companies last year, including at least three who held Department of Homeland Security (DHS) contracts in the near past. While these contracts with DOL forbid the data brokers from selling the data for immigration enforcement purposes, one of the companies, LexisNexis, has structured at least one past contract with ICE in such a way that LexisNexis would have no ability to see how ICE has been using the data. Therefore, it is impossible to be confident that ICE cannot use the data broker pathway to access Washington state driver data.

Direct agency sharing data with ICE is illegal under the Keep Washington Working Act, although that doesn’t mean it isn’t happening anyway.

However, the primary way ICE appears to be accessing DMV data in Washington state at this time is through the Nlets queries.

Governor Bob Ferguson has said that his office’s actions of canceling ICE and DHS’s access to Nlets has resulted in blocking 100,000 attempts to use Nlets to access state data. However, the UWHRC report found that from January 1, 2025 to May 31, 2026, DHS-affiliated agencies still searched the DOL database via Nlets 3,696,147 times, showing the gaping hole in the state’s data protections.

“What happens is that those arrest patrols, whether they're made of ICE, of the Border Patrol, of combined agencies, or of unknown masked men, simply log in under another agency's ORI, just like you might share your Netflix password with a family member,” Godoy said. “As a result, between January and June 2026, Washington DOL data itself shows that over one million searches were completed of Washington driver and vehicle data by agencies who are part of DHS.”

So far UWHRC has documented 38 unique ORIs, or passwords, affiliated with federal agencies prior to arrests by ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) in Washington state.

The report did find that New York State has been successful at cutting off the Nlets channel of information via robust legislation. In New York, federal agents are now only able to search out-of-state license plates via Nlets.

How Washington can do better

Pacific Rim Solidarity Network sent a statement to be read at the press conference instead of coming to speak due to fears of retaliation. They called for Ferguson to enable more transparency and accountability when it comes to DOL data sharing.

“Legislatures take time, and our communities need an answer now. We cannot wait until the next fall to have protections for Washington residents,” Rivera said. “We're asking the governor's office to act now. We're asking the governor to review how this information is being collected, how it's been shared, find any gaps or misuse, and use his authority to protect Washington residents.”

If Ferguson continues to choose not to close these documented gaps, the state legislature can act in January to make the Keep Washington Working Act more robust. Godoy emphasized that being even more explicit about the need for a court warrant in order to access state driver data wouldn’t be sufficient.

“The state has already incorporated specific requirements that Nlets comply with Keep Washington Working or face consequences, and yet has been inexplicably reticent to enforce these very agreements,” the report reads.

Accordingly, Godoy suggested adding explicit enforcement mechanisms to the Keep Washington Working Act, including a private right of action so that those harmed by the data sharing could receive restitution and potentially obtain court injunctions ordering a halt to illegal data access.

“We need to demand that Washington take action to at least protect us in the ways that it can,” Godoy said. “There's no way for Washington to just expel ICE agents from the state. That's not going to happen. But they don't need to serve us up to them on a silver platter with all of our data to make it so easy for them, to allow them to legitimate their arrests and their campaign of fear. So I think for electeds, this is your moment.”

Godoy also praised community members who have chosen to be involved in rapid response in defense of their immigrant neighbors.

“These are heroes, right?” Godoy said. “These are people putting their own life on the line to stand with people who are deeply vulnerable. So there's a lot that can be done. I think a lot of us are not doing as much as we could.”

text:
Survivors of sexual violence could wrongly be denied recognition as victims of human trafficking under credibility tests in a new UK law, the independent anti-slavery commissioner has warned.

Eleanor Lyons said the measures in the immigration and asylum bill were fundamentally unfair and could lead to many more victims of slavery and trafficking, including those allegedly abused by Mohamed Al Fayed, being denied support.

Under the legislation, Home Office officials must regard any delay to making a claim of modern day slavery or human trafficking as damaging to their credibility.

Any inaccuracy, inconsistency or omission in a person’s account, as well as any striking similarity to a claim made by someone else, must also be viewed as reasons for disbelief.

Lyons said the credibility tests would harm survivors of sexual violence who often suffered memory loss as a result of their trauma. Many were also reluctant to come forward to disclose their exploitation due to fear of reprisals by their abusers, she added.

“They are basically saying to victims, if you don’t come forward in a timely fashion not yet defined, if there are inconsistencies in your account, and if there are similarities between exploitation and [those of] others, the Home Office decision-maker must question your credibility,” Lyons said.

“For the Al Fayed victims [that] would be particularly concerning because a lot of time has passed [since the alleged abuse], a lot of them were sadly exploited in similar ways to each other, and some of the things that happened to them were completely horrific and they may not be able to recall exactly what time, which place they happened in [due to the impact of trauma].”

Several women who were allegedly sexually abused by Fayed, said they feared the measures would undermine investigations into what they described as the late billionaire’s international trafficking network.

Holly Johnson, who says she was trafficked and sexually abused when she worked at Harrods and Fayed’s Park Lane offices, said the credibility tests would re-victimise survivors.

She added: “Fayed had a specific strategy for trafficking and assaulting women, and many of our stories are really similar. To say someone shouldn’t be believed because their situation is too similar to another victim of that same abuser is absurd.”

No One Above, a collective of survivors of Fayed’s alleged abuse, said many women delayed reporting their exploitation until after his death in 2023 and Harrods’ declaration in 2024 that those who signed non-disclosure agreements would not have them enforced.

Elizabeth, an NOA member who has been recognised as a trafficking victim by the Home Office, said: “It took that for me to finally believe that I couldn’t have somebody take my house away for speaking out.”

Pelham Spong, who says she was trafficked in Paris on Fayed’s orders in 2008 before being sent to London to be sexually assaulted by him, said she did not go to the Met police until 2017 because she feared her life “was going to be ruined”.

“The thought of speaking out as a 23-year-old with no money, no resources behind me against a billionaire was unfathomable,” said Spong, whose case is being investigated by the French police. “He was so powerful.”

The government has introduced the credibility tests to close what it characterises as opportunities to misuse the National Referral Mechanism (NRM), the system for identifying potential victims of modern slavery and human trafficking in the UK, and to speed up the removal and deportation of illegal migrants.

Eleanora Fais, the anti-trafficking monitoring group coordinator at Anti-Slavery International, said: “If your primary aim is to introduce legislation that is focused on immigration enforcement, safeguarding will come in second place.

“The NRM was always meant to help survivors to disclose and be referred to support needed for the recovery. Alongside that, if they wished to, they could cooperate with police to ensure that perpetrators were brought to justice. If you introduce these criteria to weaken the system, that’s not going to happen.”

Hilary Agg, the head of policy and research at the anti-slavery charity Unseen, said the measures would allow human trafficking to thrive in the UK because fewer victims would be identified and be able to help police to pursue perpetrators.

She added that the tests would harm immigrants and the majority of trafficking and slavery victims, who are British nationals.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “Modern slavery is a barbaric crime, and the government is committed to identifying victims and ensuring they get the support they need. The immigration and asylum bill will strengthen protections and crack down on exploitation, while reducing opportunities for improper use of the system.

“The credibility considerations in the bill are well-balanced and contain appropriate safeguards, which will enhance the robustness of modern slavery decision-making.”

A Harrods spokesperson said it supported all survivors in their pursuit of justice and continued to work closely with the Met police on its investigation.

A Ritz Paris spokesperson said it was “deeply concerned by the allegations that have been reported and takes them with the utmost seriousness. We would like to express our deepest sympathy to the women who have come forward.”

The Fayed estate has been approached for comment.
