text:
This is the first time in American history that there have been zero releases at the border

WASHINGTON — The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) today announced preliminary Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 data showcasing a 95% drop in southwest border apprehensions compared to the Biden Administration, alongside the lowest annual encounters in American history and the first-ever fiscal year with zero Border Patrol releases.

Driven by President Donald J. Trump’s policies and the leadership of DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, FY 2026 combined historic low crossings with strengthened border infrastructure, disrupted cartels, and protected American trade. September marked the 17th consecutive month with ZERO releases.

“President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered. Over the past year, CBP recorded its lowest numbers in American history. A stark contrast to Biden, where CBP recorded its highest illegal immigration numbers ever,” said Secretary Mullin. “The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works. Thanks to President Trump’s leadership and the hard work of CBP and DHS law enforcement personnel, we have restored control of the border and made America safer than ever.”

“FY 2026 demonstrated what focused enforcement, strong partnerships, and the commitment of our frontline personnel can achieve,” said CBP Commissioner Rodney S. Scott. “DHS and CBP are securing the border, stopping dangerous drugs and criminals, protecting communities, and ensuring our personnel have the resources necessary for this critical mission.”

Historic Border Security Results

CBP’s enforcement posture drove U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions to their lowest level in agency history. The Border Patrol, which completed its first-ever fiscal year with no releases, recorded less than 99,000 southwest border apprehensions in FY 2026—a 95% decline compared with more than 1.8 million per year under President Biden. Total FY 2026 apprehensions (98,708) were 60% lower than the Biden Administration’s single highest month alone (249,740).

Additionally, preliminary data shows total nationwide encounters in FY 2026 were the lowest in agency history at 379,243, compared with 2.7 million per year under Biden (seven times higher). FY 2026 encounters were 88% lower than FY 2023 under Biden, which was the highest fiscal year ever.

These results reflect sustained enforcement and the deterrent effect of a secure border. Illegal aliens have received a clear message: don’t try to enter the country illegally, or you will be apprehended, detained, and deported.

A Safer Border

President Trump’s policies are also saving lives by reducing unlawful crossings, leading to a dramatic decline in border-related deaths.

Fewer unlawful crossings have contributed to a significant decline in border-related deaths. Preliminary data shows alien deaths identified by the Border Patrol fell nearly 80% in FY 2026 and since January 20, 2025, compared to the Biden Administration.

CBP personnel nevertheless remained ready to respond when lives were at risk. Across the nation, agents, officers, and air and marine personnel conducted search-and-rescue operations and delivered emergency medical aid. These efforts have included railcar rescues, a rescue effort following flooding at the Grand Canyon, and a CBP officer who responded to victims of a plane crash in Miami.

CBP’s Office of Field Operations responded to more than 3,000 medical emergencies during FY 2026, performing CPR on over 50 individuals in cardiac arrest and administering Naloxone for suspected opioid overdoses.

Stronger Infrastructure Along the Border

CBP reached a major construction milestone in FY 2026, completing 250 miles of new border barrier along the southwest border since January 20, 2025. This includes primary and secondary barriers, waterborne barriers, and supporting technology.

Funding from the Working Families Tax Cut Act enabled CBP to accelerate Smart Wall construction. From September 2025 through September 2026, CBP obligated $34.3 billion to support Smart Wall projects across all southwest border states, cementing a generational investment in physical security and operational control.

Drug Interdictions that Save Lives

As the frontline against drug smuggling, CBP is leading federal efforts to combat illicit trafficking.

CBP utilizes cutting-edge nonintrusive inspection technology and intelligence-driven strategies to seize deadly drugs, targeting not just finished products but precursor chemicals, tools, and pill presses.

As a result, preliminary data shows CBP’s drug seizures in FY 2026 totaled nearly 1 million pounds—63% higher than the 600,000-pound annual average of the last four years.

Trade and Tariff Enforcement

CBP plays a central role in enforcing trade law, supporting economic security, and interdicting counterfeit merchandise and goods made with forced labor.

In FY 2026, CBP stopped more than 4,000 shipments valued at over $325 million suspected of involving forced labor, and issued eight Withhold Release Orders along with two modifications.

CBP also seized nearly 55.5 million counterfeit goods valued at more than $12.6 billion, including 476,903 items infringing FIFA World Cup intellectual property valued at over $33 million.

By securing the border, intercepting dangerous narcotics, expanding physical barriers, and enforcing lawful trade, CBP has closed vulnerabilities across every front to ensure the long-term safety and prosperity of the American people.

title: The Odyssey of Third Country Removal - Race, Racism and the Law
description:
Abstract Excerpted From: Matthew Boaz, The Odyssey of Third Country Removal, 70 St. Louis U. L.J.
Specifically, this essay focuses on the amplified use of third country removals as part of a mass deportation campaign.
Third country removals, as they currently function, pose a real threat to noncitizens and citizens alike.
In conclusion, the increase in third country removals presents a significant legal problem.
Most of this individualized litigation has focused on ensuring proper procedure is followed, but amicus briefs in several high profile cases have also homed in on major substantive issues with the third country removal policy.
text:
Abstract

Excerpted From: Matthew Boaz, The Odyssey of Third Country Removal, 70 St. Louis U. L.J. 605 (Summer 2026) (Full Document) (244 Footnotes Omitted)

In February 2025, a hotel in Panama became a focal point for international media when a group of several hundred asylum seekers from countries such as Iran, Turkey, Nepal, Afghanistan, and Sri Lanka were suddenly sent there from the U.S. without legal recourse or notice of their destination. The majority of the migrants agreed to repatriation to their home countries, but a significant number remain, seeking to navigate an asylum system that seems intent on denying relief, with few other options available. A short time later, a similar cohort arrived in Costa Rica with an eerily familiar tale to tell.3 But public outcry rose to a fever pitch following the removal of nearly 300 individuals to the Centro de Confinamiento del Terrorism (“CECOT”), a beyond-maximum-security prison, located in El Salvador. Even more striking was that the removals occurred during court proceedings seeking to prevent the planes from taking flight, and that they relied upon the Alien Enemies Act (“AEA”), an antiquated, centuries-old law that had not been utilized since World War II. The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals later found that the invocation of the Act was unlawful in the circumstances,6 but not before months of dithering by the administration7 resulted in the imprisonment of hundreds of people by a foreign power at the behest of the U.S. government. The case remains pending after the full Fifth Circuit reheard the matter en banc in January 2026. The eventual release of those individuals and their subsequent return to Venezuela confirmed the allegations of torture and other mistreatment that many experts expected were occurring in the prison.10

Since that time, the Trump administration has sought to form agreements, both formal and informal, with dozens of countries across the globe. While *607 some, such as Nigeria and Ukraine, have declined to participate, others have expressed willingness to participate in exchange for significant sums of money and the fleeting good favor that frequently follows any “deal” struck with the president. Eswatini struck just such a deal to receive ten million dollars, though it first asked for 500 million dollars, to detain 150 future deportees. It initially imprisoned five men, originally from Cuba, Laos, Vietnam, and Yemen, who were sent from the U.S. So far, it has received fifteen individuals at a total cost to the U.S. of $5.1 million, or approximately $433,000 per person. Separately, Panama, may have agreed to accept the first removals in February in order to calm rhetoric from President Trump that focused on reasserting control over the Panama Canal. The details of many of these agreements remain disputed, and lawsuits seeking to intervene have been the primary source for obtaining illuminating details about how these accords function. As for whether these *608 agreements transgress the boundaries of domestic or international law, the devil is in the details.

This essay discusses the case of one individual, Kilmar Ábrego García, and how his story exemplifies the odyssey into which many noncitizens have been cast during the first year of the second Trump administration. Specifically, this essay focuses on the amplified use of third country removals as part of a mass deportation campaign. This essay sounds the alarm that these third country removals are likely to become more expansive because of the rapidity of the removal process, the vulnerability of affected populations, and the unwillingness of courts to intervene after the fact.

Third country removals, as they currently function, pose a real threat to noncitizens and citizens alike. Despite former Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”) Secretary Kristi Noem’s protestations that no U.S. citizens have been detained or arrested, instances of such conduct number into the hundreds during the first year of the second Trump administration. Past administrations have also, by error, arrested, detained, and deported U.S. citizens. Because the present process provides a singular mechanism to prevent removal--asserting fear of removal to a specific place--with no review, an asylum officer or Immigration and Customs Enforcement (“ICE”) officer is frequently the only person who stands between an individual and removal. Under the current administration, pressure on officers, immigration judges, and Board of Immigration Appeals (“BIA”) judges has eroded any remaining confidence that these officials employed by the U.S. Department of Justice (“DOJ”) or DHS could act in a neutral fashion as arbiters and independent decision makers.

In response to calls for creating a remedy for its wrongdoing, the U.S. alleges an inability to intervene in the affairs of foreign nations, even when it is responsible for the arrangement. The Supreme Court has seemed skeptical of this argument on at least one occasion, but intervention is not promised. Once a person has been expelled, the government knows that individual’s rights are *609 nearly nonexistent. The government claims no remedy and the courts, reluctant to interfere in foreign affairs or national security, defer to the government. However, local communities have been steadily intervening to help prevent detentions of their noncitizen neighbors, and legal actors have been successfully employing various forms of litigation to push back on these efforts. There may yet be a resistance that can adequately respond to these draconian measures.

[. . .]

Over the past fifteen months, the Trump administration has relied on inventive strategies in support of its ultimate and unreasoned goal of deporting one million people from the U.S. before the end of the fiscal year.2 One mechanism that the administration is relying ever more heavily upon is “third country removal,” wherein an individual is sent to a nation with which they have no status or connection. These removals sit at the vanguard of illegality and run contrary to domestic law and international obligations to which the U.S. is a signatory. While some third country removals are permissible, the way the present administration is utilizing a substantial proportion of these removals, including as cudgels to induce guilty pleas in federal criminal proceedings,fall far outside the bounds of lawful use. Importantly, the danger presented in the AEA cases, of U.S. citizens being sent to foreign prisons without legal recourse, remains ever present with the use of third country removals. The Supreme Court has already ratified the practice on one occasion, and federal courts, too, seem to be acquiescing to the government’s fervent desire to build up a network of willing countries to which it can send people with no connection to those places. Without some forms of intervention, the bounds of this practice appear to be limitless.

The U.S. has long relegated immigration policy and enforcement to the exclusive control of the federal government. Yet, the idiosyncrasies of the country’s vast population and diverse regional needs bode in favor of a more nuanced and individualized approach. Years of congressional and executive action have focused on broad scale efforts to deter unlawful entry and limit long-term options, reacting in unpredictable and sometimes confusing ways to various emergent crises on a case-by-case basis. For nearly two decades, the political messaging has resounded with a call for “securing the border” before any new meaningful pathways are created. At the same time, through executive action, each presidential administration has sought to remedy some small part of the immigration system, doing their level best to act in some way during a prolonged period of congressional gridlock. The result has been stagnation, with national discourse revolving around whether the border is porous and how much money should be devoted to securing it.

The U.S.’ efforts to meet lofty deportation goals have led to indiscriminate violence, and the appearance of--if not outright authoritarian *633 repression. The targeting of students, day laborers, and, allegedly, anyone who appears “to be Latino” or “an immigrant”228 has elevated the fear that noncitizens experience each day. The idea that removing people from their communities is harmful no longer rests at the margins, as major politicians decry the effects that mass deportation will have in the communities of their constituencies. In fact, many of these places extol the virtues of migration and praise their new community members who happen to be non-citizens.

In conclusion, the increase in third country removals presents a significant legal problem. As Justice Sotomayor wrote in her dissent from one of the relevant decisions, “[t]he government has made clear in word and deed that it feels itself unconstrained by law, free to deport anyone, anywhere without * notice or an opportunity be heard.” The magnitude of transgression is, for many advocates, nearly impossible to comprehend, let alone mobilize against. It is designed to promote terror and the threat of punishment. Of those who do intervene, the government seems willing to marshal its resources in favor of retribution. Courts seem to be the last bulwark against these abuses, but even they are unable to intervene in some cases.

However, all is not lost. There are several observable weaknesses to this approach of third country removals. First, many of the third countries are charging an inordinate amount of money to participate in these deals.236 When they do participate, backlash within their own borders is severe.This dynamic is not unique to the U.S. In the European Union, an agreement with Turkey in 2020 came under strain as that country’s president demanded more money to enforce Europe’s “external borders.” The region later delegated interventions to several North African countries and even non-state actors, but some countries have demanded more money for these efforts.239 Second, litigation efforts that impede the easy removal of individuals to third countries have proved successful *635 on many fronts. At the individual level, habeas corpus petitions have become a useful tool for obtaining release from detention and in preventing swift removal without an opportunity to demonstrate one’s fear of deportation to an unknown country. Most of this individualized litigation has focused on ensuring proper procedure is followed, but amicus briefs in several high profile cases have also homed in on major substantive issues with the third country removal policy. In the case of Àbrego García, amici filed a brief identifying possible Eighth Amendment violations, arguing that third country removals are being employed as punishment, a violation of the Constitution’s bounds on civil immigration enforcement.242 In another case pending before the First Circuit Court of Appeals, amici have highlighted the regulatory requirements for individualized determinations, noting that third country removal policies, as a whole, and when applied broadly, are likely violative of the regulations as written. Finally, at the local level, pushback to the president’s mass deportation agenda continues to grow within the U.S. Cities such as New Orleans, Charlotte, Chicago, and Los Angeles, for example are learning from each other and implementing communal strategies to inhibit these detentions and removals that violate due process.244 With a strategy of individual representation, class action lawsuits, and local resistance, the friction may be enough to slow down these efforts so that they can be properly adjudicated on the merits before the Supreme Court.

Assistant Professor, University of Kentucky J. David Rosenberg College of Law; J.D., Georgetown University Law Center.

text:
Joins 17 AGs in urging Congress quickly pass Epstein Files Transparency Act II, which would give state AGs and survivors the power to enforce the transparency that Congress has already demanded but Trump Administration has ignored

Under first Epstein Files Transparency Act, Trump’s DOJ was supposed to make files publicly available last December and has not done so, in violation of the Act

October 16, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) — Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison has joined a coalition of 17 attorneys general in sending a letter to congressional leadership urging swift passage of the Epstein Files Transparency Act II (EFTA II), legislation that would give state attorneys general and survivors the power to enforce the transparency that Congress has already demanded.

The letter, addressed to House Speaker Mike Johnson, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, supports H.R. 9694 and its Senate companion, S. 5005.

Congress passed the original Epstein Files Transparency Act (EFTA I), which took effect November 19, 2025 (Public Law 119-38), to give survivors and the public access to the full investigative record of Jeffrey Epstein's crimes. It passed the House on a vote of 427–1 and passed the Senate on unanimous consent. The law required the U.S. Department of Justice to make the files publicly available by December 19, 2025. Despite this requirement, nearly a year later, the Department has not met that obligation. In Phang v. Blanche, a federal court in the District of Columbia noted that the U.S. Attorney General conceded he is in violation of the Act.

"We shouldn’t be surprised — but should be shocked that — that Trump’s DOJ continues to disregard the clear requirements of the law that Congress passed nearly unanimously. Not only has the Trump Administration withheld millions of documents they were required to release, they have exposed the personal information of victims they were supposed to protect,” said Attorney General Ellison. "No federal agency is above the law and a new one shouldn’t even be necessary. But because it is, the Epstein Files Transparency Act II gives state attorneys general and survivors the tools to enforce the law Congress already passed. The public demand for this law is overwhelming and there is nothing partisan about it, so I urge Congress to act swiftly.”

As Attorney General Ellison and the coalition make clear in their letter to congressional leaders today, DOJ released only a limited portion of the files on the December 19, 2025 deadline, and later disclosures also fell short. Millions of documents remain withheld, often on the basis of legal privilege. At the same time, a Wall Street Journal review found that the personal information of at least 43 victims was exposed in the files that were released, despite the protections written into EFTA I.

In the letter, the attorneys general emphasize that the shortfall affects states directly. State law enforcement and prosecutors need full access to unredacted investigative records, including relevant FBI 302 reports, to investigate and pursue matters within their jurisdictions. Survivors, meanwhile, continue to be denied closure and control over their own records.

What EFTA II would do

Create an expedited right of action. State attorneys general, authorized state officials, victims, and members of Congress would have explicit standing to sue the U.S. Attorney General in federal court for unlawfully withholding, delaying, or heavily redacting Epstein-related records.

Protect survivor access. Victims would be guaranteed the right to access unredacted records about themselves and the harms they suffered.

Eliminate evasions. DOJ would be barred from invoking common law privileges, such as the deliberative process privilege, to avoid the disclosure requirements Congress enacted.

Enforce accountability. Federal officials who knowingly conceal, destroy, or improperly withhold mandated files would be subject to existing federal penalties.

Attorney General Ellison and the coalition stress in their letter that the pursuit of justice and public accountability transcends partisanship. They urge Congress to act so that no federal agency places itself above the law.

text:
Mayor Cherelle L. Parker’s administration told a powerful congressional oversight committee earlier this year that it does not endorse statements made by District Attorney Larry Krasner and Sheriff Rochelle Bilal about federal immigration enforcement, according to a report released Thursday.

The 18-page interim report was released by the Republican-led U.S. House Judiciary Committee less than three weeks before a midterm election when the GOP may lose its majority in the chamber. It’s part of the committee’s probe into immigration policies in Philadelphia, one of several jurisdictions that Republicans say have endangered public safety by shielding immigrants from deportation.

The report shows the Parker administration, which has largely communicated behind the scenes with the federal government about immigration enforcement, attempted to distance itself from Krasner and Bilal.

» READ MORE: House Judiciary committee criticizes Philly law enforcement over sanctuary policies

The pair each made comments about U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that went viral in January after a federal agent fatally shot a civilian in Minneapolis. Bilal called the agency “fake, wannabe law enforcement” and threatened to arrest agents.

Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel at the time released a statement clarifying that his department is in charge of municipal policing and criminal investigations, not the sheriff’s office.

A May letter to the House Judiciary Committee from then-City Solicitor Renee Garcia went further, according to the report.

“The Sheriff and District Attorney of Philadelphia are separately elected officials whose statements are wholly separate and not endorsed by Mayor Cherelle Parker’s Administration,” Garcia wrote.

A spokesperson for Bilal did not respond to a request for comment, and a spokesperson for the city’s law department declined to comment.

In an interview Friday, Krasner responded to the development that Parker’s administration had distanced itself from his comments, saying that he has spoken out against the Trump administration’s deportation campaign because “these are authoritarian times.”

“There are a lot of elected officials who have spoken and acted with courage,” he said. “Those of us who stand up and speak out with courage will be judged well by history.”

The Judiciary Committee’s report comes amid already heightened tensions between the city’s law enforcement agencies and a series of unrelated allegations of wrongdoing that have enveloped the sheriff’s office.

Earlier this week, Krasner publicly blamed the police department for botching a 2023 murder case against a man accused of fatally shooting Officer Shane Seiber on Saturday, drawing a defense from the police force that said it was not the time to be “assigning blame.”

Separately, Bilal is facing the prospect of independent, court-ordered supervision of her office, which has been accused of mishandling deed transfers for years. Earlier this month, the sheriff’s office admitted in court that it had found $20 million in sheriff’s sale proceeds that was supposed to have been transferred to the city, but had not been disbursed.

Krasner and Bilal have been confrontational toward federal immigration enforcement, with the progressive district attorney comparing ICE agents to Nazis, and Bilal saying that her message to agents is: “You don’t want this smoke.”

Parker, a centrist Democrat, has taken a quieter approach. While the mayor earlier this year signed legislation that effectively codified Philadelphia’s “sanctuary city” status, she has largely avoided directly criticizing President Donald Trump’s administration and its mass deportation campaign.

For years, Philadelphia’s policy has been that officials do not comply with detainer requests by ICE to hold immigrants who are already in city custody unless ICE produces a warrant signed by a judge.

» READ MORE: Mayor Parker’s restraint with Trump is both calculation and gamble as the president escalates against blue cities

Still, despite the Parker administration’s attempts to smooth over the city’s relationship with Washington Republicans, the House Judiciary Committee described Philadelphia’s government as part of the problem, saying the city’s policies of not cooperating with ICE in some circumstances are deliberately obstructive to federal law enforcement.

The committee in May requested a trove of records from the city, police department, sheriff’s office, and district attorney’s office after it accused Philadelphia of shielding immigrants who have committed crimes.

» READ MORE: What Mayor Cherelle Parker’s administration told the DOJ about Philly’s ‘sanctuary’ policies in a letter the city tried to keep secret

Between January 2024 — when Parker first took office — and June 2026, the city did not comply with 162 detainer requests from ICE, according to the report, which cited records provided by the city. Over the same time period, the report says, the city received seven judicial warrants, which the report said were either honored or involved people who were transferred to state prison after being convicted.

The committee wrote that the city released a handful of immigrants who had detainers and had previously been charged with crimes, such as assault. Those immigrants were later arrested by ICE, the report said.

However, city officials have in the past said that just because they do not comply with an ICE detainer request does not mean that the person is released into the community. Some continue to be incarcerated in city facilities or are transferred to other jurisdictions.

» READ MORE: Krasner rips Trump and House Judiciary Committee over ‘war against immigrants’

The Judiciary Committee was also deeply critical of both Bilal and Krasner for their offices’ respective policies toward immigration enforcement.

For Bilal’s part, the committee wrote that the sheriff, whose office secures the municipal courthouse in Center City, “actively obstructs ICE from making safe immigration arrests inside the city’s courthouse.” The committee wrote that, when ICE has a warrant to take custody of an immigrant, agents must wait to arrest the person until they’ve been transferred from the courthouse to the city’s prison complex.

And the committee took particular issue with Krasner, a frequent target of state and national Republican opposition to reformist styles of law enforcement. The report is critical of the office’s policy of reviewing cases against undocumented immigrants and at times seeking “immigration-neutral outcomes.”

“In practice, this means that prosecutors in Krasner’s office are not prohibited from crafting generous plea deals that avoid immigration consequences for even the worst offenders,” the committee wrote.

However, Krasner — who has publicly taunted Jordan for not holding a public hearing on the matter — said that it’s ICE that is treating undocumented immigrants more favorably than U.S. citizens.

He said his office provided records to the House Judiciary Committee showing that prosecutors have requested that ICE not deport immigrants facing charges for violent crimes so that they can be prosecuted, sentenced, and jailed here. Krasner said that ICE did not honor those requests.

“[Jordan] and his Judiciary Committee have written a cover-up document,” Krasner said. “Let’s just say I’m not surprised that Jim Jordan didn’t want me or many of my colleagues to be questioned or be able to answer in a public space.”

text:
The Immigrations Customs and Enforcement officer who allegedly struck a man with a vehicle during a pursuit outside Houston last weekend has been placed on administrative leave, the agency said.

The move is standard for all use-of-force incidents, according to an ICE spokesperson.

"This incident is under active internal investigation," the spokesperson said in a statement Friday.

On Saturday, Miguel Parra-Hernandez was hit by a car operated by an ICE agent during an arrest as the unidentified officer attempted to arrest him and another suspect, the agency said. Parra-Hernandez, who ICE alleged is undocumented, is currently in the hospital recovering from injuries to his legs, according to the Harris County District Attorney's office.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said Parra-Hernandez broke his leg in three places and has undergone two surgeries.

Parra-Hernandez has not been charged by any law enforcement agency as of Thursday, according to the DA's office.

ICE said in a statement that that one of its officers was pursuing Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, a Mexican national who they allege had a criminal record and a final order of removal by a judge, and observed him get in a vehicle with Parra-Hernandez Saturday morning.

The ICE officer attempted a car stop, and Mendoza-Cervantes and Parra-Hernandez fled their vehicle on foot, according to ICE and the Harris County Sheriff's Office.

Surveillance video of the incident reviewed by ABC News appears to show the ICE vehicle moving in the direction of a man running and then striking him.

An ICE spokesperson alleged in a statement that Parra-Hernandez "ran in front of an ICE vehicle" when he was hit.

"Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct," the spokesperson said in a statement Wednesday.

Mendoza-Cervantes remains at large as of Friday, according to ICE.

Teare, the DA, is currently probing the situation and told ABC News Wednesday that his office could possibly pursue criminal charges against the ICE officer.

The DA's office said two people were allegedly detained by the ICE agent prior to the incident and in the back seat of the ICE officer's vehicle when Parra-Hernandez was hit.

Teare told ABC News Thursday that his office was able to interview one of those witnesses before they were deported and that he believes the ICE officer intentionally struck Parra-Hernandez.

"Thankfully, we were able to meet with him in custody yesterday, but we were the only individuals to even speak to him," the DA told ABC News.

text:
ALBUQUERQUE, NM – The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of New Mexico filed a lawsuit on behalf of the New Mexico Immigrant Law Center (NMILC) in federal court today against Immigration and U.S. Customs Enforcement (ICE) for failing to respond to a records request. The Freedom of Information Act request was submitted with ICE over a month ago asking for records about the agency's direct contracting arrangements with CoreCivic, Inc. related to the Torrance County Detention Facility (TCDF) and Cibola County Correctional Center (CCCC).

"We’re concerned that ICE just replaced one underhanded contract with another,” said Emma O'Sullivan, staff attorney at the ACLU of New Mexico. "The state made it clear with the passage of the Immigrant Safety Act that New Mexico stands against the mistreatment and abuse of people in these detention facilities. ICE cannot continue to operate here without accountability."

The Immigrant Safety Act, passed during the 2026 legislative session, prevents ICE from contracting with New Mexico counties to use their correctional facilities as ICE detention centers. It came at a time when the Trump administration’s mass detentions and deportations were devastating the country, endangering the lives of both immigrants and citizens. The law got New Mexico out of the business of immigration detention, leaving the federal government with the limited options of operating ICE facilities directly or contracting with private entities like CoreCivic.

This spring, ICE announced that it would enter non-competitive “sole source” direct contracts with CoreCivic in both Torrance and Cibola counties to continue detaining immigrants there. ICE sidestepped important federal contracting requirements that generally require competitive bidding and a review of contractors’ safety records. Very little information about the new contracts has been made public, leaving New Mexicans in the dark about the use of taxpayer money to detain immigrants at the two facilities.

"Our communities spoke up and passed the Immigrant Safety Act to say that we refuse to be complicit in locking up immigrants, yet ICE is doing everything in its power to retain and expand Trump’s cruel detention and deportation machine in our state,” said Jessica I. Martínez, director of policy and coalition building at NMILC. “We’re requesting these documents because New Mexicans deserve to know why ICE and the Trump administration are attempting to evade our laws while they continue to subject people to inhumane detention.”

Advocates have long raised grave concerns about chronic conditions endangering the health and safety of people held at immigration detention centers in the state, including TCDF and CCCC, both operated by the private prison corporation CoreCivic. At least five people have tragically died in recent years at ICE facilities in New Mexico, including those of Kesley Vial, Roxsana Hernández, and Johana Medina León. People detained in ICE custody in our state have been subjected to some of the worst and inhumane practices by the administration, like third-country deportations and the Guantanamo Bay and CECOT prison in El Salvador deportations.

text:
NEW YORK -- Mayor Zohran Mamdani and top New York Democrats are calling on the owners of private parking lots to block federal immigration officers from using their properties as staging areas, days after immigration officers shot a man in the city.

In a Friday letter, Mamdani, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and dozens of state and local lawmakers told lot and garage owners that the city needs their “help at a critical juncture.”

“In solidarity with immigrant New Yorkers and in our shared commitment to the City we love, we ask that you do not rent, lend, or otherwise make your property available to ICE as a staging area for its enforcement operations,” the letter reads. “Make it known to ICE that it is not authorized to use your garages and lots.”

The plea came after immigration officers shot 28-year-old Dominican national Oscar Belgal during an arrest last week as he rode in a car with his young son. The shooting sparked protests and drew renewed attention to the federal government’s immigration crackdown.

The federal officers had been using a nearby private parking lot as a staging area before the shooting, according to Friday's letter.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security slammed the letter in a statement that read: “Mayor Mamdani should be grateful to our brave law enforcement officers for cleaning up the streets of NYC since he won’t. Luckily, no terminated parking will stop ICE from deporting criminal illegal aliens to make New York safe again."

Federal officials maintain the immigration officers believed their lives were in danger and opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and accelerated toward them.

New York City has previously barred outside law enforcement agencies such as DHS from setting up staging areas on city property unless they have a judicial warrant or qualify for certain “limited legal exceptions,” according to the letter. “But these laws govern City property, not the private lots and garages that you operate,” it adds.

Private businesses have at times found themselves in the middle of tense political fights over President Donald Trump's administration's immigration enforcement push.

Thwarted in its efforts to arrest refugees without a warrant, the Trump administration pressed forward on other fronts.
But the Trump administration keeps failing to offer detailed evidence that actually supports these claims.
Weaknesses in the immigration process can and should be fixed, but the all-or-nothing approach the Trump administration has used against refugees and children only leads to misery.
Unlike many former refugees and unaccompanied children targeted by the Trump administration, Ilhan Omar has the political power and the media savvy to fight back.
text:
The message: When a high profile, elected official who came to the U.S. as a child and naturalized more than 25 years ago can be threatened with deportation, no one is safe.

When ICE agents raided Representative Ilhan Omar’s (D-MN) home in Washington, D.C. this week, they didn’t just invade her privacy to further a politically motivated attack on one of Donald Trump’s staunchest critics. They were also sending a message to immigrants: when a high profile, elected official who came to the U.S. as a child and naturalized more than 25 years ago can be threatened with deportation, no one is safe. Immigrant women, Muslim immigrants, refugees and even naturalized citizens can’t help but wonder who will be next.

There are few details available about the reasons a judge authorized the warrant to search Omar’s home, but the government has conveniently let slip that it has to do with the refugee application Omar’s father submitted, which was likely filed 30 or 40 years ago. This begs the question—what evidence does DHS possibly expect to find in the Washington residence of a member of Congress from Minnesota, about paperwork her father filed decades ago? The search has expanded; a Minnesota grand jury has issued subpoenas to Omar’s family members, and the government has seized her phone. D.C.’s U.S. attorney Jeanine Pirro is making noise about criminal charges.

The spectacle will likely come to nothing, much like other politically motivated Trump prosecution efforts, but it extracts a high toll on Omar, harassing and embarrassing her just weeks before the midterm elections. It also further undermines the rule of law, as it is an attempt to undo a decision made decades ago—another signature Trump move.

While this may be the most high-profile example of targeting a former refugee, it is not the only effort to bully refugees and former refugees who have green cards or are naturalized citizens. In December 2025, the Trump administration began reviewing the files of more than 5,000 Somali refugees admitted during the Biden administration, as part of its intense campaign against immigrants in the Twin Cities. ICE agents began to arrest refugees with no basis other than their refugee status, traumatizing people who became too afraid to leave their homes and resurfacing painful memories of their past persecution. After a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction against these unlawful arrests, Omar called the administration out at a press conference organized by Minnesota’s Advocates for Human Rights,

Refugees are among the most vetted people in the entire world. People wait years, even decades to get through the vetting process. There is absolutely no reason for Trump to claim that there is rampant fraud in the refugee system, because we know this is not about fraud. This is about targeting Black and brown people from foreign countries simply because Stephen Miller doesn’t want them here.

Thwarted in its efforts to arrest refugees without a warrant, the Trump administration pressed forward on other fronts. In October 2025, Trump announced that only 7,500 refugees would be admitted in fiscal year 2026, down from 125,000 in Biden’s last year in office, with most slots reserved for Afrikaners from South Africa. (Trump subsequently added an emergency allocation of 10,000 more slots for Afrikaners in May 2026). In November 2025, the head of USCIS directed a review of all 200,000 refugee admissions approved under Biden’s watch, citing fraud and concerns that the applicants did not meet the definition of refugee. In September 2026, President Trump announced that he would rescind appropriated funds designated for refugee and unaccompanied children’s services because his border policies had been so successful that the money was no longer needed.

And, within days of the raid on Omar’s home, the administration published a regulation, effective immediately, compressing the timeline for appealing a termination of refugee status from 30 days to 10. According to the International Refugee Assistance Project, “The new regulation contains significant irregularities, including blaming the Biden Administration for definitions and practices that have been used since the Refugee Act was passed in 1980, misstating legal standards, and skipping the notice-and-comment process for the public to provide input on the regulation.”

How can anyone trust that they are safe when your new country’s government also turns on you?

Dorothea Lay, Vice President for Advocacy and Policy at Jesuit Refugee Services, said in a statement,

“This new Interim Final Rule would allow the Department of Homeland Security to fast-track the termination of refugee status and potential removal of people who fled persecution in their homelands and were lawfully admitted to this country after being thoroughly vetted. This is a violation of dictates of fairness, due process and respect for human dignity. We call on DHS to not let our country become a place where people we invite to build new lives here can’t count on us to keep our promises.”

Thirty days is barely enough time to mount an appeal against any government action, but reducing the time by two thirds is just cruel, particularly for refugees who have been permanently resettled in the United States. The promise of permanence is embedded in the Refugee Convention, as a means of ensuring safety for those who are persecuted by their own government. But how can anyone trust that they are safe when your new country’s government also turns on you?

It is becoming increasingly common for the Trump administration to rely on “fraud” as the basis for its immigration policies, in part because reliance on the national security mantra is wearing thin. Over the last two years, the public has questioned how our national security is protected by arresting five-year-olds, nursing mothers, and heads of households who support their families and have no criminal record.

While national security may be shrouded in mystery, fraud is the ultimate obfuscator, something sinister and evasive, flexible enough to mischaracterize every accident, every mistake, or every conflicting statement that an immigrant might make. This is well illustrated by the release of a “summary report” issued by the Office of Refugee Resettlement allegedly documenting fraud among unaccompanied children and their sponsors—another group the administration loves to hate.

According to this report, fraud is rampant in the unaccompanied children program: most parents have engaged in “alien smuggling” to bring their children to the U.S., most sponsors lie, and many of them are child traffickers. But the Trump administration keeps failing to offer detailed evidence that actually supports these claims. While announcing the summary report, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. seemed more interested in castigating the Biden administration for its response to the surge of children who arrived in the country in 2021 and 2022, declaring that under President Trump, the government will “never sacrifice a child’s safety for bureaucratic convenience.” But this administration, in the name of protecting children, has routinely used the allegation of fraud to justify separating children from parents, detaining children for a year or more, cutting legal and social services, and rushing to deport children whether or not they have an attorney.

Much like the attacks on refugees, claims of fraud in other parts of the immigration system are often exaggerated, frequently conflating honest mistakes with intentional acts of deceit. The public can’t parse out the facts, and without hard data, we are asked to accept policies grounded in fear or paranoia.

Weaknesses in the immigration process can and should be fixed, but the all-or-nothing approach the Trump administration has used against refugees and children only leads to misery.

Unlike many former refugees and unaccompanied children targeted by the Trump administration, Ilhan Omar has the political power and the media savvy to fight back. The raid and efforts to prosecute her should backfire on the administration; political stunts so close to an election, coinciding with new rules making it easier to deport refugees, are their own kind of fraud on the public.

The continued attempt to inject the notion of fraud into every immigration interaction grows old. The government has cried wolf too many times; and the evidence is almost never there.

While attacking refugees and children doesn’t sit well with most people, that dissatisfaction has to translate into action at the ballot box, using our votes to demand a return to a more humane and welcoming immigration system.

text:
The son of an ICE detainee who died at Miami Correctional Facility in north-central Indiana is suing the federal government, accusing it of unlawfully withholding his father’s medical information.

Viccheat Sim says the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, known as ICE, violated the Freedom of Information Act by broadly denying his requests for medical records and reports tied to the Feb. 16 death of Lorth Sim.

The lawsuit was filed in August in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. A judge gave the defendants until Oct. 22 to respond to the complaint.

The Department of Homeland Security, which includes ICE, did not respond to a request for comment Friday from The Indiana Lawyer.

Lorth Sim died Feb. 16 while in custody at Miami Correctional Facility near Bunker Hill.

A coroner ruled the death to be natural after a forensic pathologist conducted an autopsy and traced the cause to cardiovascular disease and other conditions tied to diabetes.

Sim had been diagnosed with type II diabetes and prescribed metformin to treat it, the lawsuit stated, adding that he told the staff at Miami about his condition. The lawsuit also noted that the 59-year-old Sim’s “glucose levels were markedly elevated in the hours preceding his death.”

The IndyStar has reported that Sim’s family and a nurse at the prison said Sim never received the medication.

Viccheat Sim requested any and all investigative documents and reports tied to his father’s death, the lawsuit states. He made that request under the Freedom of Information Act in April. He then made a revised request the following month seeking all records related to Lorth Sim while he was in ICE custody.

The federal agencies denied both requests and Sim’s subsequent appeals, noting that the records were compiled as part of an investigation into Sim’s death, the lawsuit states. But Viccheat Sim argued in the complaint that his father’s medical records were not prepared for law enforcement purposes.

The lawsuit noted that many records “were prepared prior to Mr. Sim’s death and were maintained in the ordinary course of his detention and medical care while in ICE custody.”

“The disclosure of a deceased individual’s central file, medical records, and disciplinary records to his son would have no effect on any alleged ongoing review of Mr. Sim’s death, not least because these records were all prepared in advance of, and independent from, his death,” the lawsuit states.

Lorth Sim came to the U.S. from Cambodia as a refugee and became a lawful permanent resident in the 1980s. In 2006, an immigration judge ordered his removal from the country and back to Cambodia following several convictions that included indecent exposure and larceny.

text:
The Maryland Office of the Attorney General lost a lawsuit Thursday alleging that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement illegally ignored a subpoena.

U.S. District Judge Julie Rubin granted ICE’s motion to dismiss the suit, which Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown said his office filed after ICE “stonewalled” a civil rights investigation into the conditions at ICE’s hold rooms in Baltimore.

Rubin ruled that Brown’s office did not have standing to sue because it based its subpoena and complaint on a law that doesn’t allow it to investigate the federal government, as well as because ICE’s denial didn’t amount to an “injury.”

“The State … issued the Subpoena to a federal agency under authority of a Maryland statute that does not authorize it to do so as a matter of law,” Rubin wrote. “The Subpoena is therefore issued outside the OAG’s legal authority pursuant to (the statute cited). Pursuant to that particular provision of the Maryland Code, OAG has no cognizable right to the information requested; there is no ‘actual harm.’”

In an email, OAG spokesperson Kelsey Hartman stated, “We are reviewing the opinion.”

ICE did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Earlier this year, the attorney general began investigating a possible pattern or practice of civil rights violations by ICE at its holding facility in downtown Baltimore, which is designed for stays of less than a day but where ICE has held people for far longer.

The lawsuit was just filed days after Rubin, in a separate case, ordered ICE to end overcrowding at the “hold rooms” in the George H. Fallon Federal Building and after a video displaying the conditions inside went viral. The video appeared to validate the allegations in a class-action case alleging that ICE deprived detainees of medicine, adequate hygiene products and access to counsel. The plaintiffs alleged that the rooms were cold, they were provided only aluminum blankets, and the lights were kept on all night.

In late September, Rubin found that the rooms were still overcrowded and that ICE had violated her order, calling the agency’s conduct a “spectacular failure.”

ICE is planning to leave the Fallon Building soon. It plans to move its Baltimore regional field office to a new facility in Elkridge. It is nearly done with construction, which was on hold amid a legal challenge by the Howard County government. U.S. District Judge Adam Abelson ruled in August that local officials couldn’t revoke construction permits.

The attorney general’s office sued under a law that allows it to issue subpoenas as part of investigations into civil rights violations. The law does not allow investigations into conduct by individual people or state and local government entities, and Brown’s team argued the lack of a mention of the federal government meant it was not exempt.

Rubin disagreed, writing that “the statutory scheme appears deliberately aimed at the potentially violative conduct of ‘person(s).’ So while the universe of violative conduct is broad, the statutory scheme focuses on violative conduct by ‘person[s]’ rather than all potential actors.”

“Accordingly,” she wrote, “the court is not persuaded that the federal government falls within the Attorney General’s enforcement power simply because the legislature did not explicitly exclude it under (the law).”

She also wrote that the attorney general’s office did not adequately plead in its complaint that it was also investigating ICE’s third-party contractors and that they were subject to subpoenas. Although that claim might be “substantially valid,” she wrote, it was “procedurally incompetent.”

text:
Mayor Cherelle L. Parker’s administration told a powerful congressional oversight committee earlier this year that it does not endorse statements made by District Attorney Larry Krasner and Sheriff Rochelle Bilal about federal immigration enforcement, according to a report released Thursday.

The 18-page interim report was released by the Republican-led U.S. House Judiciary Committee less than three weeks before a midterm election when the GOP may lose its majority in the chamber. It’s part of the committee’s probe into immigration policies in Philadelphia, one of several jurisdictions that Republicans say have endangered public safety by shielding immigrants from deportation.

The report shows the Parker administration, which has largely communicated behind the scenes with the federal government about immigration enforcement, attempted to distance itself from Krasner and Bilal.

» READ MORE: House Judiciary committee criticizes Philly law enforcement over sanctuary policies

The pair each made comments about U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that went viral in January after a federal agent fatally shot a civilian in Minneapolis. Bilal called the agency “fake, wannabe law enforcement” and threatened to arrest agents.

Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel at the time released a statement clarifying that his department is in charge of municipal policing and criminal investigations, not the sheriff’s office.

A May letter to the House Judiciary Committee from then-City Solicitor Renee Garcia went further, according to the report.

“The Sheriff and District Attorney of Philadelphia are separately elected officials whose statements are wholly separate and not endorsed by Mayor Cherelle Parker’s Administration,” Garcia wrote.

Spokespeople for Krasner and Bilal did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

A spokesperson for the city’s law department declined to comment.

The Judiciary Committee’s report comes amid already heightened tensions between the city’s law enforcement agencies and a series of unrelated allegations of wrongdoing that have enveloped the sheriff’s office.

Earlier this week, Krasner publicly blamed the police department for botching a 2023 murder case against a man accused of fatally shooting Officer Shane Seiber on Saturday, drawing a defense from the police force that said it was not the time to be “assigning blame.”

Separately, Bilal is facing the prospect of independent, court-ordered supervision of her office, which has been accused of mishandling deed transfers for years. Earlier this month, the sheriff’s office admitted in court that it had found $20 million in sheriff’s sale proceeds that was supposed to have been transferred to the city, but had not been disbursed.

Krasner and Bilal have been confrontational toward federal immigration enforcement, with the progressive district attorney comparing ICE agents to Nazis, and Bilal saying that her message to agents is: “You don’t want this smoke.”

Parker, a centrist Democrat, has taken a quieter approach. While the mayor earlier this year signed legislation that effectively codified Philadelphia’s “sanctuary city” status, she has largely avoided directly criticizing President Donald Trump’s administration and its mass deportation campaign.

For years, Philadelphia’s policy has been that officials do not comply with detainer requests by ICE to hold immigrants who are already in city custody unless ICE produces a warrant signed by a judge.

» READ MORE: Mayor Parker’s restraint with Trump is both calculation and gamble as the president escalates against blue cities

Still, despite the Parker administration’s attempts to smooth over the city’s relationship with Washington Republicans, the House Judiciary Committee described Philadelphia’s government as part of the problem, saying the city’s policies of not cooperating with ICE in some circumstances are deliberately obstructive to federal law enforcement.

The committee in May requested a trove of records from the city, police department, sheriff’s office, and district attorney’s office after it accused Philadelphia of shielding immigrants who have committed crimes.

» READ MORE: What Mayor Cherelle Parker’s administration told the DOJ about Philly’s ‘sanctuary’ policies in a letter the city tried to keep secret

Between January 2024 — when Parker first took office — and June 2026, the city did not comply with 162 detainer requests from ICE, according to the report, which cited records provided by the city. Over the same time period, the report says, the city received seven judicial warrants, which the report said were either honored or involved people who were transferred to state prison after being convicted.

The committee wrote that the city released a handful of immigrants who had detainers and had previously been charged with crimes, such as assault. Those immigrants were later arrested by ICE, the report said.

However, city officials have in the past said that just because they do not comply with an ICE detainer request does not mean that the person is released into the community. Some continue to be incarcerated in city facilities or are transferred to other jurisdictions.

» READ MORE: Krasner rips Trump and House Judiciary Committee over ‘war against immigrants’

The Judiciary Committee was also deeply critical of both Bilal and Krasner for their offices’ respective policies toward immigration enforcement.

For Bilal’s part, the committee wrote that the sheriff, whose office secures the municipal courthouse in Center City, “actively obstructs ICE from making safe immigration arrests inside the city’s courthouse.” The committee wrote that, when ICE has a warrant to take custody of an immigrant, agents must wait to arrest the person until they’ve been transferred from the courthouse to the city’s prison complex.

And the committee took particular issue with Krasner, a frequent target of state and national Republican opposition to reformist styles of law enforcement. The report is critical of the office’s policy of reviewing cases against undocumented immigrants and at times seeking “immigration-neutral outcomes.”

“In practice, this means that prosecutors in Krasner’s office are not prohibited from crafting generous plea deals that avoid immigration consequences for even the worst offenders,” the committee wrote.

However, Krasner had said his office’s policy of seeking outcomes that don’t trigger deportation apply only in nonviolent cases. And he condemned the Judiciary Committee’s probe during a news conference in May, saying it was carrying out “an untruthful, authoritarian, political campaign.”

Krasner at the time also demanded the committee hold a public hearing. No such hearing has taken place.

text:
Kamal was hopeful that his summons in April for an interview at a Minneapolis immigration office wouldn’t be an issue.

A refugee from Ethiopia, Kamal entered the United States legally in 2022. He’d gone through an extensive vetting process and around ten different interviews with refugee agencies and immigration officers, proving his case over nearly a decade. Still, he had reason for concern.

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) had sent two notices to a mailbox Kamal rarely checks. By the time he found them, he’d already missed his interview.

“I knew that I was here legally,” said Kamal, who is not being identified by his legal name because he fears retaliation for speaking about his case. “But I had no idea why they called me and what they would ask.”

Kamal immediately went to the office to try and rectify the situation, hoping it could be resolved quickly. Agents at the office instructed him to go home and said they’d be in touch soon.

Shortly after, Kamal received another letter from USCIS. They were terminating his refugee status, meaning he could face deportation.

Across the Twin Cities, attorneys and legal organizations say refugees have been receiving Notices of Intent to Terminate Refugee Status (NOITs) as a continuation of Operation PARRIS, a federal operation claiming to target fraud among legal refugees in the state. These notices have largely funneled refugees into the asylum system, which is burdened by severe backlogs and where refugees face increasingly difficult chances of being granted asylum.

For refugees in Minnesota who have fled persecution, the federal government’s latest crackdown is another challenge to overcome.

“I’m very stressed,” Kamal said. “I don’t sleep.”

Operation PARRIS’s Next Act

In January, the Department of Homeland Security announced Operation PARRIS. In the weeks that followed, federal immigration officials began detaining refugees appearing in person for interviews and promptly transferring them to detention centers in Texas.

Several court rulings in late January and February halted detentions from the operation, but re-vetting interviews for refugees across Minnesota continued in the months following. Refugees often received no more than 48 hours of notice for interviews, which lasted up to eight hours and discussed their original applications in extreme detail.

These interviews were not conducted to examine specific claims, but rather, to catch discrepancies between refugees’ new interviews and interviews they gave years earlier when they originally filed for refugee status, according to Laurie Ball Cooper, vice president for U.S. Legal Programs at International Refugee Assistance Project.

“They were absolutely a fishing expedition,” she said.

Immigrants seeking refugee status are highly vetted before entering the United States. The government assesses their identities and determines whether they pose a security threat. The government also evaluates whether they’ve experienced persecution or have a “well-founded” fear of persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, political opinion or affiliation with a particular social group.

Refugees who are admitted into the United States receive initial financial assistance for resettlement, are authorized to work and have a legal pathway to permanent residency.

Ball Cooper said interviews peaked in February and March before abruptly coming to a halt. Weeks later, USCIS began sending out the refugee termination notices from an office in Georgia tasked with conducting a computer-based review of refugee cases. The written notices outline the government’s intent to terminate someone’s refugee status, and affords them a window of time to provide evidence for why their status should not be revoked.

As was the case with Kamal, Ball Cooper said many of the notices did not reach recipients.

“They were delivered in strange ways,” she said. “Many were hand delivered to landlord offices; there were a lot of missed notices.”

Refugees receiving the notices had previously been given 30 days to respond and provide evidence to support retaining their status. However, a new interim rule posted by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday shortened the window to 10 days, citing the need to “mitigate risks to national security” and “prevent fraud and exploitation.”

The new rule makes it impossible to respond to the notices in time, said Rachel Kohler, supervising attorney at the International Institute of Minnesota, a nonprofit that supports new immigrants in the state.

Kohler said attorneys frequently need to file a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request with the U.S. government before submitting a response to the termination notice. FOIA requests provide attorneys with a copy of a client’s original interviews being scrutinized by USCIS and allow them to address specific claims levied by the agency.

With the new 10-day timeline, Kohler said requests will not arrive in time.

USCIS Spokesman Zach Kahler said in a statement to Sahan Journal that the rule is an attempt to accelerate terminations of refugee status.

“U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has found an alarming erosion of screening and vetting measures under the Biden Administration,” the statement read. “This interim final rule ensures that when DHS determines an alien did not meet the definition of a refugee at the time of admission, USCIS can now move promptly and efficiently to terminate that status.”

Kohler said FOIA requests have returned interviews that are heavily redacted by the government, leaving out key information material to USCIS’ decision to terminate an individual’s status. That means that for attorneys responding to the termination notices, there is limited recourse to address claims the government made in the notices to justify terminating a client’s status.

“It’s USCIS’s explanation of what happened at these various interviews, but we can’t see what actually happened because we can’t see the materials ourselves,” Kohler said.

Are you credible?

Attorneys and advocates say the notices have offered frivolous reasons for terminating refugee status. USCIS has based terminations on a review of refugees’ “credibility,” a highly subjective process, attorneys said.

“When they’re making these credibility determinations, it’s totally and completely discretionary whether or not an officer finds a client to be credible or not,” Koehler said. “And so our ability to request a waiver of that or to respond to that is really limited.”

Reasons for terminating status have been wide ranging, hinging primarily on differences between refugees’ interviews during their original application process or their new interviews under Operation PARRIS. In some instances, failure to provide information alone has been sufficient.

“In one of our cases, they brought up the fact that, ‘In this interview, you talked about this arrest, but in this interview, you didn’t,’” Koehler said. “So it’s not even providing different information, it’s just you didn’t tell us about this one in the second interview and you did in the first.”

Attorneys say that social media reviews have also been used as justification for deeming a refugee as not credible. Minneapolis immigration attorney Luke Srodulski said one of his clients received a termination notice that cited multiple social media posts as evidence that their risk of persecution in their home country was not well-founded.

“USCIS listed off social media posts from both before and after he was granted refugee status and used that to say, ‘Oh, you actually supported these people that you said were involved in your persecution,’” Srodulski said.

Srodulski added that the social media posts were largely reposts, and not actual opinions expressed by his client.

The scale of refugee status terminations is unclear, though Ball Cooper said the International Refugee Assistance Project has yet to see large numbers of notices outside of Minnesota.

Danielle Hendrickson, managing attorney at Mid-Minnesota Legal Aid, believes that hundreds of refugees in Minnesota are potentially affected by the notices. Hendrickson said her organization has seen subjective criteria and discrepancies between interviews used to determine whether a refugee’s fear of persecution is credible.

“They are trying to find really minute details that are different in an interview that happened 10 years ago,” Hendrickson said. “And what I have seen is that they may actually have nothing to do with the refugee claim.

“Whether there was misrepresentation in some of the cases I have seen doesn’t actually get at whether somebody was a refugee and continues to be a refugee.”

Ball Cooper and Hendrickson said the highly discretionary reviews also raise legal concerns around admissibility — an immigrant’s right to enter the country or obtain lawful permanent residence. Refugees entering the United States are extensively vetted, participating in several admission interviews and screenings from multiple government agencies. The termination notices are retroactively changing this process, Ball Cooper said.

“Often somebody at a desk in Georgia is re-evaluating the credibility of the refugee based on only information that was available at the time of the original decision,” Ball Cooper said. “[They are] overriding the decision of a specially trained refugee officer.”

New country, new challenges

Kamal left Ethiopia in 2000, fleeing political turmoil that gripped the country in violence.

Fearing further persecution, he crossed into neighboring Kenya with his family, staying at the Kakoma Refugee Camp before moving to Nairobi. As retribution for his father’s political affiliations, he spent multiple spells in prison in Ethiopia, enduring nearly two years of torture at different military camps run by the ruling Tigrayan People’s Liberation Front. Only after soldiers from the opposing Oromo Liberation Front raided the camp he was being held at in 1997 was he able to escape.

Kamal worked several jobs in Nairobi, including as a tailor and taxi driver. After years of interviews with resettlement agencies and immigration officers, he was granted admission to the United States as a refugee in 2022. Kamal resettled in Minnesota, working as a patient care assistant and driver to send money back to his children in Kenya.

After having his refugee status terminated in June, however, Kamal is now in removal proceedings in Fort Snelling Immigration Court, meaning the U.S. government is actively trying to deport him.

“I’m frustrated,” he said. “I have no idea what will happen.”

USCIS alleged that Kamal had made inconsistent statements across his interviews, determining that he had “not met his burden of establishing credibility.” Kamal vehemently denies USCIS’s allegations, saying his statements have not changed since his early interviews in Kenya.

“They are the ones actually twisted,” he said. “My statement was consistent and that’s how I came here.”

At the heart of USCIS’s allegations against Kamal are statements he gave about his role in a payment made to an individual associated with the Oromo Liberation Front. USCIS classified the group as a Tier III terrorist organization, and said the alleged inconsistencies in Kamal’s statement excluded him from refugee status when he entered the United States.

Tier III terrorist organizations are the lowest level of classified terrorist threat, do not require any official organization and fall under a broad definition of activity. Unlike Tier I and II terrorist organizations, Tier III terrorist groups are not on any official government list, and their determination is made on a case-by-case basis by immigration officers and judges.

Kamal denies sending any money to the individual in question, and maintains his statements have been consistent across interviews.

He’s now in immigration removal proceedings at Fort Snelling, where respondents face increasingly tight odds of success. He says returning to Ethiopia could be a death sentence.

“I could be disappeared at the airport,” he said.

Expanding Operation PARRIS

While cases targeting refugees have thus far been concentrated in Minnesota, several legal documents and policy memos have pointed to the Trump administration’s desire to expand operations.

In February, International Refugee Assistance Project filed a lawsuit against the administration, asking a judge to put a stop to Operation PARRIS-style detentions nationwide. A court ruling in March granted a temporary pause on detentions, but the case remains in litigation and awaits a permanent decision.

The government still wants to remove refugees from across the country, Ball Cooper said.

“They have not abandoned their desire to terrorize refugees nationwide with this,” Ball Cooper said. “They just cannot currently pursue it because of the court order.”

At the International Institute of Minnesota, Kohler said the wave of refugee terminations has unfairly targeted people who have already undergone extensive vetting prior to coming to the United States.

“They’ve done everything correctly,” Kohler said. “They have passed all of the tests and all of the vetting procedures both overseas and in the United States.”

Kamal is one of them. Today, with his future in the country hanging in the balance, he feels perpetually at risk. He said he limits his time away from home for fear of being detained by immigration authorities, and feels many of the same concerns that drove him to leave Ethiopia over 25 years ago.

“That’s why I left my home country,” he said. “If I had peace there, I wouldn’t have left. Now I am going through all this.”

text:
WASHINGTON – Representatives Brittany Pettersen (CO-07), Joyce Beatty (OH-03) and Robin Kelly (IL-02) today announced their demand for answers from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) about its failure to account for miscarriages and other pregnancy-related medical outcomes of its detainees since Donald Trump has aggressively increased the detention of undocumented immigrants, legal immigrants, and even in some cases American citizens. In a letter to Acting Director David Venturella, the lawmakers warn that a full year of pregnancy-related outcomes remains unaccounted for as reports describe pregnant women struggling to obtain basic and emergency medical care.

According to agency records, at least 18 women miscarried while in custody from January 2025 through October 3, 2025. Yet, despite these alarming and unprecedented numbers, ICE has failed to collect, maintain, or disclose data on miscarriages since the last report on October 3, 2025.

“Women are reporting pregnancy emergencies without adequate care, and ICE cannot even account for how many women have miscarried in its custody. That is appalling,” said Congresswoman Brittany Pettersen. “As a mom, I’m horrified by what these women describe. ICE must answer for these failures, provide the missing records, and ensure every person in its custody receives the care they need.”

“I’m horrified by the growing number of reported miscarriages and the blatant disregard for women’s health in ICE detention facilities,” said Congresswoman Joyce Beatty. “Donald Trump’s Department of Homeland Security has a responsibility to account for these pregnancy-related medical outcomes and ensure that women in its custody are receiving the care they need. We cannot allow a lack of transparency and accountability to put more women and unborn children at risk. We are demanding answers, and we won’t stop until we have them.”

"In the first 9 months of the second Trump administration alone, at least 18 women miscarried in ICE custody, and since then ICE has just stopped counting. Pregnant women in custody have continuously been denied access to routine and emergency medical care. Where is their humanity?" said Congresswoman Robin Kelly. "My colleagues and I are demanding accountability and real answers. Everyone – no matter where you're from – deserves to be treated with dignity and respect."

“It is well documented that incarceration significantly worsens maternal health outcomes and increases risks for pregnancy loss, including miscarriages and adverse birth events, due to high stress, poor nutrition, and limited access to quality medical care,” the members wrote in the letter. “Firsthand accounts from detainees indicate they are struggling to access routine and emergency medical care, including not being scheduled for blood tests or an ultrasound to confirm a healthy pregnancy and not receiving prenatal vitamins. The agency has also reportedly denied repeated requests for medical records from detainees, leaving them in the dark about their medical history and the need for any additional follow-up care.”

ICE’s own policy says it generally should not detain people known to be pregnant, postpartum, or nursing for administrative immigration violations, unless release is prohibited by law or exceptional circumstances exist. When those individuals are detained, the policy requires access to specialized medical care and restricts the use of certain restraints. Despite those safeguards, records cited in the letter show that the number of pregnant women and adolescents in detention rose from at least 87 in October 2025 to 101 in November 2025.

The lawmakers describe reports of delayed emergency treatment, barriers to specialist care, and people going without blood tests, ultrasounds, or prenatal vitamins. Some detainees have also reportedly been denied repeated requests for their medical records, making it harder to understand their treatment and obtain follow-up care.

The letter demands complete responses by November 6, 2026, including:

The number of pregnant people detained and how ICE justifies detention under its “exceptional circumstances” standard.

A full accounting of miscarriages, stillbirths, serious pregnancy complications, hospitalizations, and emergency transfers since October 3, 2025.

An explanation of missing data, efforts to recover it, and when agency leadership learned about reporting failures.

Records of outside medical care that was denied or delayed, complaints about pregnancy-related care, and investigations into potential violations.

Trump’s expansion of immigration detention does not give ICE free rein to disregard its own safeguards or evade congressional oversight and dehumanize those within its custody. The agency is responsible for the people it holds—and must answer for their treatment.

She has voted against enforcement funding packages, backed legislation requiring agents to visibly identify themselves, and supported restoring protections for schools, hospitals, and places of worship. Alongside Senators Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper, she demanded that the administration abandon plans for a new ICE detention facility in Hudson, Colorado. She has also pressed for answers about prolonged detention in field office holding cells and proposed safeguards to protect detained parents’ children and prevent immigration detainees from being held in federal prisons.
