title: In 100th lawsuit against Trump, California challenges immigration arrests near courthouses
description:
California sued the Trump administration for the 100th time in under two years Thursday, challenging the practice of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arresting people for alleged civil immigration violations at or near state courthouses.
Gen. Xavier Becerra, a current gubernatorial candidate — sued the Trump administration more than 120 times over four years.
Although the lawsuit focused on immigration courthouses, the ruling also covered state criminal courthouses, restoring earlier restrictions that barred civil immigration arrests in or near courthouses except in limited circumstances.
The Trump administration is appealing the ruling.
Since then, California court officials have tracked arrests by federal agents and reported them to the Judicial Council of California.
text:
California sued the Trump administration for the 100th time in under two years Thursday, challenging the practice of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arresting people for alleged civil immigration violations at or near state courthouses.

California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta said such arrests have long been barred because they are unconstitutional and deeply disruptive to the rule of law and the rights of victims, witnesses, defendants and other parties to court proceedings.

"We've seen serious criminal charges dropped and entire cases jeopardized because victims and witnesses are too scared to come to the courthouse to testify," Bonta said. "Our justice system cannot function this way."

Bonta said his office having to take the Trump administration to court 100 times in less than two years, often alongside other Democrat-led states, was a "sobering milestone" and a reflection not of political interference on California's part — as the president and his supporters have cast it — but of Trump's nearly unbridled lawlessness.

"It's very troubling when the most powerful person on the planet and the president of our country is the one trampling over the Constitution, breaking the law so blatantly and brazenly, so consistently, so frequently," Bonta said.

Independent legal experts said several factors have driven the wave of lawsuits.

Read more: With midterms underway, Justice Department presses California to withhold flagged voters' ballots

Presidents from both parties have increasingly flexed their executive power, and state attorneys general have increasingly sued in response. During Trump's first term in office, California — under the leadership of then-Atty. Gen. Xavier Becerra, a current gubernatorial candidate — sued the Trump administration more than 120 times over four years. Texas Atty. Gen. Ken Paxton — now a Republican candidate for Senate — sued the Biden administration just over 100 times in four years.

Trump in this term quickly began implementing an array of policies left over from his first term or outlined in the Project 2025 policy blueprint, many of which Bonta and other Democratic attorneys general were prepared to sue over, experts said.

Trump was also able to appoint a host of loyalists with the help of the Republican-controlled Congress, who helped advance policies that less loyal agency heads would have balked at, and which were sure to draw additional legal challenges, experts said.

Daniel Farber, a professor at UC Berkeley Law School and author of "Contested Ground: How to Understand the Limits of Presidential Power," said California's raft of lawsuits is a result of the current Trump administration "doing more aggressive things right off the starting block" — but also repeatedly targeting California specifically.

Bonta claimed in August that his lawsuits had saved California more than $200 billion, namely by reversing Trump cuts to federal funding meant for the state.

The White House has consistently derided Bonta's litigation against the administration as baseless and misguided. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis on Thursday said Bonta should stop bragging about "filing frivolous lawsuits" and "focus on addressing problems in his own state."

"The reality is, with well over 25 Supreme Court victories, the administration's policies have been consistently upheld as lawful, despite some lower courts issuing an unprecedented number of lawless injunctions," Bis said.

ICE, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment, has defended its arrests near courthouses as a "common sense" approach to apprehending offenders at times and locations where authorities know they will be.

The 100th case

Bonta's lawsuit argues that such arrests are arbitrary and capricious given the chilling effect they have on justice in the state. They violate the Immigration and Nationality Act as intended by Congress, and interfere with California's rights under the 10th Amendment to execute its "core sovereign judicial and police functions," Bonta's office said.

His arguments echo those made by other state officials in the past. During Trump's first term, for example, then-California Supreme Court Chief Justice Tani G. Cantil-Sakauye called the arrests "disruptive, shortsighted and counterproductive."

Arrests at or near courthouses began to rise again after Trump took office in January 2025. An ICE memo, issued in May 2025, said agents could conduct "civil immigration enforcement actions in or near courthouses when they have credible information that leads them to believe the targeted alien(s) is or will be present at a specific location."

Incidents quickly began cropping up. In June 2025, ICE agents arrested two women outside a Los Angeles County courthouse after a hearing in a local criminal case. The same unfolded across the state.

Alejandro Barraza, a criminal defense and immigration attorney, said he has witnessed the effect firsthand.

In October 2025, a client was arrested driving home from a hearing at the Riverside County Hall of Justice. In December, another client was arrested leaving the Rancho Cucamonga courthouse. And a third client chose to plead guilty in his criminal case rather than go to jury trial, despite Barraza's advice that the case was worth fighting, for fear of being arrested by ICE.

"The victims are losing," Barraza said. "Our clients are losing their rights to due process. Everyone is losing."

In June, U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts in San Francisco struck down ICE's expanded courthouse arrest policies nationwide. Although the lawsuit focused on immigration courthouses, the ruling also covered state criminal courthouses, restoring earlier restrictions that barred civil immigration arrests in or near courthouses except in limited circumstances. The Trump administration is appealing the ruling.

Since then, California court officials have tracked arrests by federal agents and reported them to the Judicial Council of California. Thirty people were taken into custody in June, 29 in July, 19 in August and 14 in September.

Read more: California leads lawsuit challenging Trump's rollback of fuel economy rules

State legislators have tried to push back. Last month, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a law strengthening California's protections against civil arrests for people traveling to, attending or leaving courthouses for lawful purposes. The measure extends those protections to public ways within 1,000 feet of court facilities, while preserving an exception for arrests made under a valid judicial warrant.

Bonta said his lawsuit is necessary despite the new California law, in part because the Trump administration thinks that "no state law applies to them," and courts have in some cases agreed — including the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, which this week blocked a state law that would have required federal immigration agents to display identification while working in the state.

The wider legal battle

Bonta's office has had substantial success in halting some of the Trump administration's biggest policy moves — including its plans to end birthright citizenship for the U.S.-born children of immigrants, its worldwide tariffs, its deployment of National Guard troops in Los Angeles and other U.S. cities, and its withholding of billions of dollars in federal funding allocated to the state by Congress.

Michael McConnell, director of the Constitutional Law Center at Stanford Law School, said many of California's lawsuits have been "legally meritorious," as there is a "whole lot of legal error" coming out of the Trump administration — with a "lot of the overreach" having been "facilitated by the lack of internal checks" from loyal Trump agency heads.

However, he also said that as a California taxpayer, he doesn't "appreciate having government using my tax dollars for what essentially are in many cases ideological lawsuits, even if meritorious," because private litigants can and often do bring lawsuits of their own. He said he felt the same way about many of the lawsuits brought against the Biden administration by Republican states.

Bonta said he is proud of his team for challenging the Trump administration every time they believed it had broken the law and harmed California, despite Trump's intentional effort to make that difficult.

"It was a shock and awe," he said. "It was flood the zone. It was trying to overwhelm with speed and volume, and we kept pace every time."

What happens next, he said, will depend on Trump. If he keeps breaking the law in ways that hurt the state or its residents, Bonta said he'll keep getting sued by California.

text:
Professor Margaret Satterthwaite ’99, the United Nations special rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, has been selected as a recipient of the 2026 Eleanor Roosevelt Prize for Global Human Rights Advancement. Awarded by the American Bar Association (ABA) Center for Human Rights, the prize honors those whose work has advanced the principles set forth in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which was championed by Eleanor Roosevelt.

In its announcement of the prize, the ABA referred to Satterthwaite’s work as special rapporteur since her appointment by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022. In her reports to the council and to the General Assembly, Satterthwaite has identified emerging threats and issues related to judicial systems across the globe, including improper influence exerted on the judiciary by corporations and wealthy individuals; necessary safeguards to protect judges, lawyers, prosecutors, and community justice workers from intimidation and reprisal; and Indigenous peoples’ right to develop and maintain justice systems.

In her UN role, Satterthwaite has also spoken out against threats in the United States, such as executive branch actions targeting law firms, lawyers, and federal judges, and advocated for withdrawing sanctions on International Criminal Court judges and prosecutors. She collaborated with the special rapporteur on the human rights of migrants in documenting the federal government’s efforts to execute executive policy through US immigration courts.

Satterthwaite will receive the prize during a November 30 ceremony at the New York City Bar Association along with this year’s other recipient, Lawyers for Lawyers, a nonprofit based in the Netherlands. Since its inauguration in 2018, the prize has honored individuals and organizations such as Hillary Rodham Clinton, Dr. Anthony Fauci, Billie Jean King, the American Civil Liberties Union, Amnesty International, the Elton John AIDS Foundation, Human Rights Watch, Lambda Legal, and the NAACP Legal Defense Fund.

At NYU Law, Satterthwaite serves as faculty director of the Center for Human Rights and Global Justice and the Robert and Helen Bernstein Institute for Human Rights. In the Legal Empowerment and Judicial Independence Clinic, she gives her students the opportunity to participate in her work as special rapporteur. Previously, she directed the Global Justice Clinic.

Satterthwaite, the author or co-author of more than a dozen human rights reports and dozens of scholarly articles and book chapters, has focused her recent research on judicial independence, autocratization and the rule of law, legal empowerment, and wellbeing among human rights workers. After graduating from NYU Law, she clerked for Judge Betty Fletcher of the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit and the judges of the International Court of Justice. Satterthwaite subsequently worked for human rights organizations including Amnesty International, Human Rights First, and the Commission Nationale de Vérité et de Justice in Haiti before joining the NYU Law faculty in 2006.

title: Trump administration sued over accelerated immigration process for migrant kids
description: (CNN) — A group of attorneys filed a lawsuit Thursday challenging the accelerated immigration process for unaccompanied migrant children, saying the Trump administration’s policies are unlawful.
text:
Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary, is defending her legal back…

Ukraine attacked a Russian oil refinery, abandoning a brief truce involving ener…



Migrant children as young as two are showing up at immigration courts nationwide, many without attorneys, to make their case to stay in the US.





(CNN) — A group of attorneys filed a lawsuit Thursday challenging the accelerated immigration process for unaccompanied migrant children, saying the Trump administration’s policies are unlawful.

Under President Donald Trump, unaccompanied migrant children have been increasingly forced to navigate a complicated and accelerated immigration process with dwindling help after the administration ended a long-standing contract for legal services this summer — and as administration officials try to wrap their cases at an unprecedented pace.

“This is not the immigration process that Congress intended for unaccompanied children; it is a deportation assembly line depriving them of their rights,” the lawsuit states. Thursday’s lawsuit was filed by six legal service providers who work with unaccompanied migrant kids.

It focuses on unaccompanied migrant children who are residing with family in the US or are detained, either after recently crossing the US southern border or because their guardians were picked up by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Detained children are held in shelters operated by the Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Refugee Resettlement, which is charged with their care.

CNN previously reported that children are contending with a fast-tracked immigration process, including abruptly rescheduled asylum interviews, sometimes with only a 24-hour notice — and increasingly without legal help. Migrant children as young as 2 are also showing up at immigration courts nationwide, many without attorneys, to make their case to stay in the US and avoid deportation.

Like adults, children must also go through immigration proceedings and present evidence to back up their asylum claim, and there’s no requirement for them to have legal representation throughout the process.

According to attorneys, asylum interviews have been abruptly pushed up.

“Since August 1, 2026, Plaintiffs have collectively received more than 600 notices of asylum interviews scheduled to take place in quick succession. Their attorneys are expected to represent children in multiple asylum interviews on the same day, sometimes at the same time, forcing them to forgo preparation and severely limiting their ability to effectively represent their unaccompanied child clients,” the lawsuit states.

“For these children, who risk being sent back to the countries they fled, the stakes could not be higher,” it continues.

The lawsuit calls for a return to the status quo — for example, when children were given at least 21 days notice prior to their asylum interview — and cites a federal law that’s been in place for nearly two decades, the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008, that’s supposed to provide protections for unaccompanied migrant children.

The lawsuit was filed in the US District Court for the District of Maryland.

The Trump administration has previously denied claims that cases are being fast-tracked, arguing that officials prioritize timely completion of cases. And in a statement to CNN last month, an HHS spokesperson said, “ORR will continue facilitating the ability of [unaccompanied alien children] in its custody to fully participate in immigration legal proceedings with representation by counsel, including hearings before EOIR immigration judges, who manage their own juvenile case dockets and schedules and make independent decisions on asylum claims under consideration.”

text:
SAN ANTONIO – Two days after the City of San Antonio sued to block the conversion of an East Side warehouse to a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention and processing facility, councilmembers indicated they want to explore ways to fight the agency moving into leased space at Brooks.

Councilmembers voted 9-2 Thursday approving a resolution to work and coordinate with community stakeholders on efforts to prevent or delay an ICE detention facility in the city’s urban core.

At Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones’ urging, the council first added language asking them to also take similar steps to block or delay the execution of recently reported, 15-year leases at a building at Brooks, which federal records show are linked to ICE and will reportedly be occupied by attorneys and support staff.

“I think we should take the opportunity to also communicate that we — for those of us up here that do — do not support the establishment of such a strong legal footprint. Which would again enable, I think, an even stronger presence and a type of facilitation network that would set up a larger presence here,” Jones said.

A majority of councilmembers have opposed the planned conversion of a 640,000-square-foot warehouse into a processing facility, with a planned daily population of up to 1,500 people.

On Tuesday, the city sued the Department of Homeland Security, ICE, and the heads of both agencies, arguing the government had not done a required environmental review process.

“ICE has gone rogue and at the very least, we must take action to protect all San Antonians from this threat,” Jalen McKee-Rodriguez (D2), who represents the area where the facility is planned, said at Thursday’s meeting.

Councilwoman Phyllis Viagran (D3) had pushed for Thursday’s original resolution, but she opposed the mayor’s amendment, noting “Preston Hollow holds the lease.”

“We cannot come in and say, ‘You, Preston Hollow, can’t lease out to these people.’ So that’s where it gets difficult, and that why I didn’t want to — if legally we can’t do it, I don’t want to vote for what it is,” Viagran said, though she noted she ultimately voted for the amended version.

Federal records show the leases are worth $42.5 million and $9.8 million for a combined $52.3 million.

Notice identification numbers on the documents link back to separate federal records indicating the leases were meant for ICE.

Preston Hollow Community Capital, which has a controlling interest in the WatersEdge office buildings, told KSAT the leases at WatersEdge II building on Inner Circle Drive are for administrative office space.

They said they have no involvement in the East Side detention facility.

“We recognize the community’s concerns about immigration detention facilities and want to be clear about the federal office leases at WatersEdge on the Brooks campus. These leases are for administrative office space and expressly prohibit detention facilities, holding cells, and the processing of individuals or families in custody.

We understand the space will consolidate existing San Antonio-based functions of the Department of Justice’s Executive Office for Immigration Review and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Office of the Principal Legal Advisor. The anticipated occupants are attorneys and support staff."

Preston Hollow Community Capital

The EOIR “conducts immigration court proceedings, appellate reviews, and administrative hearings,” according to its website, while OPLA represents DHS in immigration removal proceedings before the EOIR.

A DHS spokesperson told KSAT in an emailed statement that ICE would not confirm office locations, claiming a “coordinated campaign of violence” against its officers.

“Is it really news that when a federal agency hires more personnel that they need more space?” the emailed statement continues. “Thanks to the Big Beautiful Bill, we have an additional 12,000 ICE officers and agents on the ground across the country. That’s a 120% increase in our workforce.”

San Antonio’s two conservative council members, Misty Spears (D9) and Marc Whyte (D10), voted against Thursday’s resolution and have also opposed the lawsuit.

“This has nothing to do with environmental impacts. I mean, this is all ... fluff and cover and a pretext for wanting to send a certain message to people,” Whyte said.

text:
EL PASO, Texas – Legal organizations filed a motion for preliminary injunction today demanding ICE provide adequate healthcare and improve conditions for people detained at Camp East Montana, the nation’s largest immigration detention facility located on the Fort Bliss military base in El Paso, Texas.

The motion comes as ICE is on track to have its deadliest fiscal year on record, as deaths in detention have nearly doubled since last fall, including three deaths at Camp East Montana alone.

The motion, which was supported by more than 40 declarations from people currently or formerly detained at Camp East Montana, loved ones of people who have died, and correctional and medical experts, describes the government's systemic failure to provide adequate medical care and humane living conditions.

The conditions reported include medical neglect, unsanitary and unsafe conditions, confinement to windowless tents for 23 to 24 hours a day, barriers to legal counsel, and such little food that people experience substantial weight loss and other serious medical conditions. People detained at the facility also describe being physically beaten by guards and confined in extreme isolation as punishment for seeking help.

“The conditions reported in those declarations shock the conscience,” Dean Williams (he/him), a former state prison director who evaluated the conditions in Camp East Montana, wrote in support of the motion. “People describe degrading, unsafe, and unsanitary conditions, abuse by guards, and extreme restrictions and harsh treatment far beyond those of the most secure prisons I have overseen.”

In May of 2026, the American Civil Liberties Union, ACLU of Texas, Texas Civil Rights Project, and Farella Braun + Martel LLP filed their lawsuit against ICE after the federal government began detaining thousands of people in a tent encampment on the Fort Bliss military base in the El Paso desert. The facility has repeatedly come under fire since its opening in August 2025 following rampant reports of abusive, inhumane, and deadly conditions.

Quotes from named plaintiffs in the lawsuit are as follows:

“Urgent protection is desperately needed at Camp East Montana,” said named plaintiff Gerald Akari Angye. “Today, people are still being detained in this windowless camp with inadequate food, water, medicine, and recreation. People with health issues do not receive the care they need. This case remains important to me because I am a voice for those harmed by this regime. I will never be the same after the violence I experienced by guards at Camp East Montana. Many others are still being held in those horrible conditions. The United States preaches democracy and human rights, but it is separating families and torturing people who are seeking safety. The world is watching. The inhumane conditions at Camp East Montana seem to be getting worse. No one of good conscience can support what is happening there. I plead with the court to give relief to people held in the horrible Camp East Montana.”

“It’s hard for outside observers to understand what people go through at Camp East Montana,” said named plaintiff Navdeep. “That’s why we are sharing our stories. I don’t want people to continue suffering and experiencing the terrible conditions I experienced there. We need the court to take action to immediately improve conditions at Camp East Montana and to prevent additional suffering.”

“Camp East Montana is not built to accommodate the basic needs of people,” said named plaintiff ZOR. “If the court fails to intervene, things may get even worse. If nothing is done, I worry it will be a signal that it is okay that for the law to continue being ignored at Camp East Montana. I believe the conditions at Camp East Montana are meant to break people down emotionally and to punish them so they become desperate to leave. It is unbearable to be mistreated every day and trapped in a dirty room with up to 72 people. Many of us are only able to endure it because of the strength we get from the thought of our families.”

Additional quotes from co-counsel are as follows:

"The need for court-ordered relief is urgent," said Savannah Kumar (she/they), staff attorney at the ACLU of Texas. “For the past year, the government has disappeared thousands of people into its desert camp that has been the site of beatings by guards, death, disease, and hunger. The situation has continued to deteriorate. People held inside tents describe the denial of desperately needed medical care, environmental hazards, and filthy conditions. These unbearable conditions violate U.S. law and erode the moral fabric of our country. A preliminary injunction is necessary to prevent additional death and abuses at the largest immigration detention camp in the country. All of us, no matter where we were born, are created equal and are entitled to dignity that is being systematically denied at this horrific tent camp.”

“We cannot wait any longer,” said Rita Lomio (she/her), Senior Counsel at the ACLU’s National Prison Project. “ICE and the Department of Defense have long known of the cruel and deadly conditions at the tent encampment on the Fort Bliss military base. They have demonstrated time and again that they cannot or will not act to end the abuse. Former prison and jail directors have found that conditions at Camp East Montana are unprecedented and make all who live and work at the encampment unsafe. While litigation continues, a preliminary injunction is needed to end the most egregious abuses before more people needlessly suffer and die.”

“State-sanctioned violence is occurring in and outside of facilities like Camp East Montana, and the blatant disregard for human life and access to basic health care should shock the conscience of every American,” said Rochelle Garza (she/her), President of the Texas Civil Rights Project. “If we, as a society, say nothing and go along with the notion that certain lives matter less than others, the government’s abuse and neglect will continue to be normalized. Our preliminary injunction is an effort to stop ICE, and the harm that has seeped into the walls of their detention facilities, from going unchecked.”

“Detention does not strip individuals of their fundamental rights to safety, dignity, and necessary medical care,” said Cynthia Castillo (she/her), partner at Farella Braun + Martel LLP. “The record in this case shows deeply troubling medical neglect, dangerous living conditions, and mistreatment that demand immediate action. A preliminary injunction is essential to prevent further irreparable harm and to ensure that individuals detained at Camp East Montana are treated humanely while their legal claims are heard.”

title: University entanglement with carceral border institutions: Medical Education, dual loyalty ...
description:
Investigative reporting by independent Italian magazine Altreconomia recently exposed institutional proposals for medical students at an Albanian university to be placed directly within the Gjadër pre-removal detention facility.
The 2023 bilateral agreement established the two immigration detention facilities within the Albanian territory, operating under formal Italian legal jurisdiction, but outside Italian territory through physical displacement.
Drawing on concepts of structural violence, carceral geography, and medical ethics, we argue that utilising carceral border institutions as educational spaces transform the university into an infrastructural arm of a coercive border regime.
When a university inserts its students into this carceral space, it is not placing them in a neutral clinical environment.
The Italy-Albania protocol represents a political experiment of border and detention externalisation, separating the execution of domestic sovereignty from domestic territory.
text:
Guest post by Nicola Cocco, Kristina Millona, Patrizia Borsellino, Vittorio Agnoletto, Antonello D’Elia, Lara Tavoschi, Francesca Cimino, Fabio Perocco, Francesca Esposito, Chiara Montaldo, and Camilla Ponti.

Nicola is an infectious disease specialist with the Italian Society of Migration Medicine (SIMM) and an activist with Rete Mai più lager No ai CPR. Kristina is an independent researcher and journalist from Albania. Patrizia is a former Professor at the Department of Legal Philosophy and Bioethics at the University of Milano-Bicocca. Vittorio is a physician and representative of Medicina Democratica. Antonello is a psychiatrist, president of the Italian Society of Democratic Psychiatry. Lara is a Professor at the Department of Translational Research and New Technologies in Medicine and Surgery at the University of Pisa. Francesca Cimino is a researcher at the Department of Philosophy and Cultural Heritage at Ca' Foscari University of Venice. Fabio is a Professor at the Department of Philosophy and Cultural Heritage at Ca' Foscari University of Venice. Francesca Esposito is a Researcher at the Department of Psychology 'Renzo Canestrari' at the University of Bologna and a Research Associate at the Centre for Criminology at the University of Oxford. Chiara is Head of Medical Unit with Doctors Without Borders (MSF) Italy. Camilla is a psychologist and activist with Rete Mai più lager No ai CPR.

This post is part of Border Criminologies' thematic series on healthcare and detention. It was previously published in Italian in a slightly revised form on Salute Internazionale.

In contemporary migration scholarship, the concept of border externalisation has expanded significantly beyond traditional maritime interceptions and third-country readmission agreements. Today, it encompasses intricate legal, geopolitical, and structural manoeuvres designed to displace state obligations towards people on the move. Most recently, this has extended to university campuses.

Investigative reporting by independent Italian magazine Altreconomia recently exposed institutional proposals for medical students at an Albanian university to be placed directly within the Gjadër pre-removal detention facility. The facility is one of two centres established under a bilateral protocol signed in November 2023 between the Italian and Albanian governments. The rationale for the placements frames the carceral setting as a "unique didactic opportunity" and a practical laboratory for learning migration medicine and transcultural healthcare under extreme conditions. As healthcare practitioners and academics, we are extremely concerned about this framing, which normalizes an institution of structural violence under the guise of medical education.

The centre in Gjadër, and a similar facility in Shengjin, are critical manifestations of Italy’s externalisation trend in recent years. The 2023 bilateral agreement established the two immigration detention facilities within the Albanian territory, operating under formal Italian legal jurisdiction, but outside Italian territory through physical displacement.

The facility in Gjadër is a carbon copy of Pre-Removal Detention Centres in Italy (Centri di Permanenza per il Rimpatrio, or CPRs). These centres are characterised by prolonged, punitive containment policies designed to expedite deportation procedures. Legal scholars, human rights advocates, and criminologists have vigorously critiqued the Italy-Albania protocol’s violations of European and international asylum law.

Drawing on concepts of structural violence, carceral geography, and medical ethics, we argue that utilising carceral border institutions as educational spaces transform the university into an infrastructural arm of a coercive border regime. This clinical and pedagogic co-optation compromises the foundational ethical mandate of health professionals – the principle of non-maleficence – and ensnares students in structural “dual loyalty” dynamics before they develop the systemic critique necessary for professional resistance. Ultimately, when medical training is embedded within such oppressive institutions, the formation of future healthcare practitioners becomes structurally embedded in the state-sanctioned production of racist border violence.

Total institutions, carceral geographies, and structural violence

To fully understand the dangers of this pedagogical integration, we situate administrative detention centres within Erving Goffman’s sociological framework of the "total institution". Total institutions are characterised by the complete breakdown of barriers that normally separate the spheres of sleep, play, and work. In these spaces, all aspects of life are conducted in the same place and under the same single authority, strictly scheduled and enforced through a system of explicit formal rules and a body of officials. Immigration detention centres – whether located in Turin, Rome, or Gjadër – are paradigmatic total institutions. Despite their administrative, non-penal legal designation, their material reality is defined by high walls, barbed wire, heavy surveillance, restricted mobility, and the systemic stripping of individual autonomy.

Carceral geography and critical detention studies have broadly demonstrated that these spaces are inherently pathogenic. They do not merely contain people’s bodies; they actively generate physical and psychological deterioration; in other words, they expose people to the risk of premature death. The structural violence embedded in the architecture of detention sites manifests through chronic overcrowding, extreme social isolation, poor environmental hygiene, sub-standard nutrition, and pervasive uncertainty regarding one’s legal status and potential imminent deportation. These carceral determinants of health rapidly and systematically erode the biological capital of detained individuals, transforming the "healthy immigrant effect" into an accelerated trajectory of physical exhaustion, acute psychiatric distress, self-harm, and suicidal ideation.

When a university inserts its students into this carceral space, it is not placing them in a neutral clinical environment. It is introducing them into an active apparatus of state-inflicted harm. The pedagogical space merges with the carceral geography, making it impossible to separate clinical practice from the broader punitive mandate of the institution.

The bioethical crisis: co-optation, dual loyalty, and malpractice

The core bioethical dilemma for health professionals working within carceral institutions centres on the phenomenon of “dual loyalty.” Dual loyalty refers to the structural conflict between a clinician’s clinical and ethical duty to provide unrestricted care to their patient and their administrative, contractual, or political obligations to an employing authority – in this case, the state or the private entity managing the detention centre. This conflict often results in systematic pressures to subordinate patient welfare for non-clinical agendas. Within total institutions, the operational demands of security, containment, and behavioural control routinely supersede clinical priorities.

The international literature on carceral healthcare highlights severe compromises in clinical independence. In Italian detention centres, physicians are frequently pressured to perform tasks that serve carceral rather than clinical ends, such as certifying individuals as "fit for detention" or "fit for flight" prior to deportation. These practices directly conflict with the foundational bioethical tenets of beneficence and non-maleficence. Rather than serving as therapeutic agents, health professionals risk being co-opted as technical enablers of administrative violence, validating and legitimising punitive state policies through medical authority.

Introducing undergraduate medical and nursing students into these environments introduces several grave complications:

Students do not yet possess the professional autonomy, legal protections, or psychological resilience needed to navigate and resist dual loyalty pressures. They enter the clinical space in a subordinate position, bound by academic hierarchies and evaluated by supervisors who may themselves be co-opted by the carceral framework.

Exposing students to environments where the denial of adequate healthcare, the excessive use of chemical restraint, and the normalisation of trauma are standard operating procedures which desensitise them to the systemic violations of human rights.

Using carceral spaces as learning environments for students teaches them to accept clinical malpractice as an inevitable condition of institutional reality.

The Gjadër protocol: transnational de-territorialisation and clinical complicity

The specific proposal to utilise the Gjadër CPR in Albania as an educational site amplifies these ethical anomalies through transnational legal de-territorialisation. The Italy-Albania protocol represents a political experiment of border and detention externalisation, separating the execution of domestic sovereignty from domestic territory. Within this externalised space, Italian administrative laws apply, but the geographic isolation completely cuts off standard mechanisms of legal, civil, and humanitarian oversight.

For health professionals, this extreme isolation magnifies professional risks. Independent human rights monitors, journalists, and non-governmental organisations already face severe restrictions when attempting to access the Gjadër facility. The clinical data, patient records, and quality-of-care audits are shielded from public scrutiny. Consequently, the healthcare system inside Gjadër operates within a profound accountability vacuum. In such an isolated environment, the pressure on healthcare personnel to comply with securitarian directives – such as ignoring vulnerability signs during brief border screenings – becomes overwhelming.

By establishing internship programs in this extraterritorial enclave, the university becomes an active accomplice in border externalisation. It supplies a continuous stream of junior clinical labour that validates an unaccountable system. The presence of university-affiliated students provides a false veneer of humanitarian care and academic legitimacy to a structure designed for exclusion and containment.

Pedagogy of the oppressed vs. carceral pedagogy

The field of migration medicine cannot be taught separately from its political and structural context. It is inherently bound to the social, economic, and legal determinants of health. True pedagogical excellence in this discipline requires what Paolo Freire termed a "pedagogy of the oppressed" – an educational model rooted in critical consciousness, structural analysis, and a commitment to social justice and human rights. Academic faculties have a duty to train students to look beyond immediate clinical symptoms, enabling them to identify and dismantle the structural forces that produce disease, precarity, and trauma.

In stark contrast, utilising a CPR as an educational classroom models a ‘carceral pedagogy’. This model strips medicine of its social responsibilities, reducing clinical training to a narrow set of technical skills applied within a setting of institutional violence. It teaches students to accept the suspension of rights as a neutral background condition, and to view marginalised patients through a lens of containment and security. Such training violates the core mission of higher education, replacing critical thought with technical compliance.

A call for academic mobilisation and resistance

The proposed integration of medical education into the Gjadër CPR must not be treated as a routine administrative decision. It represents an urgent bioethical crisis that demands immediate mobilisation across academic, medical, and legal sectors. Universities must remain independent spaces dedicated to promoting life, human dignity, and universal human rights. They cannot serve as training grounds or logistical support for state-sponsored border control.

We call upon academic institutions, medical faculties, and professional associations – in Italy, Albania, and across the globe – to firmly reject any agreements that embed students within immigration detention centres. The clinical training of healthcare professionals must occur in environments where human life is explicitly valued, protected, and cared for. Medical education must teach students to defend human dignity, especially where it is most vulnerable. Detention facilities cannot serve as classrooms; they must remain objects of rigorous critical study, exposed for their structural harms until they are permanently closed.

text:
As the Trump administration continues to focus on increasingly aggressive immigration enforcement, two congressional candidates are set for a rematch to represent a district that stretches across Southern Arizona’s U.S.-México border

Democratic incumbent Adelita Grijalva and Republican Daniel Butierez first faced off in the 7th Congressional District special election last year after Grijalva’s father, Raúl Grijalva, — a decades-long advocate for Southern Arizona and immigrant rights — died from cancer treatment complications in March 2025.

Adelita Grijalva, a longtime Pima County elected representative, won that election with about 69% of the vote, compared with about 29% for Butierez, according to the Arizona Secretary of State website. She completed the remainder of her father’s term and made history, becoming the first Arizona Latina elected to Congress. She’s since become an outspoken critic of Trump and his administration’s policies.

Butierez has stressed his own life strides. He faced “…Pima County’s corrupt justice system, spent 10 years in prison and 30 years fighting for justice,” according to his Arizona Secretary of State candidate statement. Butierez changed his life from “a homeless drug addict” to helping others as a small business employer, he added.

In the Nov. 3 General Election, voters will decide who represents District 7 for a full two-year term beginning in 2027.

Grijalva and Butierez shared the stage at an Aug. 26 debate sponsored by the Citizens Clean Elections Commission and the Arizona Media Association, giving voters a chance to compare their positions on issues affecting Southern Arizona — a region that is majority Latino and serves parts of Tucson and communities in Pima, Santa Cruz, Cochise, Pinal, Maricopa and Yuma counties. Watch the replay here.

Immigration was among issues the candidates vastly disagreed on during the debate. Grijalva called for abolishing the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, arguing it was fundamentally corrupt and could not be reformed. Butierez pushed back. He defended ICE as a necessary law enforcement agency and argued that Congress should focus on rewriting immigration laws rather than dismantling the organization.

Unlike neighboring Congressional District 6, District 7 is not expected to be a major battleground in the national fight for control of the U.S. House. The Cook Political Report rates the seat solid Democrat, meaning Grijalva is heavily favored to win.

Still, the race determines who will represent a large swath of Southern Arizona in Congress, including borderlands communities where federal decisions about immigration and border enforcement have a direct impact.

Grijalva previously served on the Pima County Board of Supervisors and spent two decades on the Tucson Unified School District Governing Board. Before joining Congress, she worked for more than 25 years at Pima County Teen Court.

Butierez is a native Tucsonan, small-business owner and painting contractor, employing “20-63 people,” according to his Arizona Secretary of State candidate statement and Ballotpedia responses. This is his third consecutive campaign for the District 7 seat.

The candidates

Where they stand

To help Pima County voters better understand the candidates, Arizona Luminaria asked each of them three key questions. Grijalva and Butierez submitted their answers via email and were asked to keep them 250 words or less. Their responses were edited for clarity only.

ICE activity

Federal immigration enforcement has become increasingly visible in Southern Arizona, including arrests such as that of Karla Toledo. What do you think of ICE’s recent activity and what reforms or policies would you support regarding immigration enforcement actions?

Daniel Butierez: “I support ICE and the enforcement of our immigration laws, especially when it comes to violent criminals, drug traffickers, human smugglers, and individuals who have been ordered removed. At the same time, enforcement must respect due process. Karla Toledo’s removal proceedings were ultimately dismissed, which shows why individual cases need to be reviewed carefully and fairly. (Editor’s note: Two weeks after Butierez submitted his response, a federal judge declined to drop Toledo’s deportation.)

I also support the bipartisan Dignity Act of 2025, H.R. 4393, which was introduced by Republicans and Democrats to combine stronger border security with broader immigration reform.

Our representatives in Washington should be focused on fixing a broken immigration system through legislation, more judges, faster case processing, secure borders, and a workable legal pathway for people who qualify, rather than spending their time protesting in the streets of Tucson for photo opportunities.

We can enforce our laws, protect due process, and finally fix the system Congress has failed to repair for decades.”

Adelita Grijalva: “Since I was elected, I have stood up for immigrant communities against this Administration’s campaign of terror against undocumented immigrants, DACA recipients, and others who have gotten swept up in Trump’s cruel and inhumane deportation machine. ICE is an institution that is fundamentally broken and cannot simply be reformed.

It’s also important to remember that it is a relatively new agency, created in the aftermath of 9/11. I believe it is institutionally compromised, which is why it must be abolished. Then, we must comprehensively reexamine how immigration enforcement is carried out in the United States in a way that upholds the rule of law, protects civil liberties, and respects basic human dignity.

We must shift away from militarized enforcement only and invest instead in addressing root causes of immigration, adding more immigration judges, reducing backlogs and modernizing our ports of entry.”

Cost of Living and Affordability

Southern Arizona families are facing pressure from housing, food, health care, energy and transportation costs. What should Congress do to make everyday life more affordable for residents of Arizona’s 7th Congressional District, and which policies would you prioritize to lower household costs?

Grijalva: “As a mother of three kids, I am all too familiar with rising costs at the grocery store and for housing and childcare, which are more expensive than ever under Trump’s economy.

My top priorities will be to undo the damage inflicted by Trump’s tariffs and the Big Ugly Bill, including restoring cuts to Medicaid, SNAP, and Medicare. In Arizona alone, more than 400,000 people have lost food assistance, including 200,000 children. We must also end the illegal war in Iran which is skyrocketing gas and raw material prices.

Beyond undoing the harm, Democrats need to be proactive in pursuing an aggressive agenda that uplifts and empowers working people. This includes ensuring that every person in the United States has quality, affordable health care coverage by passing Medicare for All.

I support legislation to expand utility, internet, and health premium assistance programs to lower costs for families. I also support increasing the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit, as well as passing universal pre-k and affordable childcare legislation.

I am working to bring down housing costs by investing more federal dollars in affordable housing and home repairs to increase affordable housing supply. I support expanding down payment assistance and guaranteed housing for people experiencing homelessness, including veterans.”

Butierez: “Congress should focus on helping families keep more of what they earn and lowering the cost of housing, energy, health care, and transportation.

I support permanent tax relief for working families, expanding American energy production, reducing unnecessary regulations that drive up housing costs, increasing health care competition and price transparency, and controlling federal spending.

Southern Arizona families need more opportunity, lower costs, and a government that lives within its means.”

Economic Development and Environmental Protections

Southern Arizona leaders are looking for ways to attract jobs and investment, while proposed data centers have raised concerns about their electricity and water demands particularly amid Colorado River water cuts. How should Southern Arizona balance economic development with protecting its water and energy resources, and what is your position on further data center development in the region?

Butierez: “Southern Arizona should welcome new investment and good-paying jobs, but growth must be responsible.

I support additional data center development only when companies can demonstrate adequate water and power supplies and pay the infrastructure costs they create instead of passing those costs onto families and small businesses.

Arizona regulators are already examining how large-load customers such as data centers should bear more of those costs.

With the Colorado River under increasing pressure, we also need to expand our water supply through conservation, reuse, recharge, and private investment in projects such as desalination.

We can grow Southern Arizona’s technology economy without sacrificing our water security or raising utility bills for working families.”

Grijalva: “Economic development is critical to Southern Arizona’s future, and we need to continue attracting good-paying jobs and investment to our region.

We must focus on bringing economic development to Southern Arizona that makes sense for our communities. That means ensuring development does not come at the expense of public health or the cost of living.

Big data center projects threaten both. They can increase temperatures in surrounding neighborhoods, consume tremendous amounts of water and threaten our long-term water security, while also raising utility bills for families.

At the federal level, my focus will be on bringing federal dollars to Southern Arizona that make our communities attractive places for businesses to invest. I support restoring the billions of funds for green energy projects that have been cut.

Additionally, I have successfully secured $15 million in preliminary district funding for a wide range of projects, including public safety, infrastructure, and housing.

Attracting businesses also requires a strong workforce. I sit on the Education and Workforce Committee, where I have advocated for investments in K-12 and higher education to ensure we have a skilled workforce that can meet the ever-changing demands of employers.”

text:
A federal appeals court has ruled that California cannot require federal immigration officers to visibly display identification while conducting enforcement operations, finding that the state's No Vigilantes Act likely violates the U.S. Constitution's Supremacy Clause.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit directed a lower court to issue a preliminary injunction against the law, which requires plainclothes law enforcement officers to display identification while performing their duties.

The ruling, reported by The Hill, follows an earlier suspension of the measure and represents another legal development in the Trump administration's dispute with California over immigration enforcement.

The appeals court found that states cannot directly regulate federal government operations without congressional authorization, even when the same requirements apply to state officers.

The Supremacy Clause "prohibits States from directly regulating federal operations even when regulating state operations in the same manner," the court wrote.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta's office expressed disappointment with the decision."Transparency and accountability are the foundation of good law enforcement — law enforcement refusing to identify themselves undermines our collective safety," the office said in a statement to The Hill, adding that it was reviewing the opinion.

The dispute began after Gov. Gavin Newsom signed two measures in September 2025: the No Vigilantes Act, requiring visible identification, and the No Secret Police Act, restricting federal officers from wearing masks during operations. Both were scheduled to take effect January 1.

The Justice Department sued California and Newsom in November 2025, arguing that the laws unlawfully interfered with federal authority and endangered immigration agents. Attorney General Pam Bondi said at the time that the measures "discriminate against the federal government and are designed to create risk for our agents."

California officials defended the legislation as a response to immigration raids and concerns about accountability. At the September signing ceremony, Newsom said federal agents should no longer be "hidden from accountability."

The legislation followed increased immigration enforcement in Los Angeles, where protests erupted in June 2025 and Trump deployed National Guard troops and Marines over Newsom's objections. Federal authorities reported approximately 5,000 immigration arrests in the Los Angeles area between June and August.

The Ninth Circuit had already extended a pause on the identification law in April. Wednesday's ruling requires the lower court to enter a preliminary injunction but does not constitute a final judgment on every issue in the litigation.

title: Cross-continental collaboration and sensitive source work expose the human peril of third ... - AP.org
description:
In a deeply empathetic and distinctive enterprise report, Dakar-based correspondent Mark Banchereau uncovered the harrowing reality of the U.S. policy of deporting migrants to third countries.
Spotting her story on social media, Banchereau navigated erratic communications and severe access hurdles to build trust with Daniela Fuentes, a transgender Cuban woman deported by the Trump administration to the Central African Republic — a hostile environment where she survives in isolation, forced to conceal her breasts, lower her voice and wear men’s clothes to evade anti-LGBTQ persecution.
The package served as a textbook example of multi-bureau collaboration across three continents.
Directed by U.S. immigration news editor Elliot Spagat and edited by Deputy Director of Top Stories Janelle Cogan, the narrative was reinforced by Caribbean news director Cristiana Mesquita’s reporting from Fuentes’ birthplace in Cuba and immigration reporter Tim Sullivan’s contextual analysis of U.S. immigration enforcement in Washington.
Published the same day a Human Rights Watch report found more than 500 migrants had been expelled to Africa, the AP’s exclusive coverage put an unforgettable, intimate human face on a complex and fiercely contested global policy.

The Trump administration is building a case that may result in the deportation of Minnesota Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar.

Omar’s home in Washington, D.C. was raided by feds and her cell phone, notebooks and personal computer were siezed in the investigation. Omar’s sister Sahra Noor and at least one other person from the family have been subpoenaed, according to reports.

The federal investigation involves alleged false statements on Omar’s immigration paperwork.

Omar has said that she became a U.S. citizen when she turned 17 when her father became naturalized in the year 2000. The Department of Justice is searching for evidence that her claim is a lie, according to the New York Post.

Criminal charges can only be brought if alleged immigration fraud happened in the last ten years. When it comes to false statements, there is a five-year statute of limitations, defense attorney Todd Spodek told the newspaper.

Omar’s congressional office released a statement following the raid that happened earlier this week.

text:
It’s been more than a week since Oscar Belgal was shot in the neck by an ICE agent in the Manhattan and Bronx adjacent–neighborhood of Marble Hill, and the details of what happened to the 28-year-old Dominican man — whose five-year-old son was in the backseat of his car when the agents opened fire — continue to filter out. So far, immigrant advocates still haven’t heard anything that justifies the shooting.

“Regardless of what led them to this individual, there is a proper process to ascertain an individual,” explained Murad Awawdeh, the president and CEO of the New York Immigration Coalition, in an interview. “They could have gotten a judicial warrant. They didn’t. They could have sent him a notice to come in for a check-in. They didn’t. They could have done several different things instead of opening fire on Oscar and his five-year-old when schools were being let out in the Bronx.”

In a petition Belgal’s attorneys filed on Wednesday seeking his release from federal custody, they said that Belgal had picked up his son from school that afternoon and had stopped at a nearby McDonald’s before arriving home. Belgal went back outside to move his car from where it was parked near a fire hydrant when, he says, an armed, masked man suddenly approached his driver’s side window.

“The men did not identify themselves, show any documents or otherwise communicate with Oscar in any substantive way. Instead, without identifying himself, the first man struck and shattered Oscar’s window and began firing a pistol into Oscar’s car while his son cowered in the back seat,” the court filing reads. “Believing that his dad had been fatally shot, his son screamed hysterically that the masked men had killed his father.”

The filing claims Belgal was not rendered aid once he exited the vehicle and that the agents “pinned him to the ground, handcuffed him, and left him slumped and semi-conscious.” Belgal’s lawyers write that it was only after their client awoke in the hospital that the agents identified themselves as ICE.

The shooting has left Belgal with numbness in the left side of his face as well as hearing loss in his left ear, they say. Though doctors instructed Belgal to have surgery to remove the bullet from his neck within the week of October 12, he has yet to receive it and reportedly is only being offered ibuprofen for his pain. After being released from the hospital, Belgal was transferred briefly to New Jersey before being sent to the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn where he currently remains in a segregated unit. A federal judge has temporarily blocked Belgal’s deportation out of the country as well as his transfer outside of the district or the Eastern District of New York or the District of New Jersey.

In a statement, Legal Aid Society attorneys Perry McAninch and Elyssa Williams note that MDC is “notorious for medical neglect” and that “with a bullet still lodged in his neck and his serious medical needs unmet, every additional day in custody puts him at further risk.”

They allege that federal agents violated Belgal’s right to due process by attempting to arrest him without a warrant. Federal prosecutors have until Monday, October 19 to respond to the court and justify Belgal’s continued detention.

The filing is further challenging the official narrative of the incident being put forth by the Trump administration. The Department of Homeland Security has claimed that Belgal, a Dominican national, has gang affiliations and that he was the target of an investigation into the shooting of a Customs and Border Patrol officer in the city last year. Belgal’s legal team said in their filing that ICE has yet to file evidence of those ties and that their client “vehemently denies” any involvement with gangs. According to the NYPD, Belgal has two prior arrests including one in 2013 where he pled guilty to fourth-degree grand larceny and received five years’ probation and a pending case for the criminal sale of a controlled substance for which he was arrested in 2025.

During a press conference held Friday, ICE Executive Associate Director Marcos Charles said that the agents on scene used their vehicles to box Belgal in in order to make the arrest and claimed that Belgal refused orders to exit his car and then “weaponized” his vehicle by accelerating it in the direction of other officers. When the officers opened fire, Charles said, they were “using their training and believing that their life and the lives of their partners and the general public were in danger.”

Charles said Belgal was hit “superficially” in the neck and claimed ICE officers rendered aid and transported Belgal to a nearby hospital, a fact contradicted by the release of NYPD body-camera footage that showed officers arriving on the scene following the shooting and eventually transporting Belgal in their department vehicle. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin later insisted that the ICE agents didn’t know there was a child in the car.

There’s still no available video footage of the shooting itself. Surveillance footage released by the NYPD appears to show Belgal’s car accelerating forward away from officers after his window was smashed, but the moment of the shooting was not captured on camera. On Sunday, Mullin indicated that there is ICE bodycam footage from the incident that would likely be released, but suggested the timing hinged on the ongoing investigation. The Bronx district attorney Darcel Clark said her office is also investigating the shooting, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani has said that she has his full confidence.

The New York Immigration Coalition’s Awawdeh doesn’t buy DHS’s explanations. “They chose violence and they chose these theatrics because this is what ICE does now. It’s sow as much harm as they can in this moment and continue to push people further into the shadows, create more panic, more fear, and more chaos in our communities,” he said. “And it’s never been about safety and security; it’s always been about cruelty because that’s their point here.”

text:
The US Department of Justice sued California on Thursday, seeking a court order to prevent the state from tabulating certain ballots cast in the midterm elections.

The suit came two days after the department made a specious demand to the state. On Tuesday, the department sent election officials in Los Angeles county a thumb drive with a handwritten password purporting to contain the names of noncitizens registered to vote. The department asked officials to confirm the citizenship of anyone on the list and set aside ballots from those whose status could not be confirmed. It gave the state 48 hours – an extremely narrow window – to take action. It did not provide details on how it came up with the names on the list. In its lawsuit, filed in federal court in the central district of California, the justice department said it had provided the state with more than 20,000 names of likely noncitizens.

The Los Angeles county clerk and recorder, Dean Logan, said his office would not review the list, in part because it didn’t consider the USB drive secure.

“The Department of Justice has not provided the underlying evidence, source, or methodology supporting its assertions that individuals identified in its records are ineligible to vote,” Logan said in a statement. “We cannot withhold or refuse to count ballots based solely on unverified allegations, nor can we disregard the legal requirements governing our election – and we certainly have no authority to act on records that are outside of our jurisdiction.”

In a statement on Wednesday, the California secretary of state, Shirley Weber, a Democrat, said the justice department had not provided the list of voters to her office. “The [justice department’s] relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states’ protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections,” Weber said.

Justice department lawyers are asking the court to order the state not to count votes from those it had flagged.

“This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote-by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter’s citizenship status can be determined,” the lawsuit said. “This Court should order California (1) to set aside vote-by-mail ballots from persons identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens and (2) to independently – or in collaboration with the Federal Government – verify their citizenship status (beyond relying on unverified statements of citizenship necessary to registering) before tabulating their vote-by-mail ballot.”

The request to block tabulation comes amid concerns that Donald Trump and his allies will interfere in the counting of votes in the midterm elections, in which Republicans are expected to lose seats in Congress.

The Trump administration’s methodology for identifying noncitizens has come under scrutiny. Earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said there could be as many as 278,000 noncitizens on the rolls in four states, including more than 190,000 in California and about 16,000 in Nevada.

Officials at the DHS refused to share their methodology with Nevada election officials and later turned over just 185 names of people it had a strong belief were noncitizens. When Nevada officials investigated, they found every one of those people was a citizen.

Richard Hasen, an election law scholar at UCLA, described the justice department’s efforts in California as “a nice publicity stunt that gets attention for [the justice department] and reinforces the notion among the president’s most ardent supporters that California is not doing enough to combat voter fraud”.
